items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." While Rome and Persia lost some cities along the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the Sasanian Empire retains Mesopotamia, and Rome defends the cities on the western coast of the Arabian peninsula, bordering the Red Sea and Judea. The Arabian Empire is then created as a religiously fanatical, militarized, yet mercantile and diplomatic empire. Islam still spreads through Islamic traders, though not as strongly in North Africa or the Mediterranean as a whole thanks to the Roman Tribunal Republic's stability and already existing religions. [By the first millennium CE, Rome's political system works like this:] [Provinces are ruled by Provincial Tribunes, elected by the people of the province from those who have not been in the military for at least four years. Additionally, some large cities, particularly coastal entrepot cities, become provinces in their own right. Each province can pass their own laws and manage their own administration, paying taxes to the Tribunal Treasury in Rome and following senatorial law]. [Each province (plus the city of Rome) elects two senators to represent them in the Tribunal Senate. No senator may have been in the military within the previous four years. The Tribunal Senate has no Consuls, instead having an "Orator," which is basically their Speaker. The longest-serving senator automatically becomes Orator. If the Senate passes a law, it can be vetoed by Provincial Tribunes if at least half of them vote on to veto the Senate law within one year of its passing. Provincial Tribunes may vote to send a law to the Senate for consideration, and if it is sent to the Senate and the Senate approves it, it cannot be vetoed no matter how many tribunes veto it]. [Caesars are appointed by the Senate in a time of dire war with a term of two years, after which point (if the war is still ongoing) the Senate can either replace them or affirm their trust in them. This repeats until the dire war is over]. In 1000 CE, to celebrate one thousand years of popular rule following the Dimidiatio Senatus, celebrations are held across Rome, and the Roman Tribunal Republic changes its formal name to the "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIM), or "Republic between seas," for the grand republic lies between multiple seas: Mare Ponticum (the Black Sea), Mare Mediterraneus (the Mediterranean Sea), Mare Hibericum (Atlantic Ocean west of Iberia and the Canary Islands), Mare Britannicum (the North Sea and Atlantic Ocean around Britain and Ireland), and Mare Rubrum (the Red Sea and Indian Ocean). items.model_answer:
If Sulla had gone east to fight Mithridates VI while Marius, not Sulla, became the first Roman commander to march on Rome, the Republic would probably not have been saved; it would simply have broken in a different moral order. The great precedent would have belonged to the Marian-popularis side rather than to Sulla and the optimates.

The first caveat is practical: Marius could not easily “march on Rome” in 88 BCE unless Sulla had already left Italy or refused to use his army. Historically Sulla could march because he had the legions besieging Nola. Marius at that moment had prestige, veterans, allies among the populares, and support from discontented Italians, but he did not have the same ready consular army. So the plausible version is this: Sulla sails east with the Mithridatic command, and Marius, perhaps with Sulpicius or later Cinna, raises forces from veterans, Italians, and political allies and seizes Rome in Sulla’s absence.

In that case, Rome falls quickly. The city had no standing garrison capable of resisting a determined army. Marius would likely annul Sulla’s political position, declare him a public enemy, confiscate his property, and purge leading Sullan supporters. The extension of citizenship to the Italian allies would probably be protected or accelerated, because the Marian-Cinnan coalition depended heavily on Italian support. The Senate would be intimidated rather than destroyed, but its independence would be largely fictitious.

Sulla, meanwhile, would probably still defeat Mithridates. His army’s loyalty would not vanish just because Rome outlawed him. Roman soldiers followed commanders who could pay them, protect them, and lead them to plunder, and the eastern war offered all three. Indeed, if Sulla were cut off from official support, he might behave even more independently: plundering Greek sanctuaries, squeezing allied cities, and making a quick peace with Mithridates so he could return west. His settlement with Mithridates would likely remain relatively lenient, because Sulla’s main concern would become Italy, not Asia.

The crucial difference is that when Sulla returned, he would not be the man who first violated the taboo against bringing legions into Roman politics. He would present himself as the avenger of the Republic against a Marian military coup. That would give his cause greater ideological legitimacy among conservative senators and many property holders. The civil war of 83–82 BCE would still happen, but its propaganda would be reversed: Sulla could claim to be restoring legality after Marius had destroyed it.

Marius himself is unlikely to remain the decisive figure for long. He was elderly and died in 86 BCE even in the real timeline. If he marched on Rome earlier, he might enjoy a short, brutal supremacy, but the regime after him would still fall to men like Cinna, Carbo, and the younger Marian commanders. That matters because Sulla’s greatest opponent on his return would probably not be Marius, the old conqueror of the Cimbri and Jugurtha, but a divided Marian-Cinnan coalition. Against Sulla’s hardened eastern veterans, that coalition would still have a serious chance, especially if it mobilized the Italians effectively, but it would suffer from factionalism and weaker leadership.

So the most likely outcome is still a Sullan return and a Sullan victory, though perhaps after a bloodier war. Sulla’s dictatorship, if achieved under these circumstances, might be even harsher. He would be able to argue that the Marian side had committed the original sacrilege of using an army against Rome; his proscriptions could be justified as punishment for rebellion rather than as naked revenge. The constitutional reforms would probably look familiar: strengthening the Senate, weakening tribunes, restricting popular legislation, and trying to bind future magistrates more tightly to senatorial control. But because the first march had been Marian, Sulla’s “restoration” might command broader conservative support and less immediate moral embarrassment.

Long-term, however, the Republic would be no healthier. The real disease was not simply that Sulla marched on Rome; it was that Roman politics had become inseparable from personal armies, provincial commands, debt, land hunger, Italian integration, and aristocratic competition. If Marius marched first and Sulla marched later, the lesson would be even clearer: both sides had learned that legality followed military success. The taboo would not merely be broken; it would be bipartisan.

The effect on Julius Caesar is especially interesting. Caesar was connected to Marius by marriage and family politics. If Marius became the original military usurper, Caesar’s Marian association might become even more dangerous after a Sullan victory. Sulla might be less inclined to spare him. If Caesar survived, he would grow up in a world where his own political tradition, not Sulla’s, had first shown that Rome could be taken by force. In that sense, Caesar would still be an heir to Sulla’s method, but also more openly an heir to Marius’s precedent.

The broad answer, then, is: Marius marching on Rome first would change the blame, the propaganda, and possibly the fate of individual figures like Caesar, but it would not likely prevent civil war or restore the Republic. Sulla would probably still defeat Mithridates, return with a loyal army, and fight for control of Italy. The Republic would still be pushed toward military monarchy; only the name attached to the original sin would change from Sulla to Marius.

items.question: What If al-Andalus survives
human_answers: There are a number of good surviving Al Andalus timelines like moonlight in a jar on here. Obviously it can go however the author wants it- my suspicion though is that an Al Andalus which remains relatively centralised is more vulnerable than the taifas were otl to crusades- if the events over the next century don’t butterfly the Turkic incursions into Anatolia and the papal call to crusade, a crusade would certainly be directed towards Spain as well. A centralised state is often easier to conquer than decentralised ones, all you need is one battle that allows the conquerors access to the capital and central bureaucracy and you’ve done it. I think it’d be interesting to see such a fundamentally different pattern of reconquista, where instead of small northern principalities gradually extending southwards, one decisive battle/sack of Cordoba puts crusaders in charge of cordoba like happened in 1204 Constantinople, you end up with a Christian kingdom with Cordoba as its capital and likely a French king. This kingdom of Cordoba could be instantly much more powerful than the northern Christian kingdoms. Its administrative languages would be Latin and Arabic, and the language of the nobility (unlike otl) wouldn’t be an Iberian Romance language, more likely a northern French dialect, ruling over a population of Arabic and Mozarabic speakers. Unlike otl there would be no real reason for northern romance dialects to spread southwards, as even though northern Christians would settle the south, without state backing they’re more likely to assimilate to local Mozarabic or Arabic speaking Christian populations.

It wasn't unexpected, so to speak; he was ill throughout the year 1008, contracting the disease in February and dying in October. He had an angina attack. Whether this was caused by the illness, the stress of managing the country, or poisoning is difficult to say. Adding to that, instead of recovering in Cordoba, he spent a good part of the year campaigning, which probably didn't help. The reason Al-Muzaffar couldn't remain idle was the large number of problems he faced during his six-year reign. Early in his reign, there was a sharp decline in gold and silver coinage, which may indicate economic difficulties in al-Andalus or problems with the supply of gold and silver from Africa. A few months after succeeding his father, al-Muzaffar faced a conspiracy to assassinate him and his vizier, Ibn al-Qatta. The conspirators, with the commander of Saqaliba and the court secretary as the most prominent figures, intended to replace the hajib with his underage son, Muhammad, who would be a puppet (So, Puppet Squared), just as Caliph Hisham II had been. Al-Muzaffar, unlike his father, was a king-soldier, not a philosopher king (who had legal and literary training). Muzaffar had no interest in administration, politics, arts, or sciences. Leaving this to his vizier. Later, his vizier and friend, Ibn al-Qatta, who was married to his sister, organized a failed coup against Muzaffar. He had to kill people who were important to the functioning of the government during his father's era. During one of his campaigns in 1006, he attacked the territory of King Sancho Garces III of Pamplona and ended up being defeated in this campaign, which, along with his poor governance (partly due to numerous coups and open intrigue at court), brought him a bad reputation. The government would remain in crisis because al-Muzaffar's biggest problem was that he was not a Umayyad, and anyone with ambition could find legitimacy in trying to dethrone him to establish the Umayyads (on paper). This, coupled with the fact that he was not as competent as his father (who was far superior), generated this crisis. Perhaps that's quite debatable. It could have been much worse or better; it depends on many factors. I don't know if he would last the rest of the century. Seriously, the kingdom is having serious internal problems. I don't know if it would last until 1020. The kingdom would collapse; the kingdom died informally when al-Mansur exterminated the Arab elite who had maintained the emirate/caliphate for the past centuries, replacing them with enslaved soldiers and Berbers. Al-Mansur possessed exceptional skill in managing the political, military, and ethnic intrigue of the kingdom. However, his son inherited the problems without possessing the necessary competence. He had to contend with enslaved soldiers and Berbers vying to become the new Al-Mansur, the remaining Arab elite wanting to return to power, pressure from the north, and governmental instability.

I see you are having a knee-jerk reaction. We aren’t just nudging little details here and there, and historical outcomes were far from set in stone. For example when I said preventing the crusader capture of Cordova I wasn’t talking about that one specific historical one that happened after Andalusia weakness, I mean a totally different situation where crusaders target Iberia but Andalusia wins the crusades. Instead of being close-minded, let’s be more open. So imagine that the Moroccans play the role of the Turks but in Spain instead of Turkey. That is just one of many possible options Anyway, what I’m getting at is that while there is plenty of possibility space, it’s true that we can focus on what seems most plausible and believable as likely, which for me would be if the Christians are never able to establish resistance states in the North in the first place, meaning they can’t capitalize of moments of weakness when there is civil war among Muslims, though of course diminishing Muslim civil war helps, as well regular injections of fresh strength form the south such as what happened with the Almohads and Almoravids. The whole “ethnic minority exploiting the rest” is a non-issue since that’s what happens in pretty much every empire ever, and lots of them are able to persist and spread their religion/culture/civilization despite this so-called “weakness”
items.original_question: What if al-Andalus survives The 11th century was a pivotal moment in Hispanic history. At the beginning of the century, the Caliphate of Córdoba was the dominant power on the peninsula. The city of Córdoba rivaled Constantinople as the largest city in Europe. Ostensibly ruled by the Umayyads under Caliph Hisham II, in reality he was merely a puppet of his ambitious hajib (chamberlain) Abu Amir Muhammad ‘ al-Mansur ’ more famously known as Almanzor. A highly ambitious man, Almanzor would import thousands of Berber tribesmen into al-Andalus to serve in Córdoba’s army. He would utilize this army to not only keep the disgruntled Arab elites in line but also to bring the Christian north to heel through large-scale annual raids. While this arrangement put strain on the treasury and created ethnic strife, it was effective, and upon his death in 1002 AD Almanzor would be seamlessly succeeded by his son al-Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar would continue his father’s regime, continuing to import Berbers, continuing to raid the north, and keeping the state stable. It was looking like a dual-power dynamic was emerging in Córdoba just as it had back east in Baghdad. However, while on campaign against Castile, al-Muzaffar would die unexpectedly in 1008 AD. His younger brother Sanchuelo would succeed him as hajib , but he would lack the brilliance of his father or the prudence of his brother. Sanchuelo would offend the Arab nobility by having Hisham II name him as his heir as Caliph. This act would trigger the Fitna of al-Andalus, reducing the grand city of Córdoba to ruins and shattering the country into 30+ squabbling petty kingdoms or taifas. Suddenly, the power dynamic was reversed. Now the Muslim south was paying tribute to the Christian north. The north would consolidate under the Jiménez dynasty, and then push south, culminating in the capture of Toledo in 1085 AD, followed by the occupation of the rest of al-Andalus by the Berber Almoravid dynasty from Morocco. The rest of the Reconquista would unfold in the following centuries. The Fitna proved to be a lucky break for Christian Iberia, as without the might of Córdoba crushing them, the Reconquista started to truly gain steam. However, what if the Fitna was averted or delayed by having al-Muzaffar not die prematurely in 1008? Had he not died young, Sanchuelo likely never comes to power. This alone averts the triggering of the Fitna . Of course, the underlying financial issues and ethnic strife still exist, so the Fitna may still occur under different circumstances. However it’s likely to be nowhere as devestating for al-Andalus as IOTL. How would a continuing Caliphate of Córdoba navigate the rest of the 11th century? Would al-Andalus remain powerful and prosperous as we transition into the High Middle Ages? Could the Andalusi withstand pressure from both Christians and Berbers alike? Will the Reconquista ever happen without al-Andalus collapsing?

rubrics.question_focus: What If al-Andalus survives

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise specification and plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what 'al-Andalus survives' means and selects a historically plausible point of divergence, such as avoiding the Fitna of al-Andalus, preserving Umayyad/Amirid legitimacy, preventing durable northern Christian polities, or repeated North African reinforcement.
criteria.1-2: Leaves the premise vague or assumes survival by fiat with no credible divergence from real history.
criteria.3-4: Names a divergence but gives little explanation of why it would keep al-Andalus viable.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible divergence and links it to short-term survival, but leaves major vulnerabilities underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Defines survival clearly and grounds it in credible political, military, or social mechanisms.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the survival scenario, weighs alternative divergences, and justifies the chosen path against known historical pressures.

criteria.name: Internal Andalusi political and institutional dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of al-Andalus's internal stresses, including Umayyad legitimacy, Amirid rule, Berber and Saqaliba military factions, Arab elites, taifa fragmentation, fiscal capacity, coinage, court coups, and centralization versus decentralization.
criteria.1-2: Ignores internal politics or portrays al-Andalus as a stable monolith.
criteria.3-4: Mentions instability but treats it superficially without explaining factional or institutional causes.
criteria.5-6: Covers some internal dynamics, such as succession or taifas, but misses key legitimacy or military-fiscal issues.
criteria.7-8: Explains how institutions, elites, armies, and succession affect long-term survival.
criteria.9-10: Shows nuanced understanding of internal factionalism, legitimacy, administration, and how these evolve over centuries.

criteria.name: Iberian and wider Mediterranean causal interactions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for how a surviving al-Andalus affects and is affected by northern Christian kingdoms, the Reconquista, papal crusading, France, Morocco/Maghreb powers, Mediterranean trade, and possible analogies to Anatolia or the Levant.
criteria.1-2: Treats al-Andalus in isolation and ignores neighboring powers.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Christians or Morocco but with little causal interaction.
criteria.5-6: Explains some regional consequences, such as altered Reconquista or crusading, but lacks breadth or depth.
criteria.7-8: Connects Andalusi survival to Iberian, Maghrebi, and crusading dynamics in a coherent way.
criteria.9-10: Integrates Iberia, North Africa, France, papal policy, trade, and military competition into a mutually causal regional system.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage and coherence of major long-term effects if al-Andalus survives into the late medieval or early modern period, including language, religion, settlement, state formation, colonial expansion, scientific and cultural exchange, Ottoman/Atlantic geopolitics, and European balance of power.
criteria.1-2: Stops at immediate survival and gives no meaningful long-term consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few downstream effects but without causal links or historical specificity.
criteria.5-6: Covers several consequences, such as religious or linguistic change, but chains are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Develops credible long-range effects across politics, culture, religion, and geopolitics.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich, temporally extended chain showing how medieval changes reshape early modern Iberia, Europe, North Africa, and Atlantic history.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains consistent causal logic, avoids anachronism and deterministic claims, distinguishes plausible from speculative outcomes, and does not contradict the survival premise or established medieval context.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, anachronisms, or deterministic claims that break the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent ideas but frequent unsupported leaps or tension with the premise.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but under-calibrates uncertainty or leaves some contradictions unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a logical chain, flags uncertainty, and avoids most contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully balances contingency and plausibility, explicitly handles uncertainties, and keeps all causal claims consistent over the full timeline.

If al-Andalus survives, the biggest change is not that “Spain becomes Muslim,” but that Iberia remains politically and religiously plural for much longer. The consequences depend on how much of al-Andalus survives. A small surviving Granada after 1492 would matter culturally and diplomatically, but a larger Muslim state in southern or eastern Iberia would reshape European and Atlantic history much more deeply.

The most plausible version is that the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada survives as a tributary or protected state because Castile and Aragon are distracted by civil conflict, France, Italy, or dynastic instability. In that case, al-Andalus likely becomes a buffer state between Christian Iberia and North Africa, surviving through diplomacy, tribute, trade, and outside alliances with the Marinids, Hafsids, Mamluks, or later the Ottomans. It would probably be smaller than medieval al-Andalus, centered on Granada, Málaga, Almería, and perhaps parts of Andalusia.

The immediate effect would be a weaker or less unified Spain. The fall of Granada in 1492 helped the Catholic Monarchs consolidate religious and political legitimacy. Without that victory, Castile and Aragon might still unite dynastically, but the ideology of a completed Reconquista would be absent. The Spanish monarchy would have less symbolic authority, and campaigns against Muslims in Iberia would continue to consume money, soldiers, and attention.

This could affect overseas expansion. Columbus’s 1492 voyage was not caused only by the fall of Granada, but the timing mattered: the conquest freed resources and gave the monarchy confidence. If Granada survives, Spain might still sponsor Atlantic voyages, but perhaps later, with fewer resources, or under stronger competition from Portugal. A delayed or weaker Spanish Atlantic empire could mean Portugal, France, or England take a larger early role in the Americas. The conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires might still happen eventually, but not necessarily under the same Spanish leadership or at the same time.

Religiously, the survival of al-Andalus would complicate the rise of Spanish Catholic uniformity. The expulsions or forced conversions of Jews and Muslims might be delayed, softened, or applied unevenly. If a Muslim state remains next door, Spain may treat its Muslim and Jewish minorities either more cautiously, to avoid provoking war, or more harshly, out of fear of internal collaboration. Both outcomes are plausible. But the idea of Spain as a purely Catholic kingdom would be harder to enforce.

Mediterranean politics would also change. A surviving al-Andalus could become an ally, client, or contested partner of the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century. That would alarm Habsburg Spain. Instead of viewing the western Mediterranean mainly as a frontier in North Africa and Italy, Spain would face a Muslim polity inside Iberia itself. This could produce repeated wars, fortified frontiers, naval campaigns, and diplomacy involving Morocco, Algiers, Istanbul, France, and the Papacy.

Culturally, Iberia would likely remain more visibly hybrid. Arabic, Romance, Hebrew, and Berber influences would remain stronger in architecture, law, agriculture, literature, music, and urban life. Cities like Granada and Málaga could become major centers of translation, medicine, philosophy, commerce, and diplomacy between Europe and the Islamic world. Andalusi Arabic might survive longer, perhaps alongside Castilian, Catalan, Portuguese, and Romance dialects.

But survival would not necessarily mean tolerance in a modern sense. Medieval and early modern states generally organized society by hierarchy, religion, and privilege. A surviving al-Andalus might protect Christians and Jews as subordinate communities, just as Christian kingdoms often subordinated Muslims and Jews. It could be comparatively plural, but not egalitarian by modern standards.

In the long run, a surviving al-Andalus might resemble one of three things: a small Balkan-style frontier state balanced between empires; a Mediterranean Muslim kingdom tied to Morocco or the Ottomans; or, if it modernized successfully, a distinct Iberian nation-state with Islamic and Romance roots. Modern Iberia might then contain Spain, Portugal, and an Andalusi state, or Spain might eventually conquer it later under different circumstances.

So the central answer is: if al-Andalus survives, Iberia remains a contested Christian-Muslim frontier far into the early modern period. Spain’s religious unity, imperial timing, Mediterranean strategy, and national identity would all be altered. The Americas might still be colonized by Europeans, but the balance among Spain, Portugal, France, and England could shift significantly. The most durable difference would be cultural and political: southern Iberia would remain a living bridge between Europe and the Islamic world rather than becoming primarily a memory of one.

edus.text: If al-Andalus survives,
the biggest change is not that “Spain becomes Muslim,”
but that Iberia remains politically and religiously plural for much longer.
The consequences depend on how much of al-Andalus survives.
A small surviving Granada after 1492 would matter culturally and diplomatically,
but a larger Muslim state in southern or eastern Iberia would reshape European and Atlantic history much more deeply.
The most plausible version is that the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada survives as a tributary or protected state
because Castile and Aragon are distracted by civil conflict, France, Italy, or dynastic instability.
In that case, al-Andalus likely becomes a buffer state between Christian Iberia and North Africa,
surviving through diplomacy, tribute, trade, and outside alliances with the Marinids, Hafsids, Mamluks, or later the Ottomans.
It would probably be smaller than medieval al-Andalus,
centered on Granada, Málaga, Almería, and perhaps parts of Andalusia.
The immediate effect would be a weaker or less unified Spain.
The fall of Granada in 1492 helped the Catholic Monarchs consolidate religious and political legitimacy.
Without that victory, Castile and Aragon might still unite dynastically,
but the ideology of a completed Reconquista would be absent.
The Spanish monarchy would have less symbolic authority,
and campaigns against Muslims in Iberia would continue to consume money, soldiers, and attention.
This could affect overseas expansion.
Columbus’s 1492 voyage was not caused only by the fall of Granada,
but the timing mattered:
the conquest freed resources and gave the monarchy confidence.
If Granada survives,
Spain might still sponsor Atlantic voyages,
but perhaps later, with fewer resources, or under stronger competition from Portugal.
A delayed or weaker Spanish Atlantic empire could mean Portugal, France, or England take a larger early role in the Americas.
The conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires might still happen eventually,
but not necessarily under the same Spanish leadership or at the same time.
Religiously, the survival of al-Andalus would complicate the rise of Spanish Catholic uniformity.
The expulsions or forced conversions of Jews and Muslims might be delayed, softened, or applied unevenly.
If a Muslim state remains next door,
Spain may treat its Muslim and Jewish minorities either more cautiously, to avoid provoking war,
or more harshly, out of fear of internal collaboration.
Both outcomes are plausible.
But the idea of Spain as a purely Catholic kingdom would be harder to enforce.
Mediterranean politics would also change.
A surviving al-Andalus could become an ally, client, or contested partner of the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century.
That would alarm Habsburg Spain.
Instead of viewing the western Mediterranean mainly as a frontier in North Africa and Italy,
Spain would face a Muslim polity inside Iberia itself.
This could produce repeated wars, fortified frontiers, naval campaigns, and diplomacy
involving Morocco, Algiers, Istanbul, France, and the Papacy.
Culturally, Iberia would likely remain more visibly hybrid.
Arabic, Romance, Hebrew, and Berber influences would remain stronger in architecture, law, agriculture, literature, music, and urban life.
Cities like Granada and Málaga could become major centers of translation, medicine, philosophy, commerce, and diplomacy between Europe and the Islamic world.
Andalusi Arabic might survive longer,
perhaps alongside Castilian, Catalan, Portuguese, and Romance dialects.
But survival would not necessarily mean tolerance in a modern sense.
Medieval and early modern states generally organized society by hierarchy, religion, and privilege.
A surviving al-Andalus might protect Christians and Jews as subordinate communities,
just as Christian kingdoms often subordinated Muslims and Jews.
It could be comparatively plural,
but not egalitarian by modern standards.
In the long run, a surviving al-Andalus might resemble one of three things:
a small Balkan-style frontier state balanced between empires;
a Mediterranean Muslim kingdom tied to Morocco or the Ottomans;
or, if it modernized successfully, a distinct Iberian nation-state with Islamic and Romance roots.
Modern Iberia might then contain Spain, Portugal, and an Andalusi state,
or Spain might eventually conquer it later under different circumstances.
So the central answer is: if al-Andalus survives, Iberia remains a contested Christian-Muslim frontier far into the early modern period.
Spain’s religious unity, imperial timing, Mediterranean strategy, and national identity would all be altered.
The Americas might still be colonized by Europeans,
but the balance among Spain, Portugal, France, and England could shift significantly.
The most durable difference would be cultural and political:
southern Iberia would remain a living bridge between Europe and the Islamic world
rather than becoming primarily a memory of one.

items.question: What If Louis the Pious was able to successfully pass his reforms?
human_answers: Currently I cannot write a comment as it is yes it must on what Louis's successfully implemented reforms are like could upend the development not only of the Frankish Empire and the Papacy, but also of the rest of Europe ( in particular directly involving Al - Andalus, the Viking raids, the Slavic potentates and relations with Constantinople ) and how is all this it like that will influence the perception of Charlemagne's legacy, and the claim of political continuity with Rome in the Latin Christianity, so for now I will content myself with quoting some of my old comments on the era in general Yes I admit that they are a bunch of quotes, since in looking for them all I got a bad headache, but at least they cover in full the entire historical period and some hypotheses of evolution that can be generated by a different internal policy within the Carolingians

I don’t know if he’d be able to gain the loyalty of his siblings seen as Frankish traditions would still be pushed for. Even with some kind of alliance against Louis the Bald he’d need enough influence to assure that his brothers don’t turn against him afterwards but I do like the idea of him turning against his father. Another issue here is that the Frankish aristocrats would still be mostly opposed to Lothaire getting most of the empire and nominally inheriting it so he’d need to assure the aristocracy’s loyalty. I agree, the process of feudalism was already taking place and with how Charlemagne had organized his empire, it wouldn’t be far fetched to think that it’d be somewhat divided, especially with special status regions like Septimania and Bavaria existing in the empire. On the other hand if someone were to centralize power to himself, say Lothaire, I do imagine that it isn’t impossible that the Carolingian Empire is divided in subdivisions that maintain the Emperor’s loyalty and don’t solely pledge loyalty to their dukes. Charlemagne assassinated and killed those who wouldn’t integrate into his empire so it’s not that far fetched to think that the emperor would kill to maintain the empire’s loyalty.

It was never centralized though. It was extremely decentralized even back during Charlemagne's era, and he had to regularly travel around his empire as well as send his own emissaries, the Mayors of the Palace, to enforce his authority. Even in the days of the Holy Roman Empire, the position was more concentrated around the personality of an Emperor, as when Barbarossa took the throne in the 12th century, his authority was ephemeral as it existed on paper, having lapsed without a stronger monarch on the throne. Barbarossa was an extremely intelligent and energetic figure who also knew how to play the game well which was why his reforms largely endured (in Germany he was a pragmatist, but in Italy he was more of a romantic and pushed against the papacy when he didn't need to allowing Manuel Komnenos to undermine him heavily damaging Imperial rule in Italy). That was the issue with Louis the Pious, who played the game of prestige and power wrong. His blinding of his nephew Bernard while indeed a strong show of force, it came off as overly cruel to the nobility. At the same time his open display of supplication and show of piety made him seem weak. This was the issue with his sons, whom he simply failed to properly control. Funnily enough Louis the Pious was actually a very competent Emperor. He just had a lot of things going against him. And with his intellect, he often derived overly romantic solutions to certain problems he should have been more pragmatic about. His blinding of Bernard was extremely ruthless. So much so it caused quite a stir in Francia. His sons were scared of him at certain points and expected to be blinded at his hands for some of the actions they'd done. Instead of blinding, a firm punishment such as tonsuring his most rebellious sons for their pride (long hair was a cultural hallmark of the Franks) would have probably done the job. These rebellious sons being sent to a monastery close under his own influence and watch would have set a decent enough example for those who defied his will. As for the division of the Empire, if it were subdivided along reasonable lines it might have actually worked to some degree, as it would have accounted for the natural fragmentation of power and regionalism that would develop in a state like this without any sense of overarching national identity or even political capital. The fragmentation of these Kingdoms within the Empire would have unironically helped the Emperor maintain power over his kin who'd reign as subkings under his authority.
items.original_question: What if Louis the Pious was able to successfully pass his reforms? Louis the Pious had conceived the empire to never be divided. It was through this conception that he decided that power would only be relegated to his eldest son while to compensate for the lack of power, the younger sons would be gifted smaller kingdoms (like, for example, the kingdom of Italy). Nevertheless these smaller kings would still declare loyalty towards the emperor. He had also believed that imperial power came from the pope, hosting his coronation in Reims with the pope. These reforms were never truly put in place however, as the Frankish court had viewed them negatively as they did not follow Frankish tradition. In tandem, the younger brothers of Lothaire (who was meant to have the throne) played against their father. Coupled with Judith of Bavaria attempting to give her son, Charles the (eventual) Bald as much heritage as he could possibly get. Thus, progressively, until the day of Louis the Pious’ death his power was more and more fractured. Therefore, what would happen if he was more politically competent, if he was able to somehow circumvent of push back against the court politics that brought about his downfall and the division of the empire?

items.model_answer:
If Louis the Pious had successfully imposed his reforms, especially the succession settlement of the Ordinatio Imperii, the Carolingian Empire would probably have remained unified for at least another generation instead of collapsing into civil war and the Treaty of Verdun in 843.

Louis’s main problem was not simply that he was weak, but that he tried to reconcile two conflicting principles: the Frankish tradition of dividing lands among royal sons and the imperial idea that Charlemagne’s empire should remain a single Christian polity. His reform program favored unity under one senior emperor, originally his eldest son Lothair, while younger sons would receive subordinate kingdoms. If that system had been accepted by his sons and the aristocracy, the immediate result would likely have been a more stable Carolingian monarchy.

The biggest change would have been the avoidance, or at least postponement, of the partition into West Francia, East Francia, and Middle Francia. That means the later emergence of France and Germany as separate political traditions would have been delayed or taken a different form. A unified empire stretching across much of western and central Europe could have preserved a stronger sense of imperial identity, with regional kings or governors operating beneath a recognized emperor.

A successful reform would also have strengthened the alliance between the Carolingian state and the Church. Louis’s reign emphasized Christian kingship, moral reform, monastic discipline, and the idea that imperial authority had a sacred responsibility to maintain order. If these reforms had taken hold, the empire might have developed a more coherent administrative and ecclesiastical structure, making bishops and monasteries even more central to governance.

However, this would not necessarily have created a permanently united Europe. The empire still faced serious structural pressures: vast distances, powerful local aristocrats, differing regional identities, Viking raids in the west and north, Slavic and Magyar pressure in the east, and the difficulty of maintaining royal authority without a large permanent bureaucracy. Even if Louis had succeeded, later rulers would still have had to manage succession, aristocratic ambition, and military threats.

So the most likely outcome is not a stable “United States of Europe,” but a longer-lived Carolingian imperial system. Civil war would have been reduced, the Treaty of Verdun might not have happened, and the political separation of France and Germany would have been delayed or reshaped. Medieval Europe may have developed around a stronger imperial center, with feudal fragmentation occurring more slowly and under a more explicitly Christian-imperial framework.

edus.text: If Louis the Pious had successfully imposed his reforms, especially the succession settlement of the Ordinatio Imperii,
the Carolingian Empire would probably have remained unified for at least another generation instead of collapsing into civil war and the Treaty of Verdun in 843.
Louis’s main problem was not simply that he was weak,
but that he tried to reconcile two conflicting principles:
the Frankish tradition of dividing lands among royal sons
and the imperial idea that Charlemagne’s empire should remain a single Christian polity.
His reform program favored unity under one senior emperor,
originally his eldest son Lothair,
while younger sons would receive subordinate kingdoms.
If that system had been accepted by his sons and the aristocracy,
the immediate result would likely have been a more stable Carolingian monarchy.
The biggest change would have been the avoidance, or at least postponement, of the partition into West Francia, East Francia, and Middle Francia.
That means the later emergence of France and Germany as separate political traditions would have been delayed or taken a different form.
A unified empire stretching across much of western and central Europe
could have preserved a stronger sense of imperial identity,
with regional kings or governors operating beneath a recognized emperor.
A successful reform would also have strengthened the alliance between the Carolingian state and the Church.
Louis’s reign emphasized Christian kingship, moral reform, monastic discipline, and the idea that imperial authority had a sacred responsibility to maintain order.
If these reforms had taken hold,
the empire might have developed a more coherent administrative and ecclesiastical structure,
making bishops and monasteries even more central to governance.
However, this would not necessarily have created a permanently united Europe.
The empire still faced serious structural pressures:

vast distances, powerful local aristocrats, differing regional identities, Viking raids in the west and north, Slavic and Magyar pressure in the east, and the difficulty of maintaining royal authority without a large permanent bureaucracy.
Even if Louis had succeeded,
later rulers would still have had to manage succession, aristocratic ambition, and military threats.
So the most likely outcome is not a stable “United States of Europe,”
but a longer-lived Carolingian imperial system.
Civil war would have been reduced,
the Treaty of Verdun might not have happened,
and the political separation of France and Germany would have been delayed or reshaped.
Medieval Europe may have developed around a stronger imperial center,
with feudal fragmentation occurring more slowly and under a more explicitly Christian-imperial framework.

items.question: What If Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy?
human_answers: Your argument is intriguing. I wrote a post last year that made a similar argument to yours. Post in thread 'If Japan had not taken over Korea, where would they have expanded instead?' Feb 8, 2025 I feel like Korea keeping Japan from being too aggressive gives china a lot more breathing room to consolidate its own development- Seeing the modernisation happening in Korea probably strengthens reform factions in china- although if it means the Qing feel the need to reestablish control over this unpredictable vassal, could potentially lead to the sino Japanese war being replaced by a sino Korean War that also humiliates china and exposed its failure. Madhukar_Shah However, even back then, there were comments on that post saying that “even if Korea were to modernize, Japan would not abandon its ambitions toward Korea and the continent. One of the reasons for that is precisely the topic of this post. I once read a Korean alternate-history novel in which the Japanese Army and its internal factions acted as obstacles to cooperation between Korea and Japan. In the end, meaningful Korea–Japan cooperation only began to make real progress after Yamagata Aritomo fell from power following the Ōtsu Incident and was even subjected to an assassination attempt.

Huh? After the Sengoku Period Japan experienced one of the most peaceful and stable periods in its history under the Tokugawa Shogunate, which lasted lasted 250+ years. The only period in Japanese history that lasted longer was the Heian period. But that was hardly a stable regime, with regular infighting between retired emperors, the Fujiwara, and ultimately the Taira and Minamoto clans. And after the failed invasion of Korea at the end of the Azuchi-Momoyama period there were no serious Japanese attack against the mainland until the Meiji Period. ​ I am not sure why you think it was the army that uniquely pushed Japan to pursue expansionist policies? The navy was fully complicit in this as well, in fact the navy is the enabling factor in this because it's the only way for Japan to actually attack anybody outside the home islands in the first place. You use Britain and Venice as examples but how did these two powers not also use their navies for aggressive expansionism overseas? The bushi never rising in the first place, which takes you all the way back to the aforementioned Heian period. The utter failure of e.g. the Jokyu War or the Kenmu Restoration shows how powerless the court nobility became once the bakufu was established. Not to mention that the ultimate restoration of imperial power itself was enabled by the military power of the bushi, just the ones that opposed to bakufu.

I think the most interesting POD would be in the early 17th century during the first decades of the Togugawa shogunate. During the Senkaku period Japan had been relatively open to foreign trade due to the lack of central authority and when they first came to power the Togugawa tried to regulate but not stop this exchanges, including provisions such as the "Ted Seals" that allowed large Japanese merchantmen of the same name reach all the way down to Indonesia if not further. The shogunate and their allies also possessed a few European style galleons, most famously the San Juan Bautista . Now OTL the shogunate would end up halting this trade and impose the Sakoku policy which closed off Japan from almost all foreign trade, as well as starting the persecution of Christians. While the reasons behind this are still debated two of the primary reasons stated is that the Shogunate was increasingly worried about the threat that colonial European powers presented to Japan as well as the fact that a lot of this trade (including many of the Read Seal Ships) were controlled by southern houses that were not seen as loyal to the Togugawa. Now ponder a reality where the Shogunate decides a forward defense policy is better as an answer to European encroachment and that rather than cut off trade its better to let its own vassals control the Red Seals. Such a Japan would eventually have to develop the centralized naval infrastructure to protect that trade and fend of Europeans, resulting in a state for whom the navy is the central military concern (much like Britain). Edo era Japan was no economic slouch and could probably sustain a trade/semicolonial empire. Places like the Ryukyus and Hokkaido would fall under central Japanese control much earlier and sino-japanese relations would be very different. A Japanese naval empire could lead to similar responses from the Qing and the Joseon as well. Of course this would have big social ramifications within Japan: we probably wouldn't' see the same system for controlling samurai as OTL and merchants would end up much more influential much quicker. The rigid social hierarchy that the Togugawa tried to impose would fall apart before it was even properly enforced. Christianity might be more accepted but its equally possible that anti-Christianity could form the roots of an early form of Pan-Asianism.

Due to the influence of typhoons and unstable wind patterns in the East Asian seas, the region's "most strategic commercial sea lane" has historically been the trade route along the coastline, while the distant island chains have traditionally been uninhabited. Regarding the so-called "central place in trade," there were four key players in East Asian trade: mainland Japan, which produced precious metals; mainland China, which produced handicrafts (I don't believe that naval power alone could completely control trade along the Chinese coast, especially since excessive trade with China would only lead to all the precious metals flowing into China, destroying Japan's domestic industries); the Europeans; and the Spice Islands (which were within the Dutch sphere of influence, and required passing through the Philippines to reach Japan). It is clear that Japan could only control valuable trade centers if its navy surpassed the combined strength of Spain and the Netherlands; any navy less powerful than that would be meaningless. However, without any positive feedback or incentives, I don't believe it would be possible to build a navy in mainland Japan that could surpass the combined naval power of these two countries.
items.original_question: What if Japan had pursued a navy-centered national strategy? Unlike most island nations, Japan historically possessed an army with substantial political and social influence. With the emergence of the samurai class, Japan experienced prolonged periods of civil war and state formation led primarily by warrior elites. Particularly after the Sengoku period, cycles of civil war, the birth of new regimes, and expansion toward the continent were repeatedly observed. After the Toyotomi Hideyoshi regime emerged from the outcome of internal conflict, Hideyoshi employed the greatly expanded army to pursue continental ambitions, leading to the invasion of the Korean Peninsula. Following the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate and the wars that accompanied it, the Meiji government was established and Japan embarked on a program of modernization. However, unlike Britain and other island nations, Japan maintained an army with considerable autonomy and political influence despite its insular geography. Consequently, Japan’s expansionist trajectory once again focused on the Korean Peninsula, Manchuria, and the Asian continent. What I am curious about is the following. If Japan were to become a country in which the navy held complete primacy over the army, how would its history have needed to unfold differently? In this scenario, the army would be limited to roles such as suppression of internal rebellions, defense of the home islands, and naval infantry (marines), possessing only minimal status and political influence. The navy would constitute the principal military force, and national defense strategy and institutional design would likewise be shaped under naval leadership. Furthermore, the direction of external expansion would be determined from the perspective of a maritime power, rather than that of a continental state. If Japan had chosen the route of a maritime power like Britain or the Venetian Republic, or if its modernization had been deliberately oriented toward a completely navy-led military structure, how would Japanese history have unfolded differently? The Japan I'm referring to includes not only the Empire of Japan but also earlier periods of Japanese history. POD is not just in 1868 but extends to several centuries earlier.

If Japan had pursued a genuinely navy-centered national strategy, the most important change would not simply have been “more battleships.” It would have meant a different grand strategy: prioritizing sea-lane security, maritime trade, overseas commerce, island bases, and limited coastal or colonial commitments, while avoiding large continental wars in China and Siberia. In that version of events, Japan’s twentieth century could have been far less disastrous.

Historically, Imperial Japan was pulled heavily toward an army-centered continental strategy. The army saw Korea, Manchuria, north China, and eventually much of China as essential to national security and self-sufficiency. This produced the Manchurian Incident, the creation of Manchukuo, the full-scale war in China from 1937, and ultimately the strategic trap that led Japan to attack the Western powers in 1941. A navy-centered Japan would likely have been more cautious about those land commitments, because the navy’s core interest was not conquering the Asian mainland but protecting maritime access to resources and markets.

The most plausible consequence is that Japan would have tried harder to remain within the Anglo-American maritime order. It might have preserved better relations with Britain and the United States, accepted naval arms limitation treaties more pragmatically, and relied on trade rather than conquest for oil, rubber, iron, and food. If Japan avoided the invasion of China or at least avoided a prolonged China war, it probably would not have faced the same U.S. oil embargo and diplomatic isolation that made the Pacific War seem unavoidable to Japanese leaders in 1941.

Domestically, a navy-centered strategy might also have weakened the political power of the Imperial Army. The army’s semi-independent behavior, especially by the Kwantung Army in Manchuria, was one of the major reasons Japan lost control of its foreign policy. If naval officers, civilian politicians, trading firms, and industrial interests had carried more influence, Japan might have remained authoritarian and imperial, but less likely to be dominated by radical army expansionists. Party government in the 1920s and early 1930s might have survived longer.

Japan would still have had imperial ambitions. A maritime Japan would probably have retained Taiwan and Korea, sought influence in the western Pacific, and built a powerful fleet. It might have expanded commercially into Southeast Asia rather than militarily. But if it tried to seize the Dutch East Indies, British Malaya, or the Philippines by force, it would still have collided with Britain and the United States. In that case, a navy-centered strategy might only have produced an earlier or more deliberate Pacific War, and Japan would probably still have lost because its industrial base was far smaller than America’s.

So the key distinction is between a maritime-commercial strategy and a naval-militarist strategy. A maritime-commercial Japan could have become a major Pacific trading power, avoided the catastrophe of the Second Sino-Japanese War and the Pacific War, and entered the postwar world far stronger. A naval-militarist Japan, by contrast, would have built more ships and perhaps focused earlier on the “southern advance,” but it would still have faced the same fatal problem: Japan could not defeat the United States and British Empire in a long industrial war.

The broader effects would have been enormous. China might not have been devastated by Japanese invasion, which could have changed the balance between the Nationalists and Communists. The United States might never have occupied Japan, meaning no American-imposed postwar constitution, no Article 9, and a very different path to democratization. Korea and Taiwan might have remained under Japanese rule longer, unless decolonization pressures forced a later settlement. Japan itself would likely have avoided atomic bombing, firebombing, military collapse, and occupation.

In short, if Japan had pursued a navy-centered strategy in the sense of maritime trade, sea power, and limited overseas commitments, it probably would have been more secure, richer, and less isolated. If it had pursued a navy-centered strategy in the sense of challenging the Western powers for control of the Pacific, it would still have been strategically overmatched. The successful version of a navy-centered Japan would have required restraint: command of the seas for commerce, not conquest of Asia by land or a suicidal naval war against the United States.
