items.question: What If Create an exotic party system
human_answers: Led to: Independent Growers Union Party: AKA the Green Farmers Party, Green and Grow Party ... ( In derogatory terms also referred to as the Goatwool Sock Party, the goats ) A split-off from the Farmers Union Party that contends that the latter has become too subservient to the big agricultural businesses, megafarms and meat-packing plants to the detriment of small family farms and independent growers. Quickly gained a following in rural New England, Colorado, New Mexico and parts of California. Also gained support from the microbrewery industry, whole food grocery chains and Willie Nelson... However while promoting small farms and orchards, they quickly adopted ideas of sustainable green farming which lead to talk radio now openly calling them 'that other green lefties'. The fact that they are also heavily promoting the legalization of marijuana does not help and lately their appeal with traditional small family farms - once their core constituents- has waned. Many of hem now lamenting that they "revolted against being pushed out by corporate megafarms, only to now be pushed out by hippie goat farmers". Still their upward trend has slowed but not stopped andbin the last elections they managed to get as many votes as the FUP. Platform : pro small farms, pro sustainable farming, pro farm subsides but vehement watchdog making sure said subsidies are not gobbled up by large agribusiness. Socially conservative to pro-busines, pro-family and pro states rights. However also pro marijuana and against fracking, pesticides and GMO seeds. Although not official, in analogy to the Democrat's mule and the Republican's elephants, political cartoonists have taken to depicting the IGUP as a small goat or a goat Inna farmers outfit. Apparently many IGUP members liked the idea and bumper stickers of goats driving tractors, goats headbutting mules and goats p.... against the leg of an elephant have become quite popular in rural parts of the states. Closely aligned with: Fraternal Order of Local and Small Businesses: Originally an action group turned political party, the FOLSBee is - as the name implies- pro-busines but against 'big business' and megacorporations running roughshod over small neighborhood mon-and-pop stores. Unsurprisingly they have a strong following on the local levels, in several smaller towns being the biggest party in city council. Their reach however declines with each superimposed layer of government and their overall impact in the state elections I negligible. Nationally, so far they have only yielded one senator and four congressmen in their 50 years of existence. The name invokes strong images of early 1900's idyllic New England town streets with lots of stores that are just known by the family name of their owner and it must be said that the FOLSBee is quite successful in playing on the nostalgic feel of that image. Their mythical hero is George Bailey, the community banker protagonist from Frank Capra's ' It's a Wonderful Life'. And like Bailey, their main tenet is that it is a local business' task to help it's community especially when this does not exclude getting ahead themselves as well. Therefore on a national level it should be the government's task to help small businesses helping the community. As a platform, they are rather conservative, pro gun rights, pro law and order and pro-busines. However they are quite effective as a watchdog making sure that every proposed business law is effectively helping ALL businesses an not just the ones big enough to afford their own lobbyists and their idea of 'a level playing field for all' also ties in with support for education and immigrants' rights. However like the IGUP, the FOLSBee also has taken on -critics say:'has been infiltrated by' - some rather leftist and environmentalist views. So they tend to promote public transportation over new highways (there are more clients at bus stops then at parking lots) green energy over fossil fuel (no startup will come to our city thinking 'Hey, let's build a car that runs on coal') public housing, a strong social welfare net and lately even state-run healthcare. So much like conservatives paint the IGUP as the party of goat wool sock wearing weed farmers, they taken to deride the FOLSBee as the party of hippie farmers market organic bath salt sellers. Like the IGUP, this has not really affected their base and although rather small nationally, by coordinating their programs with the IGUP 'goats' they are still on of the more influntial minor pressure parties. In political cartoons to the FOLSBee is usually represented as a Norman Rockwell-esque 1920's drug store owner. Typically he is standing behind a soda fountain doling out fatherly advice to a donkey or elephant sitting at the drug store counter.

Law and Order : Center-right to right-wing, MacArthurism, law and order, strong government, agrarianism (faction) Originally formed during the Dorr Rebellion, however, they soon grew to great lengths due to the Great Rebellion. As of now, they are the party in power and have a strong grasp over the country's House of Burgesses, most likely due to the recent riots in cities such as Cleaveland and St. Elmo. The party itself campaigns on the promises of strength, justice, and keeping the radicals in check. They are currently led by Premier Joe Pennacchio. Republican Moderate : Center to center-right, liberal-conservatism, economic conservatism, social liberalism, libertarianism (faction) Created in an attempt to oppose the religious fanatics of the state along with the dictatorial Alaskan Governor Ben Stevens. However, over time they became a national party and became a party full of moderates and centrists leaning towards the right. They are also the second biggest party in the House, they support religious freedom and economic conservatism. They are currently led by Deirdre Scozzfava. Nullifier : Center-right to center-right, nullification, economic liberalism, social conservatism, free-trade, states' rights (faction) The party of nullification and free trade, the Nullifiers were strong for a good many of years before the Republic of Dixie's secession, in which they were banned for treason, however, in the early '80s, they were unbanned and forced to start from the bottom up. However, they are doing well now, and are the third biggest party in the United States' House of Burgesses. They are currently led by Peter Lawler. Solidarity : Left-wing to center-left, populism, anti-authoritarianism, left-wing populism, workers' rights, social democracy (faction) The party originated from the Illinois Solidarity Party which had been formed to oppose local lunatic Hermyle LaRouche's antics, however, they eventually moved into the national arena. For a time, they were very strong, especially during the population's progressive sway during the 1990s, they have been slowly and surely losing seats each year, They are currently led by Adlai Stevenson IV. Southern : Center-left to far-right, southern interests, social conservatism, states' rights, southern secession (faction) The Southern Party was formed for southern interests, and their interests only. It was a miracle that they were unbanned in the early 2000s by Nullifier Premier James Q. Wilson. They are especially socially conservative, however, there are a few members who could be considered left-wing populists to some extent. They only contain seats that originate from the deep south. Currently led by Roy Moore. Peoples' Constitutional : Left-wing to left-wing, Chicano nationalism, Mexican-American interests, Christian socialism (faction) And last, but also least, the Peoples' Constitutional Party. Similar to the Southern Party, the PCs were formed to protect a specific group of peoples' interests. However, unlike the Southerners, the PCs fight for the rights of minorities, well, actually just those of Hispanic origin. There is also a strong Catholic Socialist faction in the party, most likely due to former leader Dolores Huerta. Currently led by Julian Castro.

- Puritan Party: Atl scenario where the Great Awakening leads to a political movement alongside the religious revival. - National Party: Atl scenario where the military plays a more important role in early US politics. The military takes control and declares that citizenship is only given to those who serve. The US becomes a one party state dominated by military leaders. - German American Party: German immigration to America occurs in even larger numbers than otl. German Americans demand German be declared a national "protected" language. They also fight against ethnic discrimination. - Monarchist Party:. The US tries out a Monarchy but it fails and Becomes a Republic. This party tries wishes to see the return of the Monarchy. - Colonization Party: A party of early abolitionists who focus there effort on the state and local level. Try to encourage slave states to allow slaves to earn their freedom under the condition that they be sent to Liberia after their enslavement ends.

I had a rather lengthy idea I've been toying around with for a party system for a work of fiction written in my Power Without Knowledge setting that I might write out today but on an unrelated note I've been mulling over the impact of a more successful Joseph Smith presidential run . I'm not suggesting that he win, or even that he not be assassinated, I'm just trying to puzzle out the consequences of his electoral platform surviving his death. Perhaps some sort of alliance with the Liberty Party ? Smith's platform included provisions shrinking the size of Congress and docking their pay, along with the elimination of courts martial and instituting the death penalty for public officials that didn't defend their constituents' constitutional rights, but what suggests at least some buy-in from the Liberty Party was a program of complete emancipation by 1850, with at least some degree of compensation financed by the sale of public land. Smith also argued for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. I understand it's a gamble of long odds (especially regarding constitutional changes and territorial expansion) but perhaps a pragmatic move to adopt compensation as a way to attract votes in slave states that would otherwise dig in their heels at any mention of abolition? It would also almost certainly require butterflying away the LDS move to Utah, leaving them a powerful swing constituency in Illinois. The idea of an openly abolitionist party arising in and surviving the 19th century and explicitly focused on the rights of minority religious and ethnic groups has a lot of promise. *EDIT- In keeping with my new Strange Bedfellows idea for an alternate American history in party systems here's my reinterpretation of the Second Party System: Federalist Party - The sole survivor of the First Party System and the Era of Good Feelings, the Federalist Party was able to claw its way back from the brink in the wake of the shattering of the National Republican Party following the much maligned 1824 election. Advocating a strong central government, Hamiltonian economics and infrastructure spending, the party was aided in its recovery by the influx of anti-Jacksonians leaving the disintegrating National Republicans. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. While in office Jackson tended to side with Southern interests against abolitionism, opposed (but could not dismantle) the Bank of the United States and defied the Supreme Court in the lead up to the Trail of Tears. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. The Federalists would side with northern industrial interests in opposition to the spread of the Peculiar Institution, while Nullifiers, viewing such attempts as federal overreach, became adamant defenders of it. Despite this focus on the issue it wouldn't be until the 1850's that the Liberty Party, the only explicitly abolitionist party in the Union, would gain traction beyond the local level. A party of minority rights and abolitionism, the Libertarians would lead a coalition of freedmen, Mormons and Owenite socialists of all stripes to political action, parlaying a pivotal influence in several midwestern states into a coalition with the Federalists in 1860.
items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Create an exotic party system

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Divergence Logic
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer establishes a clear alternate-history or institutional premise that plausibly produces an exotic party system rather than merely listing random parties.
criteria.1-2: No clear divergence point or premise; parties appear arbitrary or unrelated to the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a premise, but the link to party formation is weak, vague, or mostly asserted.
criteria.5-6: Provides a recognizable divergence and explains some direct effects on party development.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible divergence with clear causal links to multiple party origins and alignments.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, internally grounded counterfactual premise whose institutional, social, and historical consequences strongly explain the whole party system.

criteria.name: Party System Breadth and Distinctiveness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer creates a varied, exotic, and politically meaningful set of parties with distinct identities, constituencies, ideologies, and roles.
criteria.1-2: Provides too few parties or parties are generic labels with little differentiation.
criteria.3-4: Includes several parties, but many overlap ideologically or lack clear bases of support.
criteria.5-6: Creates a functional multiparty system with some distinct platforms and voter blocs.
criteria.7-8: Offers a diverse party ecology with clear ideological niches, regional bases, factions, and political functions.
criteria.9-10: Presents a vivid, memorable, and exotic party system where each party has a distinctive history, constituency, symbolism, and strategic role.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms by which the new parties emerge, compete, evolve, and affect governance over time.
criteria.1-2: Little or no explanation of how parties form, gain support, or influence politics.
criteria.3-4: Gives limited mechanisms, mostly party platforms without electoral or social dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic formation causes, voter bases, and some electoral consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers party origins, coalitions, regional strength, factional drift, electoral incentives, and policy effects.
criteria.9-10: Traces long-range dynamics across generations, including realignments, splinters, alliances, media framing, institutional pressures, and governing consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the created party system remains coherent across time, geography, ideology, and institutions without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible timelines, or mutually incompatible party claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent elements but frequent inconsistencies in ideology, chronology, or influence.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor unexplained jumps or tensions between party traits and outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains strong consistency across party histories, platforms, regions, and electoral status.
criteria.9-10: Shows excellent systemic coherence, with tensions explicitly explained as factions, compromises, historical legacies, or strategic adaptations.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Constraint Awareness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer balances imaginative exoticism with plausible political sociology and acknowledges uncertainty where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Wildly implausible or deterministic; ignores political constraints and social realities.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible ideas, but relies heavily on unsupported leaps or overconfident claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, though some assumptions or long-range outcomes are underjustified.
criteria.7-8: Balances creativity with realistic voter behavior, institutions, regional interests, and contingency.
criteria.9-10: Highly imaginative yet disciplined; clearly distinguishes likely outcomes from speculative ones and explains constraints, tradeoffs, and alternative possibilities.

items.model_answer:
An exotic party system could be imagined as a political system where parties are not permanent ideological blocs, but temporary, issue-based alliances that form and dissolve around specific public problems.

In this system, voters would not choose one party for everything. Instead, each voter could divide their political support across several “policy parties”: for example, an environmental party for climate issues, a labor party for workplace rights, a localist party for regional policy, and a civil-liberties party for rights and justice. Parliament or congress would then be composed not only by general party vote, but also by strength in different policy areas.

The most unusual feature would be that parties would have expiration dates. Every few years, they would need to re-register, prove public support, and clearly define their current goals. This would prevent parties from becoming old machines that survive only through loyalty, money, or identity. New movements could enter more easily, while obsolete parties would disappear.

Government would be formed through “modular coalitions.” Instead of one ruling party controlling all policy, different coalitions could govern different domains. A green-left coalition might control climate policy, a centrist-business coalition might control trade, and a civil-rights coalition might control constitutional issues. The prime minister or executive would coordinate these coalitions rather than command a single majority.

The benefit of such an exotic system would be flexibility. It would better reflect voters who are not purely left-wing, right-wing, liberal, conservative, nationalist, or socialist, but mixed in their views. It could reduce polarization because parties would need to cooperate across issues.

The danger is instability. If parties constantly form and dissolve, voters may become confused, governments may become fragmented, and accountability may weaken. It might be hard to know who is responsible when policy fails. Wealthy groups could also create short-lived parties to influence one issue and then vanish.

So, an exotic party system could be creative and more representative, but it would need strong rules: transparency in funding, clear coalition agreements, independent election supervision, and mechanisms to hold temporary parties accountable. Otherwise, it could become chaotic rather than democratic.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

I actually like the idea of an improved dragon better than what we have with Starship (assuming it ever carries humans). As for using it for lunar missions. Do we need to recreate the Apollo Mission profile or can we build some sort of transfer craft a sort of tug or booster that can be docked with and used to get to and from the moon. We would need a way to refuel it in earth orbit but it may be one way to get Dragon to the moon. And long term it may be better. I have always thought that we needed some sort of “space craft” vs the way we do everything with the vehicle we use to get up and down from earth. That would I suppose be a big task to build and maintain and refuel this transfer vehicle. But it may allow a less powerful system to do the job. And once you have the hardware it is harder to cancel the thing. So we may actually get some long term use.

All true of course, also fully ignored in most cases and specifically in the articles/videos I cited above The "mantra" is simply that Dragon is cheaper and therefor better than Orion. Similar statements about Falcon versus SLS. One of the videos I didn't cite was in fact one that suggests Lunar HLS "Starship" will be used for ferrying the landing party from LEO to LLO where they would use Dragon to land on the Moon and then return to the HLS "Starship" to be ferried back to LEO where Dragon would be used to land on Earth. Ya, IIRC you lose the core stage. Ya it would be 'neat' but keep in mind the Super Draco's are not actually "throttleable" since they are supposed to be used as abort rockets and not landing rockets. The way the propellants are stored at very high pressures in order to get that high thrust for abort and I think that precludes landing use so they likely would have to be redesigned.. Randy
items.original_question: What if Falcon/Dragon to the Moon? Kind of bouncing off this thread as I've run across some of the usual "hype" sources such as this and this , (nothing from SpaceX though which I think is telling) "bragging" about SpaceX's "great new plan" to send crew Dragon to the Moon "sooner than NASA or China" etc, et-al. (Of course they all simply ignore the issues with Dragon going beyond LEO and the fact Orion and SLS are designed to do exactly that but what would I expect ) So the question is essentially "What if SpaceX had continued to iterate and improve Dragon and Falcon Heavy for use in Lunar missions? Granting that as I pointed out here that there's likely no "place" for such a move since the SpaceX to Mars focus was pretty much baked in since the start and with such a short timeline getting a plausible POD is going to be problematic I do wonder if a bit more focus on "Dear Moon" along with Cargo/Crew Dragon couldn't set up a premise where the eventual "HLS" might end up more realistic? Anyway, open for thoughts and comments Randy

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had kept developing Falcon Heavy and Crew Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions instead of shifting that role to Starship, the most likely result would have been a more modest but earlier commercial lunar capability: crewed lunar flybys and possibly lunar-orbit missions, but not a full reusable Moon-landing system without major additional hardware.

Falcon Heavy could plausibly send a modified Crew Dragon on a free-return trajectory around the Moon. That was the basis of SpaceX’s 2017 plan to fly private passengers around the Moon using Falcon Heavy and Dragon 2. To make that real, SpaceX would have needed to human-rate Falcon Heavy, validate Crew Dragon for deep-space reentry speeds, expand life support duration, improve radiation protection, add deep-space communications and navigation, and certify mission profiles beyond low Earth orbit. None of those are trivial, but they are much less ambitious than building Starship.

The first likely outcome would have been a commercial circumlunar flight sometime in the early-to-mid 2020s, assuming SpaceX prioritized it and NASA or private customers accepted the risk. It would have resembled Apollo 8 in broad outline only in the sense of sending humans around the Moon, but technically it would probably have been simpler: no lunar orbit insertion, no landing, just a free-return loop around the Moon and back to Earth. Dragon’s heat shield technology was probably adaptable to lunar-return speeds, but it would have required testing and certification.

Going beyond a flyby would have been much harder. Crew Dragon does not have the propulsion capability to enter and leave lunar orbit by itself. For a true lunar-orbit mission, SpaceX would have needed an additional propulsion module, a larger service module, or a separately launched stage that Dragon could dock with in Earth orbit. Falcon Heavy could support such an architecture, but it would become a multi-launch mission with orbital rendezvous, docking, and perhaps propellant-management challenges. It would still be feasible in principle, but no longer as clean as “Falcon Heavy launches Dragon to the Moon.”

A crewed lunar landing using Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have required an entirely separate lunar lander. Dragon could perhaps serve as the crew transport from Earth to lunar orbit, while a lander launched separately would handle descent and ascent. That architecture would look more like a commercialized Apollo-style system: Dragon as the command module, Falcon Heavy as the heavy launcher, and another vehicle as the lunar module. SpaceX could have developed or partnered on such a lander, but Falcon Heavy’s payload limits would likely force multiple launches, tight mass constraints, or expendable launch profiles.

The biggest strategic effect is that SpaceX might have become a serious near-term competitor to Orion/SLS for some lunar missions. A Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar flyby would likely have been far cheaper than an SLS/Orion mission, and if demonstrated successfully it would have increased pressure on NASA to buy commercial crewed deep-space transport. However, it probably would not have fully replaced Orion for NASA’s Artemis architecture without extensive redesign, because Orion was built for longer-duration deep-space operations, lunar orbit, and integration with NASA’s broader exploration plans.

The tradeoff is that Starship would likely have been delayed or deemphasized. SpaceX would have gained a more conservative, incremental lunar program, but at the cost of pursuing a less transformative system. Falcon Heavy and Dragon could have delivered impressive “Apollo 8-class” missions and perhaps supported early commercial lunar-orbit operations, but they would not have offered the same payload capacity, reusability, surface cargo delivery, or Mars ambitions that Starship was intended to provide.

So the counterfactual answer is: SpaceX probably could have flown people around the Moon with Falcon Heavy and a modified Dragon earlier than Starship will fly crewed lunar missions, and it might have created a lower-cost commercial alternative for lunar flybys and perhaps lunar orbit. But crewed landings would still have required a separate lander and a more complex multi-launch architecture. It would have been a nearer-term, narrower lunar program—not a full replacement for Starship’s long-term ambitions.

edus.text: If SpaceX had kept developing Falcon Heavy and Crew Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions instead of shifting that role to Starship,
the most likely result would have been a more modest but earlier commercial lunar capability:
crewed lunar flybys and possibly lunar-orbit missions,
but not a full reusable Moon-landing system without major additional hardware.
Falcon Heavy could plausibly send a modified Crew Dragon on a free-return trajectory around the Moon.
That was the basis of SpaceX’s 2017 plan to fly private passengers around the Moon using Falcon Heavy and Dragon 2.

To make that real, SpaceX would have needed to human-rate Falcon Heavy, validate Crew Dragon for deep-space reentry speeds, expand life support duration, improve radiation protection, add deep-space communications and navigation, and certify mission profiles beyond low Earth orbit.
None of those are trivial,
but they are much less ambitious than building Starship.
The first likely outcome would have been a commercial circumlunar flight sometime in the early-to-mid 2020s,
assuming SpaceX prioritized it and NASA or private customers accepted the risk.
It would have resembled Apollo 8 in broad outline only in the sense of sending humans around the Moon,
but technically it would probably have been simpler:
no lunar orbit insertion, no landing,
just a free-return loop around the Moon and back to Earth.
Dragon’s heat shield technology was probably adaptable to lunar-return speeds,
but it would have required testing and certification.
Going beyond a flyby would have been much harder.
Crew Dragon does not have the propulsion capability to enter and leave lunar orbit by itself.
For a true lunar-orbit mission, SpaceX would have needed an additional propulsion module, a larger service module, or a separately launched stage that Dragon could dock with in Earth orbit.
Falcon Heavy could support such an architecture,
but it would become a multi-launch mission with orbital rendezvous, docking, and perhaps propellant-management challenges.
It would still be feasible in principle,
but no longer as clean as “Falcon Heavy launches Dragon to the Moon.”
A crewed lunar landing using Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have required an entirely separate lunar lander.
Dragon could perhaps serve as the crew transport from Earth to lunar orbit,
while a lander launched separately would handle descent and ascent.
That architecture would look more like a commercialized Apollo-style system:
Dragon as the command module, Falcon Heavy as the heavy launcher, and another vehicle as the lunar module.
SpaceX could have developed or partnered on such a lander,
but Falcon Heavy’s payload limits would likely force multiple launches, tight mass constraints, or expendable launch profiles.
The biggest strategic effect is that SpaceX might have become a serious near-term competitor to Orion/SLS for some lunar missions.
A Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar flyby would likely have been far cheaper than an SLS/Orion mission,
and if demonstrated successfully it would have increased pressure on NASA to buy commercial crewed deep-space transport.
However, it probably would not have fully replaced Orion for NASA’s Artemis architecture without extensive redesign,
because Orion was built for longer-duration deep-space operations, lunar orbit, and integration with NASA’s broader exploration plans.
The tradeoff is that Starship would likely have been delayed or deemphasized.
SpaceX would have gained a more conservative, incremental lunar program,
but at the cost of pursuing a less transformative system.
Falcon Heavy and Dragon could have delivered impressive “Apollo 8-class” missions and perhaps supported early commercial lunar-orbit operations,
but they would not have offered the same payload capacity, reusability, surface cargo delivery, or Mars ambitions that Starship was intended to provide.
So the counterfactual answer is:
SpaceX probably could have flown people around the Moon with Falcon Heavy and a modified Dragon earlier than Starship will fly crewed lunar missions,
and it might have created a lower-cost commercial alternative for lunar flybys and perhaps lunar orbit.
But crewed landings would still have required a separate lander and a more complex multi-launch architecture.
It would have been a nearer-term, narrower lunar program—
not a full replacement for Starship’s long-term ambitions.

items.question: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?
human_answers: The only time Aircraft Carriers carry out multi-day attacks on the same location is when they either are providing air cover to an invasion force or have total air superiority. If Pearl Harbour had been a single raid each day for two days the raid on the second day would have suffered serious losses and the patrol aircraft may have located the Carriers which then becomes a very big question of risking a Carrier. Aircraft Carriers are great at projecting power in that they represent overwhelming firepower from unexpected directions at any time. For example look at the exercises carried out between the cold war Royal Navy and the USA. I think it was HMS Ark Royal which involved HMS Ark Royal being the aggressor and striking US bases on the US Eastern Sea Board. up to a week of operations with strikes on a daily basis and undetected due to sneaky sneaky tactics. Aircraft Carriers are also hideously vulnerable to attrition and easily overwhelmed while in contact with shore based aircraft. Naval Aircraft are compromises due to structural needs and limitations caused by operational environment. The exact same engine in an airframe designed with the same technology will result in a land based aircraft of higher basic capability. The further technology has improved the smaller the difference in performance. During 1940's this difference was massive. Size constraints include wingspan, height and weight. Takeoff distance is also important. Range suffers because you need to hit takeoff speed much sooner. What all of this leads to is the fact the Royal Navy could not safely carry out more than a single night of attacks. The Raid was split into two waves due to time it took to launch the loaded aircraft then spot the next wave on the flight deck. Number of aircraft in an attack is also determined by speed at which aircraft could be launched. Even today the raid count is determined by rate of aircraft launch and form up time. j If the Royal Navy had 4 Fleet Carriers available the raid would still have been a single night. However the number of aircraft in each raid would have changed. With 4 carriers the raid would have likely been 80 Swordfish in two waves and it would also have been possible to attempt to wipe out the local airbases in order to do a daylight follow up. The Fighters from 4 Carriers would have been able to fend of larger opposition. If the aircraft compliment was the same as HMS Ilustrious then you could plan on 60 Fulmar's to be available. The likelihood is however that had 4 Carriers been available the air group would be Swordfish, Fulmar's and Sea Gladiators with 60 fighters in Fleet being impossible at this time of the war. 40 Swordfish with Torpedo's and 40 with bombs and flares equals Taranto being removed as a Naval Base for a full year with few Oil storage tanks remaining and the ships in the harbour being severely damaged and total constructive losses. Photos of Taranto pre war show the ships moored stern in at a the docks and essentially tied together. This being hit by 250 or 500lb bombs would decimate the Italian ships due to very week deck armour. 20 to 50 mm is very light and even a 250lb SAP bomb should go through. If 6 ships and tied together you create a 60m by 140m target square as a minimum with plenty of HE and fuel to burn in the ships. Swordfish Dive Bombing was fairly accurate. 40 Torpedo armed and 32 bombers with 8 Flare dropping aircraft equals insane damage levels.

The Brits achieved miracles with a bunch of obsolete biplanes ... The first wave, 12 aircraft, consisted of 6 Swordfish armed with torpedoes, 2 two with flares plus four 250 lb (110 kg) bombs, and 4 with six bombs. The second wave , 8 aircraft, 5 with torpedoes, 2 with flares pus four bombs. Total attack force, 20 aircraft, of which only 11 actually carried a torpedo ! (contrast Pearl Harbor, Japanese attack force= 353 aircraft) The Brits don't need more 'waves', they need more aircraft and more carriers... criteria.name: Operational feasibility of a second Taranto strike
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically evaluates whether the Royal Navy could mount a second attack on Taranto given 1940 carrier operations, aircraft availability, launch cycles, night operations, fuel, maintenance, and risk to HMS Illustrious.
criteria.1-2: Treats a second attack as trivially possible or impossible with little reference to carrier operations or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some limits such as aircraft numbers or danger but gives a shallow or partly inaccurate feasibility assessment.
criteria.5-6: Explains key constraints, including limited Swordfish numbers, night attack requirements, and carrier vulnerability, with some gaps.
criteria.7-8: Provides a well-grounded assessment of sortie generation, aircraft losses, rearming, scouting risk, and why repeat attacks were difficult.
criteria.9-10: Integrates carrier doctrine, launch/recovery cycles, maintenance, surprise, Italian response, and force protection into a highly plausible feasibility judgment.

criteria.name: Damage mechanisms and immediate military effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains what a second attack would likely damage at Taranto and how that would affect the Italian fleet, harbor infrastructure, oil stores, repair capacity, and naval operations.
criteria.1-2: Gives vague claims such as 'Italy would be destroyed' or 'nothing changes' without explaining damage mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Identifies possible extra ship damage but neglects infrastructure, repair limits, ordnance types, or harbor conditions.
criteria.5-6: Discusses additional torpedo or bomb damage to ships and some operational consequences, though with limited specificity.
criteria.7-8: Covers ships, docks, fuel, repair facilities, anti-air defenses, and how torpedoes, bombs, and flares could alter outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced damage model tied to aircraft loadouts, target layout, shallow-water torpedo use, deck armor, fires, and Italian recovery timelines.

criteria.name: Causal chain from Taranto to Mediterranean strategy
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible downstream consequences for the Mediterranean war, including Italian fleet availability, British convoy operations, Malta, North Africa, Axis naval behavior, and German intervention.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to broad conclusions about winning the war without a credible chain from the second attack.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Mediterranean consequences but relies on loose speculation or skips major intermediate steps.
criteria.5-6: Connects heavier Taranto damage to Italian naval weakness and some effects on convoys or North Africa, but incompletely.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain involving fleet attrition, convoy security, Malta pressure, Axis logistics, and likely German countermeasures.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a long-range, conditional chain that weighs British gains against Italian adaptation, Luftwaffe deployment, resource limits, and theater-wide feedback effects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and counterfactual restraint
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes under the counterfactual, avoids overclaiming, and handles dependence on assumptions such as aircraft numbers, timing, surprise, and Italian readiness.
criteria.1-2: Presents a single deterministic outcome with no uncertainty or caveats.
criteria.3-4: Uses occasional hedging but still makes unsupported or overconfident claims.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some uncertainty around losses, detection, and damage but does not structure alternatives clearly.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely outcomes from contingent ones and explains which assumptions drive different scenarios.
criteria.9-10: Provides calibrated scenario ranges, identifies sensitive variables, and avoids claiming effects beyond what the premise can support.

criteria.name: Historical consistency and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer remains consistent with known facts about the Taranto raid, British and Italian capabilities in 1940, aircraft types, fleet dispositions, and the limits of the counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Contains major factual errors or contradictions, such as wrong belligerents, anachronistic aircraft, or impossible force levels without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Includes several inaccuracies about Taranto, Swordfish, carriers, Italian defenses, or Mediterranean context that weaken the reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Mostly respects the historical setting but has minor errors or unsupported assumptions about forces, tactics, or timelines.
criteria.7-8: Accurately uses historical details and keeps the counterfactual changes limited and internally consistent.
criteria.9-10: Demonstrates strong command of the actual raid and 1940 naval aviation, explicitly controls deviations from history, and avoids internal contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a follow-up attack on Taranto soon after the November 1940 raid, the most likely result would have been a larger but still not war-deciding Italian naval disaster.

The first Taranto attack succeeded because it achieved surprise. It damaged three Italian battleships—Conte di Cavour, Littorio, and Caio Duilio—and temporarily shifted the naval balance in the Mediterranean toward Britain. A second raid, especially the following night, might have finished off already damaged ships, hit repair facilities, or possibly damaged one or more of the remaining operational battleships such as Vittorio Veneto or Giulio Cesare. If that had happened, the Regia Marina’s battleship force could have been crippled for many months rather than merely reduced.

That would have made Britain’s position in the Mediterranean stronger. Malta convoys, movements to Greece and Egypt, and Royal Navy operations in the central Mediterranean would have faced less danger from Italian heavy surface forces. Italy might have become even more cautious than it already was, and a later action like Cape Matapan in March 1941 might either not have happened or would have occurred under even worse conditions for the Italians.

But the second attack would also have been much harder. The Italians would no longer have been surprised. Anti-aircraft crews would have been alert, smoke screens and defenses improved, and British aircraft losses probably higher. HMS Illustrious would also have had to remain in dangerous waters longer, increasing the risk from Italian air attack, submarines, or surface forces. The British carrier force in the Mediterranean was too valuable to risk casually.

So the likely answer is: a second Taranto attack might have deepened the Italian defeat and given Britain a stronger short-term naval advantage, perhaps delaying Italian fleet operations for months. But it probably would not have knocked Italy out of the war or solved the wider Mediterranean problem. Axis convoys to North Africa still depended heavily on smaller ships, submarines, destroyers, aircraft, and later German air power. The strategic balance would improve for Britain, but the campaign would not be decided by Taranto alone.

items.question: What If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944?
human_answers: When the Allies invaded NW Africa, the French colonies of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia Kesselrings command was approved to recruit patriotic French to resist the Allies. The proposed infantry division never materialized. Enough men were found for a weak battalion, but after the unhealthy and unreliable were rejected there were enough to form a single over strength company. Given the German shortage of up to date equipment, particularly artillery and motor transport. The extra 100,000 French would be armed with the usual mix of older & obsolescent weapons, often in inferior numbers, like most other ground combat formations in Rundsteadts OB West. Just maybe there would be a SS 'Frankreich' division with good equipment, but otherwise its going to be leftovers, horse drawn artillery, little or no medium and heavy artillery, no supporting armor other than a few obsolescent R35 or D2 tanks, pitiful air support, inferior AT guns, French made MG vs the MG 34 or MG42. Compounding all this is the chronic German shortages of artillery ammunition and fuel. If the 100,000 French soldiers are used to offset other soldiers who are then sent to other front the questions is who? The overaged German reservists of the Bodenstang formations? The Ossies from Poland, Urkraine, Beylo Russ, ect... ? The elite Panzer Truppen? If the French are just added on top of the others, with no transfers, then its just the same inadequate equipment spread across a increase of 5% or 10% of men. A second given is the relatively small number of French soldiers who volunteered for the crusade in the east. The members of the Charlemagne division totaled far less than 100,000 through the entire war. Probably less than 50,000 served in that formation. While volunteers could be found to fight in the east, there was no similar movement in the west. The Milcie managed to recruit young men who wanted to avoid labor service, but that relatively large body failed to volunteer or participate in the battle of France. Most deserted long before the Allied armies over ran the police districts the Milcie units were assigned to.

items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow provided 100,000 troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, it probably would have made the Normandy campaign bloodier and possibly slower, but it would not likely have changed the final outcome of the war.

The first issue is plausibility. By 1944 Vichy France no longer had real military independence. After the Allied landings in North Africa in 1942, Germany occupied the previously “unoccupied” zone of France and disbanded most of the Vichy armistice army. Vichy could supply police, militia, labor, and small collaborationist formations, but raising and deploying 100,000 reliable French troops for coastal defense would have required German approval, German equipment, German command integration, and a major political decision to trust French units with weapons. That trust was doubtful, because many French soldiers were anti-German, pro-Allied, or at least unwilling to die defending German occupation.

Assuming the 100,000 troops existed, their effect would depend heavily on where they were placed. If they were spread thinly along the whole Atlantic Wall from the Netherlands to southern France, their impact on D-Day would have been limited. The Atlantic Wall was enormous, and 100,000 men across such a front would mostly improve local garrison strength without solving Germany’s main problems: Allied air superiority, naval gunfire, logistical weakness, poor mobility, and uncertainty about where the invasion would land.

If, however, they were concentrated in Normandy, the effect could have been more serious. One hundred thousand men is roughly the equivalent of several infantry divisions. Additional defenders in the Cotentin, around Caen, or behind Omaha and Juno beaches could have increased Allied casualties, slowed the beachhead expansion, and made German counterattacks more dangerous in the first days after 6 June. Omaha Beach in particular was already a near-run battle; stronger defenses there could have made the landing still more costly and might have forced a local evacuation or temporary failure.

But even in that stronger scenario, the Allies would still have held major advantages. They controlled the air and sea, could bombard coastal positions heavily, and had immense reserves of men, ships, vehicles, and supplies. German armored reserves were constrained by Hitler’s command system, Allied deception, fuel shortages, and air attack. Additional French infantry would not solve those structural problems. Unless those troops were unusually well-trained, well-equipped, highly motivated, and positioned exactly at the decisive points, they would probably delay the Allies rather than defeat them.

Morale and loyalty would be the biggest weakness. Many French soldiers ordered to fight Americans, British, Canadians, and Free French forces on French soil might have surrendered quickly, deserted, passed information to the Resistance, or fought half-heartedly. Allied psychological warfare would have emphasized that they were Frenchmen dying for Germany. The Resistance would likely have targeted them, and German commanders might have distrusted them enough to assign them static or secondary roles, reducing their battlefield value.

Politically, the consequences would have been severe. Vichy’s collaboration would have appeared even more direct and military, not merely administrative or police-based. The postwar reckoning in France would probably have been harsher, with deeper purges, more trials, and a sharper civil conflict between Resistance forces and collaborators. De Gaulle’s claim that Vichy was illegitimate would have been strengthened, while any later attempt to portray Vichy as a shield for French interests would have been much harder to sustain.

So the most likely result is: the Normandy invasion becomes more costly and perhaps slower, especially if the French troops are concentrated near the landing zones, but Germany still loses France. The larger strategic balance in 1944—Allied material superiority, Soviet pressure in the east, Allied air power, and German logistical collapse—would not be reversed by 100,000 Vichy troops. At most, they might have delayed liberation by weeks or possibly a few months; they probably would not have prevented it.

Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. items.original_question: What if World War I had occurred 9 years earlier? The First Moroccan Crisis occurred between 1905 and 1906 during the Russo-Japanese War. Although this event did not escalate into a full-scale military conflict, it was resolved through the Algeciras Conference. However, tensions between the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente grew stronger. Then, in 1911, the Second Moroccan Crisis took place. At this time, there were talks of a potential war, but ultimately it was resolved through international negotiations. Despite these series of events, in 1914, World War I broke out due to the assassination of the Austrian Archduke and the subsequent invasion of Serbia. This raises an interesting question. During the July Crisis in the OTL, there were numerous efforts to avoid war, but in the end, the arrogance of autocratic monarchs and the complex web of interests caused tensions to escalate and ultimately explode. What if such a chain reaction and explosion had occurred during the First Moroccan Crisis? What if the First Moroccan Crisis had escalated into a full-blown war, leading to World War I happening 9 years earlier than in the OTL? What could have been the consequences of such a scenario? Here are the questions in English: 1. In 1905, how does the military strength of countries such as the United Kingdom, France, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the Kingdom of Italy compare to that of 1914 in OTL? Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? And how would Roosevelt's vision for the post-war world differ from Wilson's? 3. The Russian Empire, after the Russo-Japanese War in OTL, pursued reforms like constitutional monarchy changes and Stolypin’s agricultural reforms. However, in this TL, war breaks out before such reforms happen. What impact do you think this would have on Russia? I believe Russia would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL. However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?

items.model_answer:
If World War I had broken out nine years earlier, in 1905 rather than 1914, it would probably have been a very different war: more favorable to Germany, less globally mobilized, and less likely to produce the exact chain of outcomes that led to the Russian Revolution, Versailles, fascism, and World War II as we know them.

The most plausible spark would have been the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905 or a Balkan crisis involving Austria-Hungary and Russia, not the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Europe already had dangerous alliance structures: Germany and Austria-Hungary were tied together, France and Russia were allied, and Britain had recently reached the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904. But the alliance system was not yet as hardened as it became by 1914. Britain was not as firmly committed to France, Anglo-German rivalry was serious but less intense, and military coordination between Britain and France was less developed. That means a 1905 war might not automatically have become the same full-scale “Triple Entente versus Central Powers” conflict.

Germany would likely have been in a stronger relative position. Russia had just been badly weakened by the Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 Revolution. Its army, navy, finances, and domestic stability were in poor condition. In 1914 Russia was still inefficient but much stronger than in 1905. France, therefore, would have faced Germany with a weaker Russian partner. If Germany attacked France through Belgium, Britain might still have entered the war to defend Belgian neutrality, but British involvement would have been less certain and probably slower. If Britain stayed neutral, France would have been in grave danger.

The war itself would probably have been less technologically advanced but still extremely deadly. Machine guns, rapid-fire artillery, rail mobilization, barbed wire, and modern rifles already existed, so it would not have been a purely nineteenth-century war. However, aircraft, tanks, poison gas, advanced submarines, and the enormous shell-production systems of 1914–1918 were either absent or immature. The conflict might have been somewhat more mobile at first, but trench warfare could still have emerged if offensives failed. The great difference is that governments and economies were less prepared for a long “total war,” so political pressure for a negotiated peace might have come sooner.

A German victory would have been more likely than in 1914, especially if Britain did not intervene decisively. Germany might have defeated France quickly, imposed indemnities or colonial concessions, and strengthened its dominance in continental Europe. Russia, already unstable in 1905, might have been forced into humiliation, deeper revolution, or major internal reform. Austria-Hungary might have survived longer under German protection, though its ethnic tensions would not have disappeared.

If Britain did enter, the war could still have widened into a major European and imperial conflict, but the balance would be different. Britain’s navy was still superior, and Germany’s dreadnought challenge had not yet fully developed. A British blockade would have hurt Germany, but Germany’s submarine campaign would have been far less effective than in the later war. The United States would almost certainly have remained neutral; in 1905 it was less prepared and less politically inclined to intervene in a European war.

The biggest long-term change is that the familiar twentieth century would likely not unfold the same way. A 1905 war would probably not produce the exact conditions of 1917–1919: no identical Russian Revolution, no Versailles settlement in the same form, no Weimar Republic created by defeat in 1918, and therefore no Nazi rise in the same way. Instead, Europe might have seen either an earlier German-dominated order or a shorter, negotiated war that postponed the great reckoning rather than resolving it.

So, if World War I had occurred nine years earlier, it would likely have been less global, less technologically “total,” and more favorable to Germany. It might have prevented the specific disasters that followed the real First World War, but it would not necessarily have made the twentieth century peaceful. The underlying rivalries—German power, Russian weakness and ambition, French revanchism, British fear of continental domination, and Balkan nationalism—would still have remained.

edus.text: If World War I had broken out nine years earlier, in 1905 rather than 1914,
it would probably have been a very different war:
more favorable to Germany,
less globally mobilized,
and less likely to produce the exact chain of outcomes that led to the Russian Revolution, Versailles, fascism, and World War II as we know them.
The most plausible spark would have been the First Moroccan Crisis of 1905 or a Balkan crisis involving Austria-Hungary and Russia,
not the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand.
Europe already had dangerous alliance structures:
Germany and Austria-Hungary were tied together,
France and Russia were allied,
and Britain had recently reached the Entente Cordiale with France in 1904.
But the alliance system was not yet as hardened as it became by 1914.
Britain was not as firmly committed to France,
Anglo-German rivalry was serious but less intense,
and military coordination between Britain and France was less developed.
That means a 1905 war might not automatically have become the same full-scale “Triple Entente versus Central Powers” conflict.
Germany would likely have been in a stronger relative position.
Russia had just been badly weakened by the Russo-Japanese War and the 1905 Revolution.
Its army, navy, finances, and domestic stability were in poor condition.
In 1914 Russia was still inefficient but much stronger than in 1905.
France, therefore, would have faced Germany with a weaker Russian partner.
If Germany attacked France through Belgium,
Britain might still have entered the war to defend Belgian neutrality,
but British involvement would have been less certain and probably slower.
If Britain stayed neutral,
France would have been in grave danger.
The war itself would probably have been less technologically advanced but still extremely deadly.
Machine guns, rapid-fire artillery, rail mobilization, barbed wire, and modern rifles already existed,
so it would not have been a purely nineteenth-century war.
However, aircraft, tanks, poison gas, advanced submarines, and the enormous shell-production systems of 1914–1918 were either absent or immature.
The conflict might have been somewhat more mobile at first,
but trench warfare could still have emerged if offensives failed.
The great difference is that governments and economies were less prepared for a long “total war,”
so political pressure for a negotiated peace might have come sooner.
A German victory would have been more likely than in 1914, especially if Britain did not intervene decisively.
Germany might have defeated France quickly, imposed indemnities or colonial concessions, and strengthened its dominance in continental Europe.
Russia, already unstable in 1905, might have been forced into humiliation, deeper revolution, or major internal reform.
Austria-Hungary might have survived longer under German protection,
though its ethnic tensions would not have disappeared.
If Britain did enter,
the war could still have widened into a major European and imperial conflict,
but the balance would be different.
Britain’s navy was still superior,
and Germany’s dreadnought challenge had not yet fully developed.
A British blockade would have hurt Germany,
but Germany’s submarine campaign would have been far less effective than in the later war.
The United States would almost certainly have remained neutral;
in 1905 it was less prepared and less politically inclined to intervene in a European war.
The biggest long-term change is that the familiar twentieth century would likely not unfold the same way.
A 1905 war would probably not produce the exact conditions of 1917–1919:
no identical Russian Revolution,
no Versailles settlement in the same form,
no Weimar Republic created by defeat in 1918,
and therefore no Nazi rise in the same way.
Instead, Europe might have seen either an earlier German-dominated order
or a shorter, negotiated war that postponed the great reckoning rather than resolving it.
So, if World War I had occurred nine years earlier,
it would likely have been less global, less technologically “total,” and more favorable to Germany.
It might have prevented the specific disasters that followed the real First World War,
but it would not necessarily have made the twentieth century peaceful.
The underlying rivalries—German power, Russian weakness and ambition, French revanchism, British fear of continental domination, and Balkan nationalism—would still have remained.

items.question: What If A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections
human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. Combine that with the endemic corruption issues that come from twenty years in power, and you've got a recipe for a one term president. A distinct but similar dynamic appears with the coming of Nixon. Nobody believed LBJ about anything by 1968, and that rubbed off on Humphrey, who was (ironically) more upright but much weaker than Johnson, and the Hump never could shake the Credibility Gap issues he inherited. The loss of trust on all fronts created widespread anger and chaos followed in the wake of that anger. Add to that the endemic corruption issues that come from eight years of Kennedy and Johnson, and you've got a recipe for a Nixon win. No surprise, this is basically the exact same setup that takes down Nixon and Ford. What you might notice here is that the personality flaws of the individual in the White House combine with the problems of institutional corruption that arise after years in power to create a scandal unique to the time and place that ends up consuming everyone involved. I would imagine that a Bush I who gets a second term--by *some* miracle--is going to make some similar mistakes to the ones his son made. They had many of the same advisors, after all. Here, Bush I had none of Bush II's cocksure self assurance to distract from whatever Middle East quagmire he drags the US into, and I think he would crash and burn more quickly in terms of public approval. You might imagine a scenario where Clinton's scandals + much better Perot popular vote= an apparent Bush landslide, where Bush makes the error of mistaking his opponents' divisions for his own strength. I won't get into details because it's current politics, but if you want an example of just such an outcome, look at the results of the last UK general election. The bigger question to me is why America would turn to a plutocrat like Rockefeller after 16 years of "Greed is Good."

Okay, the idea is that this story is loosely based on some ideas from other users who wrote their stories*. The general idea is to create a story with some overall meaning using all of this. So, the story is about how, before the 1988 elections, a recession (like the one in the 90s) occurs. This causes Bush to win by a much smaller margin than OTL (301-236 EVs), resulting in the Democrats gaining more seats in the Senate and the House. This leads to Bush panicking, causing him to try to appease both Reaganite Republicans and more moderate Republicans, although I haven't decided what his cabinet would look like. Anyway, because of this, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is delayed until August 18, 1991. Furthermore, Iraq decides to invade the east coast of Saudi Arabia on December 26, 1991, that is, 130 days after the invasion of Kuwait. This leads to larger chain reactions overall, but they are not important at this moment. Two important points should also be added: 1. There were no Yugoslav Wars, therefore Bush was perhaps less concerned about the situation developing in the Balkans and set an earlier deadline (than OTL) for a ceasefire in Iraq, which ended on February 24, 1992. 2. The Iraqi Civil War did not end until 1993, so there was an incentive to be more attentive to the problems of other countries. This resulted in a much more effective Gulf War, and Saddam was overthrown a few days before the coalition reached Baghdad, but these are details. What you're probably wondering is... how did Bush win the 1992 election? Well, it was for several reasons. Like the Gulf War, the fact that the Soviet Union was doing stupid things, that the US was able to recover from the recession thanks to contracts with Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and most importantly, that each and every one of Bill Clinton's sex scandals was revealed. Ultimately, the election ended in a landslide victory for Bush (343-195 EVs). Bush's second term was relatively fruitful**. In foreign policy, he had some relative successes, such as Somalia, and some major successes, such as Rwanda. The economy was booming, and everything was going well. But people were starting to get tired of 16 years of Republican presidency and a Democratic option that wasn't showing it could win 4 elections in a row. Therefore, the Democratic primaries would be an opportunity to determine who could win the 1996 election once and for all. I have a vague idea of who the Democratic candidates might be in the primaries; they would be: ● Jay Rockefeller – He would be the one to win because of his establishment base and because he represents a remnant of the New Deal era, making him the best candidate. ● Henry Cisneros – The surprise candidate of the primaries, someone no one expected to win so many states, even though he's a senator who won the 1990 midterm Senate elections. I think he would come in second or third. ● Jesse Jackson – I'm sure he would see this as the perfect opportunity to run in the 1996 elections. He would run with the rainbow coalition and say that the reason they didn't win the last election was because Bill Clinton was a moderate white Southerner and, above all, a womanizer. Therefore, I see him coming in second or third, but I highly doubt the establishment would want him as their candidate. ● Bill Bradley – He would be the progressive candidate the establishment would prefer over Jackson, but I doubt he would win many states, to be honest. ● Joe Biden - Same as Bradley, but being liberal, not progressive. ● Kent Conrad - Okay, I'd have to justify myself here. I'm actually basing this on some hypothetical 1996 primaries , and I thought it would be interesting and funny to add him as a wildcard candidate. I think he could win Iowa, but I doubt it. In the end, Jay Rockefeller won the primaries, with Jackson and Cisneros coming very close to victory. The Democratic national nomination process ended with Jay Rockefeller as the presidential candidate, and, as happened in the 1988 nomination, a Texan (Henry Cisneros) was chosen, while the protesting defectors voted for Jesse Jackson. The Republican primaries and nomination process is simpler. All the candidates who ran in the 1996 primaries OTL are running ITTL, the difference being that Dan Quayle runs and wins the primary and the Republican nomination. Lamar Alexander came in second in the primaries and became Quayle's running mate. Now, some details I'd like to add are that a) Jesse Jackson would say a few words that would unify all racial demographics in the Rockefeller/Cisneros formula, and Dan Quayle would say something so stupid/racist against Chicanos that it would be repudiated by all centrists; that would be very funny. items.model_answer:
Assuming “Rockefeller” means Senator Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia and the 1996 race is an open contest rather than Bill Clinton seeking reelection, a Rockefeller/Cisneros Democratic ticket would probably defeat a Quayle/Alexander Republican ticket, but by a narrower margin than Clinton/Gore’s real 1996 victory over Dole/Kemp.

Jay Rockefeller would have run as a moderate-to-liberal Democrat with strong credentials on health care, poverty, and social policy, plus personal wealth and establishment credibility. Henry Cisneros, former mayor of San Antonio and Clinton’s HUD secretary, would add urban-policy experience and Latino representation, helping Democrats especially in the Southwest and among Hispanic voters. The ticket would likely emphasize economic stability, welfare reform with a softer edge, health care, education, and continuity with the general direction of the Clinton years, but without Clinton’s personal charisma.

Dan Quayle heading the Republican ticket would be a major liability. Although he had conservative credentials and name recognition as George H. W. Bush’s vice president, by 1996 he was still widely mocked as inexperienced and gaffe-prone. Lamar Alexander as running mate would help somewhat: he was more serious, competent, and associated with education reform and moderate Southern Republicanism. But Alexander probably would not fully neutralize doubts about Quayle at the top of the ticket.

The campaign would likely be less about ideology than competence. Rockefeller would attack Quayle as unready to be president, while Quayle would portray Rockefeller as an out-of-touch liberal heir from one of America’s richest families. Republicans would also likely attack Cisneros over the personal and legal controversies that surrounded him in the mid-1990s. That could damage the Democratic ticket, but probably not enough to make Quayle look like the safer choice.

Regionally, Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely hold most of the Democratic base: the Northeast, the Pacific Coast, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and probably much of the Upper Midwest. Rockefeller would be especially strong in West Virginia and could help in nearby Appalachian or working-class states, though he would not have Clinton’s Southern appeal. Cisneros could help in California, New Mexico, and among Latino voters generally, but Texas would probably still vote Republican.

Quayle/Alexander would likely do better than Dole/Kemp in parts of the South and among social conservatives, and Alexander might help in Tennessee and neighboring states. The GOP would probably carry most of the Great Plains, Mountain West, and Deep South. But Quayle’s weaknesses would make it hard to win enough swing states such as Pennsylvania, Michigan, New Jersey, Wisconsin, or Florida.

A plausible result would be a Democratic victory with something like 300 to 330 electoral votes, rather than Clinton’s real 379. The popular vote might be roughly Rockefeller/Cisneros 49–51%, Quayle/Alexander 42–45%, with Ross Perot or another Reform Party candidate still taking a smaller but meaningful share.

The broader consequences would be significant. Without Clinton’s personal dominance, the Democrats would probably have a less charismatic but more technocratic presidency. A Rockefeller administration might focus more heavily on health care, anti-poverty policy, education, and incremental welfare-state reform. Cisneros could push housing and urban investment higher on the agenda. Republicans, meanwhile, might conclude after a Quayle defeat that the party needed a fresher, more disciplined conservative standard-bearer in 2000, possibly accelerating the rise of George W. Bush or another governor-style Republican.

In short: Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely beat Quayle/Alexander in 1996 because the economy and national mood favored Democrats and because Quayle would be a weak Republican nominee. But the Democratic win would probably be smaller, less personal, and less Southern-based than Clinton’s real-life victory.

edus.text: Assuming “Rockefeller” means Senator Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia and the 1996 race is an open contest rather than Bill Clinton seeking reelection,
a Rockefeller/Cisneros Democratic ticket would probably defeat a Quayle/Alexander Republican ticket,
but by a narrower margin than Clinton/Gore’s real 1996 victory over Dole/Kemp.
Jay Rockefeller would have run as a moderate-to-liberal Democrat with strong credentials on health care, poverty, and social policy,
plus personal wealth and establishment credibility.
Henry Cisneros, former mayor of San Antonio and Clinton’s HUD secretary, would add urban-policy experience and Latino representation,
helping Democrats especially in the Southwest and among Hispanic voters.
The ticket would likely emphasize economic stability, welfare reform with a softer edge, health care, education, and continuity with the general direction of the Clinton years,
but without Clinton’s personal charisma.
Dan Quayle heading the Republican ticket would be a major liability.
Although he had conservative credentials and name recognition as George H. W. Bush’s vice president,
by 1996 he was still widely mocked as inexperienced and gaffe-prone.
Lamar Alexander as running mate would help somewhat:
he was more serious, competent, and associated with education reform and moderate Southern Republicanism.
But Alexander probably would not fully neutralize doubts about Quayle at the top of the ticket.
The campaign would likely be less about ideology than competence.
Rockefeller would attack Quayle as unready to be president,
while Quayle would portray Rockefeller as an out-of-touch liberal heir from one of America’s richest families.
Republicans would also likely attack Cisneros over the personal and legal controversies that surrounded him in the mid-1990s.
That could damage the Democratic ticket,
but probably not enough to make Quayle look like the safer choice.
Regionally, Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely hold most of the Democratic base: the Northeast, the Pacific Coast, Illinois, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and probably much of the Upper Midwest.
Rockefeller would be especially strong in West Virginia
and could help in nearby Appalachian or working-class states,
though he would not have Clinton’s Southern appeal.
Cisneros could help in California, New Mexico, and among Latino voters generally,
but Texas would probably still vote Republican.
Quayle/Alexander would likely do better than Dole/Kemp in parts of the South and among social conservatives,
and Alexander might help in Tennessee and neighboring states.
The GOP would probably carry most of the Great Plains, Mountain West, and Deep South.
But Quayle’s weaknesses would make it hard to win enough swing states such as Pennsylvania, Michigan, New Jersey, Wisconsin, or Florida.
A plausible result would be a Democratic victory with something like 300 to 330 electoral votes,
rather than Clinton’s real 379.
The popular vote might be roughly Rockefeller/Cisneros 49–51%, Quayle/Alexander 42–45%,
with Ross Perot or another Reform Party candidate still taking a smaller but meaningful share.
The broader consequences would be significant.
Without Clinton’s personal dominance,
the Democrats would probably have a less charismatic but more technocratic presidency.
A Rockefeller administration might focus more heavily on health care, anti-poverty policy, education, and incremental welfare-state reform.
Cisneros could push housing and urban investment higher on the agenda.
Republicans, meanwhile, might conclude after a Quayle defeat that the party needed a fresher, more disciplined conservative standard-bearer in 2000,
possibly accelerating the rise of George W. Bush or another governor-style Republican.
In short: Rockefeller/Cisneros would likely beat Quayle/Alexander in 1996
because the economy and national mood favored Democrats
and because Quayle would be a weak Republican nominee.
But the Democratic win would probably be smaller, less personal, and less Southern-based than Clinton’s real-life victory.
