items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?

items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and survived, the history of mountaineering would have changed dramatically, though the broader course of world history probably would not.

The immediate result would have been a huge British triumph. In the 1920s Everest was closely tied to imperial prestige: Britain had failed to reach the North Pole and South Pole first, and Everest had become a symbolic “third pole.” A successful Mallory-Irvine ascent would have been celebrated as one of the great achievements of the British Empire. Mallory, already famous, would likely have become a national hero on the scale later occupied by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay.

It would also mean that the first ascent of Everest occurred nearly thirty years earlier than in our timeline, using far more primitive equipment. That would have transformed perceptions of what was possible in high-altitude climbing. Their success would have validated the use of early oxygen apparatus and the northern route from Tibet. The famous question of whether Mallory and Irvine reached the top before dying would never have become one of mountaineering’s great mysteries.

The 1953 ascent by Hillary and Tenzing would still have been important, but it would not have been the first ascent. It might be remembered instead as the first confirmed postwar ascent, the first ascent from Nepal by the South Col route, or the ascent that reopened Everest to the modern era. Tenzing’s role as a Sherpa climber would still have mattered greatly, but the symbolic breakthrough would have been different: less “humanity conquers Everest for the first time,” more “Everest is climbed again by a new route and a new generation.”

Mallory’s survival could also have influenced later climbing culture. He might have written and lectured extensively, shaping mountaineering ethics and technique. Irvine, only twenty-two, might have become a major figure in expedition engineering or high-altitude climbing. Their account would have provided invaluable details about the Second Step, oxygen use, weather, and human performance near 29,000 feet. If they proved that the Second Step could be climbed with 1920s equipment, later debates about the feasibility of their real-life attempt would never have arisen.

There would likely have been fewer British expeditions obsessively focused on “finishing” Everest in the 1930s, since the main prize would already have been won. However, Everest would not have become easy or routine. The mountain would still have killed many climbers, and Himalayan mountaineering would still have developed slowly because of weather, altitude, politics, and limited access to Tibet and Nepal.

Politically, the achievement would have reinforced British imperial confidence in the interwar period, but it would not have stopped the decline of empire, the rise of nationalist movements, or the coming of World War II. Its effects would have been cultural rather than geopolitical: a powerful myth of British courage and endurance, added to the heroic memory of the First World War generation.

In short, if Mallory and Irvine had summited and survived, they would be remembered as the undisputed first conquerors of Everest, the 1953 Hillary-Tenzing ascent would lose its “first ascent” status, and the mythology of Everest would center on a 1924 imperial-era triumph rather than a postwar Commonwealth achievement. The biggest change would be in mountaineering history and national symbolism, not in the fundamental trajectory of the twentieth century.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. Rating Indicator ​ Rating Description ​ G ​ General Audiences - All Ages Admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children whether viewing together with parents or by themselves. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. R ​ Restricted - Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them with proper legal identification at the box office. NC-17 ​ Adults Only - No One 17 Years And Under Admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not legally admitted and all adults must have legal identification at the box office. With the Film Rating System in place to ensure film producers and film distributors have the creative freedom to pursue the projects they want to make, there could be other ways for the Legion of Decency and various religion and social rights groups could clean up Hollywood for film, radio and eventually television without hampering creative freedom. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. Entertainment, education and information fit for religious viewers. They would take in the various technological and artistic talents and know-how from the secular Hollywood studios and apply them towards delivering motion pictures (narrative feature and even the documentaries) with high production standards and quality to deliver their messages to the masses while showing religion on the side of freedom versus tyranny. This would also filter down to local radio stations (and eventually television stations starting in the late 1940s) that would choose to become affiliates of the religious non-denominational Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) which would be listener and eventually viewer-supported to broadcast religious services, national and international news along with news analysis and commentary, local community sports highlights and commentary, charity events, and even motion pictures from the Holy Light library after they finish their original theatrical runs come the advent of television. Local, state and federal non-partisan movements and educational institutions such as colleges, universities, trade schools and public schools would take advantage of the creative and editorial freedoms to organize radio (and eventually television) stations under one coast-to-coast network to provide listener/viewer-supported entertainment/culture, public affairs, educational and community outreach programming for the masses. National Public Radio (NPR) and the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) would both provide alternatives to the commercial broadcast radio (and eventually television) networks found in the American Broadcasting Company (ABC - formerly NBC Blue), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC - formerly NBC Red). All of them would agree, however, that their news reporting standards were to be "factual, fair and without bias" and any commentary and analysis from a partisan political viewpoint should be "clearly defined as such". While NPR and TBN were listener and eventually viewer-supported from the beginning; ABC, CBS and NBC would ensure that commercial time would be limited during hours when children and teenagers would be most likely to be tuning in. The commercial networks would choose to give fair and equal time, coverage and analysis of viewpoints and educational/informative programs to keep up with NPR and TBN's higher standards. However, there was another effect of the Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio decision - the major movie studios could not buy and own the cinema companies that their films would be released to. This would be an antitrust compromise with the governments so that no corporate body could block the release of a film in a release slot that could pose a risk to another company's releases. What would the ripple effects of all this combined be on the motion picture and radio studios and distributors of the time (20th Century-Fox, Columbia, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Paramount, RKO, Republic, United Artists, Universal, Walt Disney and Warner Brothers) on the content in the films they would release to the public? How might some of your favorite films and other pop culture installments from the early 20th Century and beyond have gone if all their makers and distributors were given maximum creative freedom within reason to make what they wanted to? Feel free to discuss this entire ATL in the comments.

items.model_answer:
If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had received strong First Amendment and union protections much earlier in the twentieth century, American mass culture would probably have become more politically open, more artistically experimental, and less dominated by a few corporate gatekeepers. But it would not simply have become free or egalitarian; market pressure, racism, sexism, advertiser power, and anti-radical politics would still have mattered.

For film, the biggest change would have been the weakening or possible prevention of the studio-era censorship system. In actual history, the Supreme Court held in 1915 that motion pictures were not fully protected speech, which helped justify state and local censorship boards. Hollywood responded with self-censorship, culminating in the Production Code, or Hays Code, which restricted sex, profanity, interracial relationships, homosexuality, criticism of religion, sympathetic criminals, and many forms of political radicalism. If film had been clearly protected by the First Amendment from the 1910s or 1920s, local censorship boards would have had less power, and the studios would have had less incentive to impose such a strict national code. American movies might have addressed labor conflict, racial violence, sexuality, abortion, queer life, police corruption, and political repression decades earlier and more openly.

That said, studios still would have self-censored to protect profits. Catholic organizations, Protestant reformers, women’s clubs, segregationists, and local politicians could still organize boycotts. The major studios, seeking national distribution, would still avoid controversy in many cases. So the result would not have been a fully “modern” cinema in the 1920s. But the line between mainstream and independent film would likely have shifted: more adult dramas, political films, and formally experimental work might have survived inside commercial cinema rather than being pushed to the margins.

Earlier union protections would also have changed Hollywood labor. Actors, writers, directors, animators, technicians, and extras would have had a stronger position sooner against the studio system. Contracts might have been less coercive, working hours safer, credits more reliable, and residuals or profit participation negotiated earlier—especially once radio and then television created new markets for reused performances and scripts. A stronger labor movement in Hollywood could also have made the anti-communist blacklist harder to impose in the late 1940s and 1950s. It probably would not have eliminated red-baiting, but studios would have found it harder to quietly fire writers, actors, and directors for political association if unions and courts had already established stronger protections.

For comics, earlier First Amendment protection would likely have prevented or softened the moral panic that led to the 1954 Comics Code Authority. In real history, horror, crime, romance, and socially critical comics were pushed out or sanitized after Senate hearings and industry self-regulation. If comics had been recognized early as protected expression rather than disposable juvenile material, publishers would have been less vulnerable to censorship campaigns. The medium might have developed “adult” genres much earlier: political satire, horror, memoir, war criticism, erotic humor, and literary comics could have become mainstream by the 1940s or 1950s rather than gaining legitimacy much later.

Union protections in comics would have been especially important for creators. Many early comic-book writers and artists worked under harsh work-for-hire conditions, often losing control over characters that became enormously profitable. If unions had formed earlier and been legally protected, creators such as Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster, Jack Kirby, Bill Finger, and many others might have received better credit, royalties, health benefits, and bargaining power. The superhero industry might still have existed, but ownership and compensation would likely have been less one-sided. There may also have been a larger independent or creator-owned comics sector much earlier.

Broadcasting would have changed in a more complicated way. Radio and later television were regulated under the idea that the public airwaves were scarce and that license holders had public obligations. If broadcasters had received stronger First Amendment protection much earlier, federal agencies would have had less authority to police content in the name of morality, balance, or “public interest.” Labor, socialist, Black, immigrant, religious minority, and other dissident voices might have found more room on radio in the 1920s and 1930s, especially if union and community broadcasters were also protected.

But stronger First Amendment protection for broadcasters could have cut both ways. It might have reduced government censorship, but it might also have weakened public-interest regulation meant to prevent monopoly or require balanced coverage. Large networks and advertisers could still have dominated access to the airwaves. Earlier broadcasting freedom might therefore have produced a more open political culture in some respects, but also a more commercialized and possibly more partisan one.

The combined effect across film, comics, and broadcasting would have been a faster maturation of American popular culture. Themes that emerged publicly in the 1960s and 1970s—civil rights, sexual freedom, antiwar politics, feminist critique, queer identity, distrust of police and government, and sympathy for outsiders—might have appeared in mass media decades earlier. American audiences would have encountered a broader range of social realities before the postwar period, and the divide between “high art” and “popular culture” might have weakened sooner.

Politically, earlier protections could have strengthened democratic debate. Mass media would have been harder to use as a tightly managed instrument of moral conformity. Labor movements, civil rights organizations, antiwar activists, and minority communities might have had better access to cultural production and distribution. The Red Scare and Cold War consensus would probably still have happened, but they would have faced stronger legal and institutional resistance.

Economically, the entertainment industries might have been less centralized. Stronger unions and creator rights would have raised costs for studios, networks, and publishers, but also created more stable professional careers. Some companies might have produced less material or taken fewer risks financially, but creators would have had more leverage and more incentive to innovate. The studio system, comics publishers, and radio networks would still have sought control, but they would have had to negotiate more often with organized creative labor.

The most likely overall result is not a radically liberated twentieth-century media landscape, but an earlier and broader opening. American film would have become more adult sooner; comics would have avoided decades of infantilization; broadcasting would have allowed more dissenting voices; and creative workers would have had greater power over their labor and intellectual contributions. The United States would probably have developed a more pluralistic, contentious, and politically self-aware popular culture earlier in the century.

items.question: What If the Haber process is never invented?
human_answers: there are very very very few inventions that are so dependent on one person or group or situation that they wont get invented without them. Frankly i am not sure i can think of any. Yes it may get delayed but never invented? seams doubtful Now this isn't my area of expertise but. Usually when it is time to railroad you can pretty much count n somene inventing and building a railroad. This is why we often get similar inventions in multiple locations. Even back in the day a lot of inventions that get credited to one country and that other counties then “stole them” probably had more then a few cases of contry B finally get to the same level of knowledge in that area and this leads to someone figuring it out. The differencecis that as we get to more modern times the knowledges of 1st world countries gets closer and closer and spreads thoughout . This is why things like nuclear science, jet engines and radar were all “sort of” being looked at in multiple countries with a relatively short time span. So unless there are some very unusual circumstances odds are someone will eventually figure it out.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.

items.model_answer:
If the Haber process were never invented, the modern world would be smaller, hungrier, less industrially agricultural, and probably less able to wage long industrial wars.

The key reason is nitrogen. Plants need fixed nitrogen, but most atmospheric nitrogen is unusable by crops. Before Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis, societies got usable nitrogen from manure, crop rotation with legumes, guano, Chilean nitrate deposits, and a few expensive industrial methods such as electric-arc fixation. Those sources were valuable but limited. The Haber process made it possible to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia cheaply and at enormous scale, which then made modern nitrogen fertilizer possible.

Without it, 20th-century agricultural yields would have been much lower. The Green Revolution would either not happen or would be far less successful, because high-yield wheat, rice, and maize varieties depend heavily on synthetic fertilizer. Food would be more expensive, famines more frequent, and meat production much lower because feeding livestock requires large amounts of fertilized grain and forage. Global population would likely be far below today’s level; not because billions would suddenly die, but because over the century food constraints would raise mortality, lower fertility, slow urbanization, and limit economic growth. A world without industrial ammonia could plausibly have several billion fewer people by the 21st century.

There would also be major geopolitical effects. Germany’s ability to keep fighting in World War I depended heavily on synthetic ammonia, because the British blockade cut off access to Chilean nitrates needed for explosives and fertilizer. Without Haber-Bosch, Germany might have faced a munitions and food crisis much earlier, making World War I shorter or forcing very different military strategy. More broadly, countries with nitrate deposits, guano islands, or strong manure-based agricultural systems would become more strategically important.

Agriculture would look very different. More land would be devoted to legumes, pasture, and green manure crops simply to maintain soil fertility. Human and animal waste would be recycled more aggressively. Cities might be designed around nutrient recovery rather than treating sewage as waste. There would be much more pressure to cultivate marginal land, likely causing more deforestation and habitat loss in some places, even though total population and consumption would be lower.

Environmentally, the result would be mixed. The world would have far less nitrogen runoff, fewer algal blooms and dead zones, less nitrate-contaminated groundwater, and lower nitrous oxide emissions from fertilizer use. Fossil fuel consumption by the fertilizer industry would also be lower. But the need to compensate with more farmland, guano extraction, and intensive manure use could create other ecological damage.

The biggest caveat is that if “the Haber process” specifically were never invented, some alternative synthetic nitrogen technology might eventually replace it. Scientists knew that fixed nitrogen was a critical bottleneck, so enormous effort would have gone into electric-arc fixation, calcium cyanamide, biological nitrogen fixation, or some other catalytic ammonia route. In that case, the main effect might be a delay of decades rather than permanent absence. But if no similarly cheap industrial nitrogen fixation ever appears, the modern high-population, high-yield, fertilizer-dependent world simply does not emerge.

edus.text: If the Haber process were never invented,
the modern world would be smaller, hungrier, less industrially agricultural, and probably less able to wage long industrial wars.
The key reason is nitrogen.
Plants need fixed nitrogen,
but most atmospheric nitrogen is unusable by crops.

Before Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis, societies got usable nitrogen from manure, crop rotation with legumes, guano, Chilean nitrate deposits, and a few expensive industrial methods such as electric-arc fixation.
Those sources were valuable
but limited.
The Haber process made it possible to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia cheaply and at enormous scale,
which then made modern nitrogen fertilizer possible.
Without it, 20th-century agricultural yields would have been much lower.
The Green Revolution would either not happen or would be far less successful,
because high-yield wheat, rice, and maize varieties depend heavily on synthetic fertilizer.
Food would be more expensive,
famines more frequent,
and meat production much lower
because feeding livestock requires large amounts of fertilized grain and forage.
Global population would likely be far below today’s level;
not because billions would suddenly die,
but because over the century food constraints would raise mortality, lower fertility, slow urbanization, and limit economic growth.
A world without industrial ammonia could plausibly have several billion fewer people by the 21st century.
There would also be major geopolitical effects.
Germany’s ability to keep fighting in World War I depended heavily on synthetic ammonia,
because the British blockade cut off access to Chilean nitrates needed for explosives and fertilizer.
Without Haber-Bosch, Germany might have faced a munitions and food crisis much earlier,
making World War I shorter or forcing very different military strategy.
More broadly, countries with nitrate deposits, guano islands, or strong manure-based agricultural systems would become more strategically important.
Agriculture would look very different.
More land would be devoted to legumes, pasture, and green manure crops simply to maintain soil fertility.
Human and animal waste would be recycled more aggressively.
Cities might be designed around nutrient recovery rather than treating sewage as waste.
There would be much more pressure to cultivate marginal land,
likely causing more deforestation and habitat loss in some places,
even though total population and consumption would be lower.
Environmentally, the result would be mixed.
The world would have far less nitrogen runoff, fewer algal blooms and dead zones, less nitrate-contaminated groundwater,
and lower nitrous oxide emissions from fertilizer use.
Fossil fuel consumption by the fertilizer industry would also be lower.
But the need to compensate with more farmland, guano extraction, and intensive manure use could create other ecological damage.
The biggest caveat is that if “the Haber process” specifically were never invented,
some alternative synthetic nitrogen technology might eventually replace it.
Scientists knew that fixed nitrogen was a critical bottleneck,
so enormous effort would have gone into electric-arc fixation, calcium cyanamide, biological nitrogen fixation, or some other catalytic ammonia route.
In that case, the main effect might be a delay of decades rather than permanent absence.
But if no similarly cheap industrial nitrogen fixation ever appears,
the modern high-population, high-yield, fertilizer-dependent world simply does not emerge.

because the British blockade cut off access to Chilean nitrates needed for explosives and fertilizer.
Without Haber-Bosch, Germany might have faced a munitions and food crisis much earlier,
making World War I shorter or forcing very different military strategy.
More broadly, countries with nitrate deposits, guano islands, or strong manure-based agricultural systems would become more strategically important.
Agriculture would look very different.
More land would be devoted to legumes, pasture, and green manure crops simply to maintain soil fertility.
Human and animal waste would be recycled more aggressively.
Cities might be designed around nutrient recovery rather than treating sewage as waste.
There would be much more pressure to cultivate marginal land,
likely causing more deforestation and habitat loss in some places,
even though total population and consumption would be lower.
Environmentally, the result would be mixed.
The world would have far less nitrogen runoff, fewer algal blooms and dead zones, less nitrate-contaminated groundwater,
and lower nitrous oxide emissions from fertilizer use.
Fossil fuel consumption by the fertilizer industry would also be lower.
But the need to compensate with more farmland, guano extraction, and intensive manure use could create other ecological damage.
The biggest caveat is that if “the Haber process” specifically were never invented,
some alternative synthetic nitrogen technology might eventually replace it.
Scientists knew that fixed nitrogen was a critical bottleneck,
so enormous effort would have gone into electric-arc fixation, calcium cyanamide, biological nitrogen fixation, or some other catalytic ammonia route.
In that case, the main effect might be a delay of decades rather than permanent absence.
But if no similarly cheap industrial nitrogen fixation ever appears,
the modern high-population, high-yield, fertilizer-dependent world simply does not emerge.

items.question: What If one people, two nation-states
human_answers: Italy would be easy to do, even with a recent-ish POD: there were proposals floating around in the mid-19th century, concerning Victor Emmanuel II crowning himself king of the Two Sicilies rather than annexing the place outright, while keeping the local government around; since Cavour himself was hesitant to annex the South, and only did so because Garibaldi was becoming too much of a loose cannon, if things had gone slightly differently, this could've happened, and since the South had its own distinct identity and history (even though it used Tuscan as its own official language, as every other state in the peninsula did), this could've stuck, with northern and southern Italy becoming kind of like Australia and New Zealand, independent countries closely tied to each other and under the same monarch. Ironically, the Third War of Independence could've gone better for northern Italy, since northern and southern troops couldn't integrate well IRL, and Italy could've gained Trento and Trieste before World War I, butterflying away the need for intervention; the Two Sicilies could have eventually gained a protectorate of sorts over Albania (history would rhyme there, since Skanderbeg had ties to the Neapolitan royals of his era and fled to Naples when his anti-Turkish uprising failed) and would've surely annexed the Papal enclaves once the north annexes Rome. Garibaldi's OTL expedition to Trento might instead take place in Pola or even Fiume but, as I stated earlier, northern Italy could be more willing to just accept territorial bribes from Austria here, since most of the Irredenta would've been gained already.

Faroese should linguistic be seen as a dialect of Western Norwegian. You could pretty much write Faroese with Nynorsk (the written standard the dialects in this region use) and vice versa. Where Faroese differ from Icelandic is that like Norwegian it have seen near complete replacement of vocabulary with Danish vocabulary thanks to the use of Danish Bibles, while on Iceland the Bible was translated into Icelandic early on and the Danish state supported the existence of a distinct Icelandic language for ideological reasons.. The main reason why Danes and Norwegians have trouble reading Faroese is because it use a it own variation of the Latin alphabet which is different from the one Danes and Norwegians use, while even if Icelandic was written using Danish or the different Norwegian written standards, it would be hard to understand it because of the difference in vocabulary. If the Danish-Norwegian Union had survived the Faroese Island would simply have been seen as part of Western Norway.

If the Prussians had done a better job containing the Great Northern War plague, then there might have been far more Prussian Lithuanians, who differ from Lithuanians in that they are Lutheran, strongly influenced by German culture, and speak a Germanized register of Lithuanian. While they kept the Lithuanian language alive during the Russian repression, the Prussian Lithuanians actually opposed Lithuaniation nationalism and explicitly refused to live in an independent Lithuanian state, accepting nothing else than German rule. Thus, when the Memel Territory was established, the Prussian Lithuanians declared themselves to be "Memellanders". Subsequently, after WW2, the Soviets saw them as Germans and expelled them from East Prussia. IOTL, the GNW plague absolutely decimated the Prussian Lithuanians, who comprised nearly 90% of its victims. Had it been contained effectively, and a butterfly net used afterwards, there would've been far more Prussian Lithuanians in East Prussia, perhaps enough to cause a national awakening. The Soviets likely would've propped up "Prussia" as a separate SSR from Lithuania while still expelling the Germans, and supported Prussian Lithuanian nationalism to divide and conquer (having just annexed resistive Lithuania). Basically Moldovenism, though in this case with genuine religious and cultural differences (plus a very different standard language).
items.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?

items.model_answer:
If one people were divided into two nation-states, the result would be a mismatch between cultural nationhood and political sovereignty. The people might share language, history, religion, or ethnic identity, but live under two separate governments, legal systems, armies, borders, and international alignments.

The main consequence would be a tension between shared identity and separate state interests. Each state might claim to represent the “true” nation, producing rivalry and possible reunification movements, as in divided Germany or Korea. Families, trade, migration, and culture could be disrupted by the border. Over time, however, the two states could also develop distinct political identities: different institutions, education systems, economic models, and foreign alliances could make the populations increasingly different despite common origins.

Whether this arrangement is peaceful depends less on the fact of being “one people” and more on political conditions. It can be stable if both states recognize each other, allow cross-border contact, protect rights, and do not use national unity as a reason for war. It becomes dangerous if one or both states deny the other’s legitimacy, militarize the border, or are backed by rival great powers.

So “one people, two nation-states” is possible, but it challenges the nationalist idea that every people should have exactly one state. It can produce either peaceful plural statehood or a persistent struggle over reunification, depending on institutions, leadership, and international context.

edus.text: If one people were divided into two nation-states,
the result would be a mismatch between cultural nationhood and political sovereignty.
The people might share language, history, religion, or ethnic identity,
but live under two separate governments, legal systems, armies, borders, and international alignments.
The main consequence would be a tension between shared identity and separate state interests.
Each state might claim to represent the “true” nation,
producing rivalry and possible reunification movements,
as in divided Germany or Korea.
Families, trade, migration, and culture could be disrupted by the border.
Over time, however, the two states could also develop distinct political identities:
different institutions, education systems, economic models, and foreign alliances could make the populations increasingly different despite common origins.
Whether this arrangement is peaceful depends less on the fact of being “one people” and more on political conditions.
It can be stable
if both states recognize each other, allow cross-border contact, protect rights,
and do not use national unity as a reason for war.
It becomes dangerous
if one or both states deny the other’s legitimacy, militarize the border,
or are backed by rival great powers.
So “one people, two nation-states” is possible,
but it challenges the nationalist idea
that every people should have exactly one state.
It can produce either peaceful plural statehood or a persistent struggle over reunification,
depending on institutions, leadership, and international context.

items.question: What If Reverse Cuba and the Philippines
human_answers: American interest in Cuban had been more or less secured after the Span-Am War, so it'll be difficult for them to justify annexation, which could earn the ire of the Cuban independentists and the Southern States. But the Philippines presented some once in a lifetime opportunity for the US to finally gain their own foothold in the China market, instead of lurking around ports under the jurisdiction of other great powers. In a relatively practical POV, the US didn't need to annex the whole islands. Why waste men and money against the people that's prepared to fight to the last man to preserve their freedom (some historians even claimed that the Fil-Am War was the US first taste of a Vietnam scenario)? They could just let them be, make some economic agreements with them, get some ports, etc. and voila, they've got themselves a permanent presence in the Pacific without too much blood. Heck they could even convince the Brits to recognize the Republic and establish relations hoping to have Germany (or Japan) to back down from doing anything funny (although that may be a long shot).

Well, these few regions can try to secede. The issue is if they can maintain status quo. Malolos Republic controlled the navy or whatsoever left of the Spanish Navy. The government also controlled majority of the population of the Philippines. The Malolos republic can raise 100k men while your local provinces seceding have that same or lower population than the opposing army with your army having no or minimal rifles whatsoever. Your opponents have also better and well educated generals compared to you. You got also the issue of loyalty of your populace if they are more loyal to your seceding province or Malolos Republic. It is simple reality of warfare, you can try but the question is if you can succeed. It is pure imagination that civil war is because some or one provinces seceded. The only way that Civil war will happen is if Luna or Aguinaldo or anyone in the army fights among themselves. Or if you got a PoD that will butterfly away anything the resembles OTL 1890s Philippines.

Not really. The mood in the US was generally fairly pro-Cuban, and many of the Yellow Journalists of the time were agitating for Cuban independence. Plus, the labor unions in the US were also tied pretty closely to the Cubans. The whole reason the Maine was in Cuba was because the US had much more vested in what happened there than in the Philippines, due to the proximity to Florida. They were very concerned that the violence in the island might damage US investments further, and they were determined that either Cuba would remain Spanish or that Cuba would be in the US sphere somehow. Given that 6 decades later, human civilization nearly ended with a foreign threat got a foothold on that island, that was a fairly prescient concern. The US didn't care much about the Philippines until they managed to sink the Spanish fleet and realized that nothing was stopping them from taking the islands, so they did. So, in summation, if you want the US to annex Cuba and liberate the Philippines, you'd have to change things much earlier than the war.

AHC: Reverse Cuba and the Philippines

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.

items.model_answer:
If the United States had “reversed” its treatment of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War—annexing Cuba while granting the Philippines independence—the biggest result would have been a much more openly Caribbean-focused American empire and a much less direct American role in Asia.

Cuba was geographically close to the United States, economically tied to it, and strategically important for control of the Gulf of Mexico and the future Panama Canal. If Washington had annexed Cuba instead of making it formally independent under the Platt Amendment, Cuba probably would have become something like Puerto Rico: a U.S. territory with limited self-government, heavy American investment, and strong military control. It might eventually have been offered statehood, but that would have been politically difficult because of race, language, party balance, and the power of Cuban sugar interests. More likely, Cuba would have remained a long-term territory or protectorate.

This would have changed Cuban history profoundly. There likely would have been no independent Cuban republic in the same form, no Batista regime in the same way, and probably no 1959 Castro revolution as we know it. But annexation would not necessarily have meant stability. Cuban nationalists had fought Spain for independence, not to become an American colony. A U.S. annexation could have triggered a serious anti-American insurgency, especially if Cuban elites and veterans felt betrayed. Over time, Cuba might have developed politics similar to Puerto Rico’s: divided between statehood, independence, and commonwealth-style autonomy.

For the Philippines, early independence after 1898 would have avoided the Philippine-American War, which in reality killed hundreds of thousands of Filipinos and created deep resentment. Emilio Aguinaldo’s republic or a successor government might have tried to build an independent Filipino state immediately. But it would have faced major problems: regional divisions, weak institutions, landed elites, Muslim resistance in the south, and the threat of foreign powers such as Germany or Japan. The United States would probably still have demanded naval access, commercial privileges, or a protectorate-like relationship, because the Philippines were strategically valuable as a gateway to China.

The major danger for an independent Philippines would have been Japan. Without formal U.S. colonial rule, the Philippines might have been more vulnerable to Japanese pressure or invasion before or during World War II. The United States might still have defended it if it had treaty rights or bases there, but the defense would have been less automatic. Alternatively, Japan might have moved against the islands earlier if they seemed weak and not fully protected by Washington.

For the United States, the reversal would have made its imperialism look different. It would have avoided the costly and morally damaging war of conquest in the Philippines, reducing anti-imperialist criticism at home. But annexing Cuba would have made the U.S. appear more blatantly expansionist in the Americas. Latin American distrust of Washington would likely have intensified even earlier, because Cuba was the symbolic prize of the war against Spain and had been promised freedom under the Teller Amendment.

The broader twentieth century would also change. A U.S.-controlled Cuba would make the Caribbean even more of an American military lake. The Cuban Missile Crisis almost certainly would not happen in the same form, because the Soviet Union would not have had an independent Cuban government to ally with. But if U.S. rule produced a strong Cuban independence movement, Cuba could still become a major Cold War flashpoint—more like Algeria or Vietnam than like Castro’s Cuba.

In short, reversing Cuba and the Philippines would probably mean a U.S. Cuba resembling Puerto Rico, with intense debates over autonomy and statehood, and an earlier independent Philippines that would be freer from American colonial rule but more exposed to regional instability and Japanese imperialism. The United States would be less of a formal Asian colonial power, but more openly an annexationist power in the Caribbean.

items.question: What If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset?
human_answers: That would fall under the bad economics heading. Germany and Italy might well have a good aircraft industry but for something of the Tornado's complexity and expense, they would need partners to spread the burden. Germany previously partnered with Fairchild-Hiller-Republic prior to Panavian efforts and as much as I like the G.91, it isn't really in the Tornado's league. In terms of a precedent for an Italian combat twin, the closest I can get is the PD.808GE which was of course originally a joint-venture between Piaggio and Douglas. If a number of nearby industrial/aerospace powerhouse nations have approximately compatible requirements, not to mention nations that you have other economic partnerships with in mind, why on earth wouldn't you consortium-up? Germany would not be so fiscally inept as to squander the opportunity and go it alone. Why would they choose to build an inferior type that their singular budget would necessitate? I know the popular narrative has Germany as the unwilling partner but much like the recent-ish Typhoon discussion, the narrative isn't bone out by the facts. The reality was Germany studied cheaper, less capable alternatives such as single-seat, fixed wing etc. and then ploughed right on with the full capability. Eminently logical and seemingly blown out of proportion by two generations of media. A simple question. If Germany were errmming and ahhhing so, why is it Panavia GmbH ? I realise that this thread is probably designed to engender responses like: RAF F-15Bs! Yeah, man, cool! Fine as far as it goes but not very probable. From my perspective, the premise is more like what if money, industry and defence stop mattering in Europe in the 1970s and my response is

The Marineflieger simply wanted a replacement for the F-104 but that doesn't matter because as OTL showed, whatever the airforce (both branches) wanted it didn't matter because the politicians decided. As an example of this look at the text below: Spoiler: text At least the VAK 191 would fulfill some of the requirements of the Luftwaffe and the Marineflieger. Both coming in single and two-seat variants, fighter/interceptor configuration and nuclear capable strike bomber. Supersonic and subsonic variants. And if the German aerospace industry lobbies enough, they might see one variant put into production as they actually have an existing product that consumed tons of R&D funds and ended up flying. Well, conventional wisdom showed that the single-seat, single-engine, fixed-wing design ended up outliving the variable-geometry twin-engined two-seater one. Yeah I doubt they were happy with their low-level supersonic strike F-104s and F-4s... The VAK 191 could fulfill the low-level supersonic strike-aircraft role.

IIRC the British Taxpayer paid 48% of the R&D cost of the Tornado IDS and I definitely remember that it paid 100% of the ADV's R&D cost. I don't know if HM Treasury could have paid the other 52% of the R&D cost of the IDS and that's the expensive one because it includes the cost of developing the engines and airframe. If that's correct which defence projects have to be cancelled to pay the difference? Then there's the cost of building them. My guess is that the assembly cost of the aircraft would be the same because they were made in three different factories and the same number of RAF aircraft are built in the same factory IOTL and ITTL. The British factory also built all the IDS and ADV that were exported too. However, the economies of scale for the engines, avionics and the "bits" of the airframe will be lost because the number built will be cut from nearly 1,000 to about 550. A lot fewer aircraft to support may put the operating cost up too by increasing the price of spares. Also the British defence industry may not have enough scientists and engineers to do the R&D on its own. Which may mean it takes longer and costs more. Or other defence projects have to be cancelled so the scientists and engineers can be concentrated on the Tornado IDS. OTOH I've heard people say that collaborative projects cost more and take longer than national projects. That's partially because of the extra layer of bureaucracy and mainly for political reasons. Each nation (naturally) wants its share of the work to be the same as the amount as it pays. That produces a less than optimal distribution of the R&D and production contracts. Or at least a worse distribution than a purely national distribution, as national politics means the best firm for the job doesn't necessarily get the contract either. Is there any truth to that? Or is it a false memory?

items.model_answer:
If West Germany and Italy had withdrawn from the PANAVIA Tornado program at the outset, the Tornado as it actually existed would almost certainly never have been built.

The central reason is cost and scale. The Tornado was viable because Britain, West Germany, and Italy shared development costs, production work, and a large combined order. West Germany was especially important: it was not just a partner but the largest customer, needing a low-level strike and reconnaissance aircraft to replace types such as the F-104 in NATO’s central front role. Italy added further production volume and political-industrial weight. Without those partners, Britain would have been left trying to fund a sophisticated variable-geometry strike aircraft almost alone, only a few years after cancelling TSR-2 and then the F-111K on cost grounds. That would have been politically and financially very difficult.

The most likely outcome is that Britain would either have cancelled the project or drastically reduced it into a smaller, cheaper national aircraft. A purely British “Tornado” would probably have suffered the same fate as TSR-2: rising costs, shrinking orders, Treasury opposition, and eventual cancellation or heavy compromise. The RAF would then have had to extend the lives of existing aircraft such as the Buccaneer, Phantom, Jaguar, and Canberra while looking for foreign alternatives.

For Britain, the practical replacement options would probably have been American or Anglo-French. A renewed purchase of an American strike aircraft—perhaps the F-111 in some form, or later an aircraft such as the F-15E, F-16, or F/A-18—would have become more likely. Alternatively, Britain might have leaned harder on the Jaguar for tactical strike and kept the Buccaneer in service longer, but that would not have fully replaced the Tornado’s low-level, all-weather interdiction capability. The later Tornado ADV interceptor would also not have appeared, so Britain would have had to keep Phantoms longer or buy an imported air-defence fighter.

West Germany and Italy would also have had to find different solutions. West Germany would probably have become more dependent on U.S. aircraft for strike, reconnaissance, and nuclear-delivery missions. It might have bought more Phantoms initially and then moved earlier toward F-16s or another American platform. Italy, with a smaller budget and force requirement, would likely have extended the F-104 even longer and later sought a cheaper mix of F-16s, AMX-type light attack aircraft, or another imported fighter.

The industrial consequences would have been large. PANAVIA, Turbo-Union, the RB199 engine, and the multinational production structure that sustained major parts of British, German, and Italian combat-aircraft industries would either not have existed or would have been much smaller. British Aerospace would have lost one of its most important Cold War programs, while German and Italian firms would have had less experience in advanced combat-aircraft collaboration. That could also have affected later European projects, including Eurofighter, because Tornado created habits of cooperation, work-sharing, and joint procurement that helped make later programs politically possible.

Militarily, NATO in Europe would have been more dependent on U.S. aircraft for deep interdiction and low-level nuclear strike. The Tornado gave European NATO members a capable indigenous all-weather strike aircraft designed specifically for the Central European battlefield. Without it, the force mix would probably have been more fragmented: more Phantoms, Jaguars, F-111s, F-16s, and later other U.S.-supplied types, but no common European strike platform.

So the short answer is: West German and Italian withdrawal at the start would probably have killed the Tornado program. Britain alone was unlikely to sustain it, and NATO air forces would have filled the gap with longer-lived legacy aircraft and more American purchases. The result would have been a weaker European combat-aircraft industrial base, greater dependence on the United States, and no Tornado IDS, ADV, or ECR as known historically.
