items.question: What If No nuclear weapons?
human_answers: As has been noted it is pretty much impossible to avoid having nuclear weapons ever being created. The science is pretty obvious. What CAN be altered, to a degree, is the "when". The U.S. threw a dramatic amount of funding at the effort, along with huge amounts of resources (Manhattan literally built the entire city of Oak Ridge TN to house the workers on the project. It was farmland, with about 3,000 people living in the area then in less than 2 years, it was a city with a population of 75,000. Government just walked in and "acquired" 59,000 acres, evicted everyone in the local farms and villages, and started building a fence (BIG ASS fence). The same thing happened in Washington with Hanford, except it was 500,000 acres and 39,000 people, Just a little less funding, or a project manager less driven than General Groves and the Bomb isn't ready.

Based on the described scenario, the USSR becomes the first country to test a nuclear weapon in the early 1950s, whereupon the US and UK governments demand an explanation for who filed the relevant reports in the wrong section back in 1940. In the case of the US, it's probably Lyman Briggs, who in OTL actually did lock away a key report in his safe without showing it to anyone else, which may have delayed the start of the Manhattan Project by several months. But even then, uranium fission was discovered in France in December 1938. The Einsten-Szilard letter warned the US government of the possibilities in August 1939. The Frisch-Peierls memorandum, the first description of a nuclear weapon, was written in March 1940 for the British government. By Frisch's own description, the work he and Peierls did was straightforward for any competent nuclear physicist. There might be a PoD wherein Frisch and Peierls are interned as enemy aliens and not allowed to work as physicists. Oliphant is focussed on the higher priority radar work, so Thomson's conclusion that it was not worth pursuing a chain reaction in uranium is accepted by the British government. There is therefore no MAUD committee, no report for Briggs to ignore, and no reason for Oliphant to kick things into gear. Instead, what is likely to happen is that eventually someone in the US does ask the questions that Frisch and Peierls asked, and they reach similar answers. Given OTL's trajectory, it's hard to see why that would happen any earlier than August 1941, given that US research was initially largely concerned with power plants rather than weapons. If we say it does, it might take the best part of a year for a US equivalent of the MAUD report to be carried out and an atomic weapons programme started. That puts a US weapons programme without the MAUD input as starting in mid-1942 - so about a six month delay. An arbitrarily longer delay is entirely plausible, but eventually - and probably sooner rather than later - someone is going to ask the right questions, and then things will start moving very quickly.

I do wonder if we don’t get the examples of nuclear destruction at the end of WW2 and if we delay the development of the bombs a bit so that by late 50s to mid 60s they are not quite as destructive as they were in real life if we don’t end up with a nuclear war. There are several reasons why WW3 was avoided. The example of how destructive the first generation bombers were, knowledge that the bombs were getting more powerful. Then the jump in power to the H bomb. Russia knowing that until the advent of ICBM they were behind the U.S. because their bombers sucked. The general aftermath of WW2 and no one really wanting to fight as a result. Russian back propaganda against nuclear weapons. Etc. All of this delay a possible WW3 until the combination of ICBM and drastically More powerful bombs made WW3 really unthinkable. But in a world we’re nuclear weapons are (somehow) drastically delayed we won’t see a lot of this, you are not seeing photos of nuked cities, you are getting 1st gen ICBMs with smaller nukes until h bombs get small enough to fit on ICBMs. Etc. So the taboo of a nuclear war is probably not built up soon enough to prevent a nuclear war. In fact they probably don’t segregate “conventional” war from “nuclear” as soon as we did otl. So we probably do see a WW3. Edited to add: BTW I think it is very unlikely to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1949. And almost impossible to keep nuclear weapons from being developed by 1955. And I thin it would be ASB to push them farther out then that. Physics simply allows for them so once you get the combination of the understanding of physics and the industrial/technical ability to make them you are getting them. And it is not exactly all that high tech to build a gun type nuke. So I just don’t see how you delay the development all that long. You would need the U.S. and the USSR to both come out of WW2 in much much worse shape to the point that they simply can’t afford to build nukes and I don’t see that happening.
items.original_question: What if No nuclear weapons? No Tubes Alloy or Los Alamos, and no German atomic research. Sadly, Japan is invaded - high causalities on both sides especially Japanese civilians much of it from starvation. No organised surrender, just quiet acceptance from district, to town, then the next. Japanese Americans were 'encouraged' to return to the homeland and rebuild - from the stone age! But what happens - with no nuclear umbrella - no ballistic missiles. WMD were confined to the Grandslams & Tallboys, with fuel air explosives via aircraft bombs or short range (V2) missiles. Research was more focused on better guidance for V1 type cruise missiles, and other ASM. Would the Berlin Blockade still happen, would it get hot? How would this affect Defence spending? Where would the focus on the difference between here and OTL?

rubrics.question_focus: What If No nuclear weapons?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Feasibility and Point of Divergence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer treats 'no nuclear weapons' as a constrained counterfactual requiring a plausible mechanism, rather than simply assuming physics or institutions change without explanation.
criteria.1-2: Assumes nuclear weapons never exist with no mechanism, or relies on impossible changes to physics without acknowledging them.
criteria.3-4: Gives a vague reason for nondevelopment but ignores known scientific discoveries and wartime incentives.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible delay mechanism, such as bureaucratic failure or reduced wartime mobilization, but leaves key feasibility issues underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains a credible point of divergence involving Manhattan Project, MAUD, Soviet espionage, funding, or personnel, while noting permanent nondevelopment is unlikely.
criteria.9-10: Precisely distinguishes permanent absence from delayed invention, grounds the divergence in real institutions and scientists, and clearly bounds what the premise can plausibly change.

criteria.name: Scientific and Industrial Causality
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer accounts for the physics, engineering, and industrial requirements that made nuclear weapons difficult but ultimately discoverable.
criteria.1-2: Ignores nuclear science and treats bombs as arbitrary political choices.
criteria.3-4: Mentions uranium or atomic science superficially but misses why discovery would likely recur.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that fission knowledge and industrial capacity matter, but gives only a partial account of enrichment, plutonium, reactors, or bomb design.
criteria.7-8: Connects fission discovery, critical mass reasoning, enrichment/reactor infrastructure, and state resources to likely development timelines.
criteria.9-10: Shows strong causal command of why gun-type and implosion weapons, wartime megaprojects, and postwar superpower capacity make indefinite prevention highly implausible.

criteria.name: World War II and Early Cold War Timeline Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives a coherent alternate timeline for WWII's end, the first successful nuclear program, and early US-UK-Soviet strategic behavior.
criteria.1-2: Produces a timeline that conflicts with basic WWII chronology or gives no sequence of events.
criteria.3-4: Mentions WWII or the Cold War but with major gaps or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Sketches plausible changes to Hiroshima/Nagasaki, Japan's surrender, or Soviet development, but lacks integration across actors.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent sequence linking delayed Manhattan work, Soviet/UK/US programs, espionage, Japan, and early Cold War military planning.
criteria.9-10: Builds a tightly reasoned timeline with actor-specific incentives, technological bottlenecks, and plausible dates for delayed or first nuclear tests.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and Strategic Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of major downstream consequences, especially deterrence, nuclear taboo formation, conventional war incentives, arms races, alliances, and possible WWIII risk.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'no Hiroshima' or gives simplistic utopian/apocalyptic outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Identifies one downstream effect but ignores deterrence, Cold War strategy, and military substitution.
criteria.5-6: Covers several effects, such as conventional warfare, superpower rivalry, or arms racing, but mechanisms are uneven.
criteria.7-8: Explains how absence or delay affects deterrence, taboo formation, bomber/ICBM strategy, NATO-Warsaw tensions, and risk of major war.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced long-range chain showing how delayed weapons could either reduce early nuclear trauma or increase conventional/nuclear escalation risk, with multiple interacting mechanisms.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles uncertainty honestly, avoids overclaiming, and maintains internal consistency across the counterfactual chain.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or ignores the speculative nature of the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Uses some cautious language but contains major unsupported certainties or inconsistent assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and alternative paths, though some claims remain overconfident or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while keeping assumptions consistent over decades.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous uncertainty calibration, explicitly flags branch points, avoids hidden contradictions, and explains why some outcomes are more plausible than others.

items.model_answer:
If nuclear weapons had never existed, the world would likely have been less at risk of sudden civilization-ending catastrophe, but not necessarily more peaceful. The main difference is that great-power war after 1945 would have been more thinkable.

In World War II, Japan probably still would have surrendered, but the path could have been much bloodier. Without the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the United States would likely have continued conventional firebombing, naval blockade, and preparations for invasion. Soviet entry into the war against Japan would still have mattered greatly. Japan’s surrender might have come after more destruction, famine, or a negotiated shift around the emperor’s status. The war could have ended later and with higher Japanese, American, Soviet, and civilian casualties.

After 1945, the biggest change would be the Cold War. Nuclear weapons made direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union terrifyingly risky. Without them, NATO and the Warsaw Pact might have been more willing to fight a large conventional war in Europe, especially during crises such as Berlin, Korea, Cuba, or later confrontations. A Third World War would have been more plausible. It would not have destroyed humanity instantly, but it could have killed tens of millions through conventional bombing, invasion, famine, chemical or biological weapons, and economic collapse.

The Korean War and Vietnam War might also have unfolded differently. Nuclear weapons helped set limits: leaders feared escalation. Without that ceiling, major powers might have intervened more directly with conventional forces. China, the Soviet Union, and the United States could have been more willing to test each other militarily. Some wars might have expanded rather than remaining “limited.”

On the other hand, many countries would not have pursued nuclear deterrents, so there would be no nuclear arms race, no Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it, no fear of accidental nuclear launch, no nuclear proliferation crises involving India, Pakistan, Israel, North Korea, or Iran, and no long-term risk of terrorists acquiring a nuclear device. The immense resources spent on nuclear arsenals might have gone to conventional forces, space programs, welfare, infrastructure, or other military technologies.

But the absence of nuclear weapons would not remove the underlying causes of war: nationalism, ideology, territorial disputes, fear, imperial decline, resource competition, and regime insecurity. States would likely compensate with larger conventional armies and perhaps more chemical, biological, cyber, or precision-strike weapons. The taboo against weapons of mass destruction might be weaker or might attach instead to chemical and biological warfare.

Nuclear energy would also be affected depending on the exact counterfactual. If nuclear physics still existed but weapons were never developed, civilian nuclear power might still emerge, perhaps with stricter international control. If nuclear fission itself were impossible, the world would rely even more on coal, oil, gas, hydro, and renewables. That could mean higher carbon emissions unless renewables and efficiency developed faster.

Overall, a world without nuclear weapons would probably have less existential risk from instant nuclear annihilation, but a higher chance of direct great-power conventional wars. Nuclear weapons have been horrifyingly dangerous, but they also created a powerful deterrent against total war between major powers. So the counterfactual is not simply “a safer world.” It is more likely a world with fewer apocalyptic standoffs, but possibly more large wars.

edus.text: If nuclear weapons had never existed,
the world would likely have been less at risk of sudden civilization-ending catastrophe,
but not necessarily more peaceful.
The main difference is that great-power war after 1945 would have been more thinkable.
In World War II, Japan probably still would have surrendered,
but the path could have been much bloodier.
Without the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the United States would likely have continued conventional firebombing, naval blockade, and preparations for invasion.
Soviet entry into the war against Japan would still have mattered greatly.
Japan’s surrender might have come after more destruction, famine, or a negotiated shift around the emperor’s status.
The war could have ended later and with higher Japanese, American, Soviet, and civilian casualties.
After 1945, the biggest change would be the Cold War.
Nuclear weapons made direct war between the United States and the Soviet Union terrifyingly risky.
Without them, NATO and the Warsaw Pact might have been more willing to fight a large conventional war in Europe,
especially during crises such as Berlin, Korea, Cuba, or later confrontations.
A Third World War would have been more plausible.
It would not have destroyed humanity instantly,
but it could have killed tens of millions through conventional bombing, invasion, famine, chemical or biological weapons, and economic collapse.
The Korean War and Vietnam War might also have unfolded differently.
Nuclear weapons helped set limits:
leaders feared escalation.
Without that ceiling, major powers might have intervened more directly with conventional forces.
China, the Soviet Union, and the United States could have been more willing to test each other militarily.
Some wars might have expanded rather than remaining “limited.”
On the other hand, many countries would not have pursued nuclear deterrents,
so there would be no nuclear arms race,
no Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it,
no fear of accidental nuclear launch,
no nuclear proliferation crises involving India, Pakistan, Israel, North Korea, or Iran,
and no long-term risk of terrorists acquiring a nuclear device.
The immense resources spent on nuclear arsenals might have gone to conventional forces, space programs, welfare, infrastructure, or other military technologies.
But the absence of nuclear weapons would not remove the underlying causes of war:
nationalism, ideology, territorial disputes, fear, imperial decline, resource competition, and regime insecurity.
States would likely compensate with larger conventional armies
and perhaps more chemical, biological, cyber, or precision-strike weapons.
The taboo against weapons of mass destruction might be weaker
or might attach instead to chemical and biological warfare.
Nuclear energy would also be affected depending on the exact counterfactual.
If nuclear physics still existed but weapons were never developed,
civilian nuclear power might still emerge,
perhaps with stricter international control.
If nuclear fission itself were impossible,
the world would rely even more on coal, oil, gas, hydro, and renewables.
That could mean higher carbon emissions
unless renewables and efficiency developed faster.
Overall, a world without nuclear weapons would probably have less existential risk from instant nuclear annihilation,
but a higher chance of direct great-power conventional wars.
Nuclear weapons have been horrifyingly dangerous,
but they also created a powerful deterrent against total war between major powers.
So the counterfactual is not simply “a safer world.”
It is more likely a world with fewer apocalyptic standoffs,
but possibly more large wars.

items.question: What If the USSR was leaked information about OB just before it happened and were thus better prepared and more competent in 1941? (No strike though)
human_answers: A couple days or weeks isn’t really enough if you’re going with the “Stalin finally makes a good decision” scenario. You need at least a couple months to have the Soviets dug in and prepared at more defensible spots further east than iotl, and considering the German initial manpower advantage (to say nothing of the purges creating widespread incompetence in the red army and said incompetence making their logistics horrible), they still probably lose pretty hard, although not quite as much as iotl. I think at least 6 or so (probably a bit more) months is needed to help close the manpower gap and create a Minsk-Kiev line that the Germans can’t penetrate if you don’t want Soviet losses to be seen as proportionally a lot bigger (though there’s a strong chance they still are in this scenario, just not enough to give the impression that all you need to do is kick in the rotten door enough and it’ll fall).

The Soviet Union possessed highly precise intelligence indicating that the German military's logistics were insufficient to sustain a protracted war and that its armaments factories had not yet shifted to a wartime footing. (This intelligence was derived from the infiltration of German industry by communist sympathizers.) Hitler also couldn't been so foolish as to believe that the mighty Soviet Union could be conquered within three months—at least, no analyst would have dared to venture such an insulting conjecture. Consequently, the less reliable intelligence from military and western country must have been false, and war is in next year. This chain of logic is remarkably robust; You cannot convince the Soviets that Germany is about to attack without introducing collateral changes—and different changes would inevitably lead to different outcomes in the war. Would they perceive their own military as weaker? Would they place their trust in Anglo-American intelligence while disregarding the Comintern’s own network? Or would they have managed to plant exceptionally reliable spies deep within the German military itself? Each of these scenarios would necessitate a distinct defensive strategy, thereby altering the very trajectory of the conflict. One thing, however, remains certain: if the Soviet Union were to lose the war while the United States remained an active belligerent, the Americans would undoubtedly drop the nuclear bomb.

I don't think there's an obvious way for the USSR to react to knowing war is coming. The Germans were much more ready for war. The USSR reaction will probably be a more planned withdrawal in the earliest days of the conflict, blowing some bridges behind their retreat, getting troops out of the pockets where they were surrounded and surrendered. Also less of the air force blown up on the ground in the opening days of the war. A better USSR reaction to Barbarossa might mean, 5,000 planes destroyed on the ground, 500,000 less troops taken as prisoners of war and a German advance that is stopped 100 miles from Moscow. That would probably look disasterous to the USSR and to historians looking backwards but would be a massive improvement over our time line. That said I've no idea how things would progress through the war. There's a lot of decisions to be made. I suspect the Germans might balance a stronger Soviet advance by putting more troops on that front which might make things easier on the Western front. No one really knows. Theres a long war and its all possibilities only.

As noted this ultimately may be worse for the USSR (but probably not) As Stalin had pretty well decimated his military command, So you have a lot of folks that either are no good at the job or have to little experience at the job or both. And if they know it is coming they may as noted by others be more forward deployed and more “aggressive” so they may not fall back as much. A good part of the beginning of the war for the USSR was the learning curve and while they were getting their butt kicked early on this did give them practice that they slowly implemented. In effect trading territory for “reduced” casualties. Compared to how bad they would have been clobbered if the tried to hold the liner harder the OTL. This is obviously exchanged for not getting surprised in this timeline. The question is which did more damage to the USSR the poor leadership needing time to find better officers or to at least get some learning in or the surprise? I tend to think it is a very minor advantage to the USSR to know ahead of time. But I think the poor leadership will mean that 90% of the advantages they get from not being surprised is tossed out the window by leadership that doesn’t know what it is doing. I suspect you will see more troops over run or surrender or otherwise forced to surrender as the order to not retreat will comedown and that there will be bigger battles sooner and closer to Germanies support system any anything that results in Germany have a shorter support line while still getting yo fight big battle vs the zuSSR is probably an improvement for Germany. Plus the war will be fought “faster” if the USSR is less inclined to pull back so the two don’t spend as much time traveling (retreating/advancing). So they are probably bigger battles sooner and more troops committed vs falling back so Germany by should able to kill more Russians faster. That being said it still ultimately sees Germany grind to a halt and it will see the USSR build enough troops and equipment and what have you to stop Germany so Germany will ultimately do better in terms of inflicting casualties on the USSR but they won’t get as far into the USSR. One thing I don’t know is if this fighting closer to the border will result in the German advance stoping before it gets so close that the USSR has to move its factories. Not moving a factory or two could make a big difference.

Again, as usual these scenarios entirely depend on one or both sides failing to react to changing circumstances. Firstly, USSR had information about possibility of German attack and was reacting. 'Stalin refused to believe the intelligence' is basically a myth. Soviet problem was not lack of the information or anyone's willingness or unwillingness 'to believe'. Soviet problem was lack of definitive information because everything that they had on Barbarossa was either utterly wrong, contaminated with enough false intelligence to make discerning what is true and what is not quite impossible or simply arrived too late for any sort of meaningful reaction. Secondly, USSR primary issue was that Germans at any point of preparation to Barbarossa were in position to speed these preparations up if they see an obvious Soviet reaction . And Germans were positioned to attack better than Soviets were positioned to defend. Let's say USSR starts mobilizing mid-April. Germany will not wait until June 22nd to attack because reality is not Hearts of Iron 4 game on a historical rails. Germans will simply attack in May before Soviet mobilization finishes. And yes, it could screw Mussolini by preventing Germany from bailing him out, but it was simple question of Germany already having mobilized army and having a better logistical infrastructure on their side of the border, so whatever obvious thing Soviets would do, Germans will have an opportunity to react. P.S. And no, Stalin will not give orders to pre-emptive attack against Germany for the very same reasons. Red Army was not in the position to attack anyone and everyone in Soviet leadership, including Stalin knew about that.

(But they don't do a preemptive strike though. This question is not about that. Thats a whole different story) 1)Would this lead to an earlier Soviet victory in WW2? Could the USSR gobble up more of theBalkans and potentially more of Germany and perhaps parts of Italy and entire Greece? 1.2)How much sooner could the USSR relalistically win due to this? OR 2)Could this actually lead to a better German performance as the USSR initially performs better but this means that the more decisive battles are fought closer to German soil which leads to Hitler paradoxically winning the war? criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity and feasibility of Soviet reaction
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the scenario: the USSR receives credible information about Operation Barbarossa shortly before it begins, becomes somewhat better prepared and competent in 1941, but does not launch a preemptive strike.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise, assumes a Soviet first strike, ignores the timing, or treats the leak as irrelevant or magical.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges warning but gives vague or implausible Soviet reactions with little attention to Stalin’s prior skepticism or short lead time.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that days or weeks of warning allow limited improvements but not full transformation of Soviet readiness.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes effects of different warning windows and explains why preparation is constrained by command, logistics, and politics.
criteria.9-10: Precisely handles the no-strike premise, credibility problem, Stalinist decision-making, and realistic limits on what can change before June 1941.

criteria.name: Coverage of Soviet military mechanisms in 1941
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains concrete ways Soviet preparation and competence could alter the opening phase of Barbarossa.
criteria.1-2: Offers only broad claims such as 'the USSR does better' with no military mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few generic improvements but not how they affect the campaign.
criteria.5-6: Covers plausible measures such as dispersing aircraft, alerting troops, evacuating supplies, or avoiding some encirclements.
criteria.7-8: Connects Soviet measures to specific effects: fewer prisoners, less aircraft loss, better withdrawals, bridge demolitions, defense in depth, and delayed German advances.
criteria.9-10: Deeply integrates Soviet manpower, purges, command competence, rail logistics, mobilization timing, frontier deployments, and defensible fallback lines.

criteria.name: German operational constraints and adaptive response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for German strengths, limitations, and possible reactions to a better-prepared USSR.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Germany as either effortlessly defeated or omnipotent, ignoring actual 1941 operational realities.
criteria.3-4: Mentions German superiority or logistics only superficially.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes German initial advantages and logistical limits while explaining that Soviet preparation likely reduces but does not erase early losses.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes effects on key dynamics such as encirclements, pace of advance, supply strain, air losses, Minsk/Kiev/Smolensk/Moscow, and German redeployment choices.
criteria.9-10: Balances Wehrmacht tactical-operational competence against strategic overreach, showing how German plans might adapt and where they remain structurally vulnerable.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream war outcomes
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the coherence of the projected consequences beyond the opening weeks, including the Eastern Front, Allied strategy, and the wider war.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to an unsupported ending, such as instant Soviet victory or guaranteed German conquest.
criteria.3-4: Gives a short-term outcome but little explanation of how the war develops afterward.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible medium-term trajectory, such as reduced Soviet losses, a slower German advance, or Moscow being less threatened.
criteria.7-8: Extends the chain coherently into 1942 and beyond, considering attrition, mobilization, Lend-Lease, German force allocation, and Western Allied implications.
criteria.9-10: Builds a nuanced long-range scenario with contingent branches, showing how early Soviet improvements reshape but do not mechanically determine the entire war.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, evidence use, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer expresses appropriate uncertainty, avoids internal contradictions, and grounds claims in the historical context of Barbarossa.

criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but makes overconfident or contradictory claims.
criteria.5-6: Uses cautious language and mostly plausible historical assumptions, with minor gaps or unsupported numbers.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely, possible, and speculative outcomes while avoiding contradictions with the no-strike and short-warning constraints.

items.model_answer:
If the USSR received credible, detailed information about Operation Barbarossa shortly before 22 June 1941 and Stalin actually acted on it, the invasion would still be extremely dangerous, but the opening catastrophe would likely be much less severe.

The biggest change would be in the first days. Historically, Soviet units on the western frontier were caught in a confused half-peace, half-war posture. Aircraft were parked wingtip-to-wingtip, ammunition and fuel were poorly distributed, communications were fragile, commanders were afraid to act without permission, and many forward armies were positioned in ways that made them vulnerable to encirclement. If Moscow had accepted the leak as real, the USSR could have quietly put frontier forces on alert, dispersed aircraft, loaded ammunition, prepared demolitions, moved headquarters, activated air defenses, and warned commanders to expect immediate German attack.

That alone would probably prevent one of the worst historical disasters: the destruction of much of the Soviet air force on the ground. The Luftwaffe would still win air superiority, but not as cheaply. German spearheads would still break through in places, but they would face more organized resistance, more blown bridges, more prepared artillery, and fewer Soviet formations frozen by contradictory orders.

The main strategic effect would be fewer giant encirclements. Historically, the Germans annihilated huge Soviet forces at Białystok-Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, Vyazma-Bryansk, and especially Kiev. If the Soviet leadership were more competent in 1941, it might withdraw from exposed salients earlier rather than ordering doomed stands. Avoiding or reducing the Kiev encirclement alone could preserve hundreds of thousands of men and large amounts of equipment. That would seriously weaken Germany’s chance of reaching Moscow in force.

Germany would probably still advance deep into Soviet territory. The Red Army in 1941 had real structural problems: poor communications, inexperienced officers, incomplete mechanized formations, weak logistics, and the aftereffects of purges and rapid expansion. A warning would not magically fix those. German armored and air doctrine was still superior at the start, and the Wehrmacht would retain the initiative. So this is not a scenario where the USSR easily stops Germany at the border.

But Barbarossa depended on destroying the Red Army quickly. If the Soviets are prepared enough to avoid the worst opening losses, the German plan begins to fail even earlier. Army Group Center might still take Minsk and reach Smolensk, but later and at higher cost. Army Group North might struggle more to isolate Leningrad. Army Group South would have a much harder time achieving a massive Kiev-style victory. By autumn 1941 the Germans would likely be exhausted farther west than they were historically, with fewer Soviet losses and stronger Soviet reserves.

The Battle of Moscow might either not happen in the same form or would be much less favorable to Germany. Instead of German forces reaching the outskirts of Moscow after months of huge encirclements, they might stall earlier, perhaps around Smolensk, the upper Dnieper, or short of the historical Moscow line. If they still tried for Moscow, they would face a larger and less shattered Red Army.

The war would probably still be long, but shorter and less catastrophic for the USSR. A better-prepared Soviet Union in 1941 might save millions of soldiers and civilians, preserve more industry and equipment, and begin counteroffensives from a stronger position in 1942. Germany would have less captured Soviet matériel, fewer prisoners, and less time to exploit Ukraine and western Russia. The Wehrmacht’s failure before winter would be clearer and more damaging.

A plausible outcome is that the Eastern Front turns against Germany earlier, perhaps in 1942 rather than after Stalingrad in late 1942–43. Stalingrad as we know it might not happen, because Germany may never reach the Volga in such strength. The decisive Soviet counteroffensive could occur farther west, or Germany might be forced into a defensive war much sooner.

Politically, the Allies still side with the USSR because Germany still invades. Since there is no Soviet first strike, Hitler cannot credibly claim a defensive war. Japan probably still avoids attacking Siberia, especially if the USSR looks more resilient from the beginning.

The broader consequence is that Nazi Germany likely loses faster. The USSR emerges from the war less devastated and possibly stronger diplomatically. Depending on the timing of Germany’s collapse, Soviet armies might either occupy even more of Eastern and Central Europe, because they advance earlier, or the Western Allies might adjust their plans to land sooner. But the central point is clear: a prepared, competent Soviet response in June 1941 would not stop Barbarossa at the frontier, but it would probably prevent the worst Soviet disasters of 1941 and make Germany’s invasion fail sooner and more decisively.

edus.text: If the USSR received credible, detailed information about Operation Barbarossa shortly before 22 June 1941 and Stalin actually acted on it, the invasion would still be extremely dangerous, but the opening catastrophe would likely be much less severe.
The biggest change would be in the first days.
Historically, Soviet units on the western frontier were caught in a confused half-peace, half-war posture.

Aircraft were parked wingtip-to-wingtip, ammunition and fuel were poorly distributed, communications were fragile, commanders were afraid to act without permission, and many forward armies were positioned in ways that made them vulnerable to encirclement.

If Moscow had accepted the leak as real, the USSR could have quietly put frontier forces on alert, dispersed aircraft, loaded ammunition, prepared demolitions, moved headquarters, activated air defenses, and warned commanders to expect immediate German attack.
That alone would probably prevent one of the worst historical disasters: the destruction of much of the Soviet air force on the ground.
The Luftwaffe would still win air superiority.
But not as cheaply.
German spearheads would still break through in places.
But they would face more organized resistance, more blown bridges, more prepared artillery, and fewer Soviet formations frozen by contradictory orders.
The main strategic effect would be fewer giant encirclements.
Historically, the Germans annihilated huge Soviet forces at Białystok-Minsk, Smolensk, Uman, Vyazma-Bryansk, and especially Kiev.
If the Soviet leadership were more competent in 1941, it might withdraw from exposed salients earlier rather than ordering doomed stands.
Avoiding or reducing the Kiev encirclement alone could preserve hundreds of thousands of men and large amounts of equipment.
That would seriously weaken Germany’s chance of reaching Moscow in force.
Germany would probably still advance deep into Soviet territory.
The Red Army in 1941 had real structural problems: poor communications, inexperienced officers, incomplete mechanized formations, weak logistics, and the aftereffects of purges and rapid expansion.
A warning would not magically fix those.
German armored and air doctrine was still superior at the start, and the Wehrmacht would retain the initiative.
So this is not a scenario where the USSR easily stops Germany at the border.
But Barbarossa depended on destroying the Red Army quickly.
If the Soviets are prepared enough to avoid the worst opening losses, the German plan begins to fail even earlier.
Army Group Center might still take Minsk and reach Smolensk, but later and at higher cost.
Army Group North might struggle more to isolate Leningrad.
Army Group South would have a much harder time achieving a massive Kiev-style victory.
By autumn 1941 the Germans would likely be exhausted farther west than they were historically, with fewer Soviet losses and stronger Soviet reserves.
The Battle of Moscow might either not happen in the same form or would be much less favorable to Germany.

Instead of German forces reaching the outskirts of Moscow after months of huge encirclements, they might stall earlier, perhaps around Smolensk, the upper Dnieper, or short of the historical Moscow line.
If they still tried for Moscow, they would face a larger and less shattered Red Army.
The war would probably still be long.
But shorter and less catastrophic for the USSR.
A better-prepared Soviet Union in 1941 might save millions of soldiers and civilians, preserve more industry and equipment, and begin counteroffensives from a stronger position in 1942.
Germany would have less captured Soviet matériel, fewer prisoners, and less time to exploit Ukraine and western Russia.
The Wehrmacht’s failure before winter would be clearer and more damaging.
A plausible outcome is that the Eastern Front turns against Germany earlier, perhaps in 1942 rather than after Stalingrad in late 1942–43.
Stalingrad as we know it might not happen.
Because Germany may never reach the Volga in such strength.
The decisive Soviet counteroffensive could occur farther west, or Germany might be forced into a defensive war much sooner.
Politically, the Allies still side with the USSR.
Because Germany still invades.
Since there is no Soviet first strike, Hitler cannot credibly claim a defensive war.
Japan probably still avoids attacking Siberia.
Especially if the USSR looks more resilient from the beginning.
The broader consequence is that Nazi Germany likely loses faster.
The USSR emerges from the war less devastated and possibly stronger diplomatically.
Depending on the timing of Germany’s collapse, Soviet armies might either occupy even more of Eastern and Central Europe, because they advance earlier.
Or the Western Allies might adjust their plans to land sooner.
But the central point is clear.
A prepared, competent Soviet response in June 1941 would not stop Barbarossa at the frontier.
But it would probably prevent the worst Soviet disasters of 1941 and make Germany’s invasion fail sooner and more decisively.

The causal chain is mostly consistent: better alertness reduces initial losses, which weakens encirclements, which worsens German logistics and reduces chances at Moscow, potentially altering 1942. However, it is not exceptional enough for 9-10 because it gives few explicit estimates, does not deeply analyze how much could realistically be changed with only short warning, and makes some broad claims such as saving millions or Germany losing faster without tightly flagging their dependence on warning length, Stalin's behavior, Soviet command competence, and German adaptation. Still, it strongly satisfies the criterion with only minor unsupported leaps.

items.question: What If Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley.
human_answers: No Elvis will have minimal effect. Yes he was a popular Singer but he didn’t write anything. So the songs he is famous for will still exist. Will his lose have effects on music? Obviously. But it is not like music won’t more or less still evolve as it did. The lost of one singer is not going to have that drastic an effect there are simply to many of them. And as such someone else will slot in to become the “it” singer of that time. This is Not Like removing a given general from a given battle. In a battle the general has direct influence on the fighting. Swapping him out with someone else can have drastic effect. Who sings Hound Dog… not so much. Yes the song may or may not do worse at the charts and it may or may not have an impact on a company or a song writers career, But the removal of a singer is not effecting WW2. Singers and actors while obviously famous people in general are a dime a dozen! And pretty replaceable in most circumstances. Yes they have impact but is is hard to quantify. Yeah someone else singing a sang may mean that two people that loved that song and it formed the core of how they hooked up may not get it on in the back of a 1953 Chevy but… how the hell would anyone know that for certain? The impact of actors and singers and other people who are famous because they are famous has little impact if they are changed. You want an example of an impact from no Elvis? My uncle and his friend would not have had weekend gigs playing in the band of an Elvis impersonator. And I would have been able to stay home and avoid going to a really dull county fair that my folks dragged me to. And who knows I may have gotten farther with the pretty blonde next door sooner. But I doubt it. I know we have all heard of Elvis but he was simply not that important. I challenge you to tell me what he actually did that has a significance to history, or music. Yes a lot of folks imitated his style and his look and yes a lot of people bought his music. But if anything he had a negative knock on in music as his manager was an As$#@&*(. Of the first order and screwed many a song writers over big time. So there is a reasonable likelihood that some songwriters may have done better. Now the Beatles are a bit different. They wrote a LOT of music and some of that music had an impact on other writers. Once again the impact of them not being around has a knock on in pop culture in that you don’t get impersonator and it will effect in minor ways various individuals when they have to listen to different singers or whatever. But as with Elvis that has minimal influence on anything. And is almost impossible to document. But the lose of the songs that they wrote will have an effect on the evolution of music much more then not have an inspiration for singers shacking their hips. For example the Beach Boys will be effected as the album Pet Sounds was a direct response to some of the work the Beatles were doing. Writers have a more significant impact on music as they tend to influence each other a lot and it is simpler to replace the person singing any given song then the person that wrote it. Just look at how many people have success doing covers of songs. So the problem with this kind of post is twofold. One it is very very very hard to predict exactly what will change. For example will not having the song Dont Stop (thinking about tomorrow) influence the outcome one of the 1992 presidential election? Probably not. So you are dealing with things that are very nebulous. And if it just a singer that is even hard to say as it is possible that some unknown singer could get a break with the song instead. Elvis didn’t write his music so pretty much all his songs would be song by someone else if he disappeared. And the second problem with this kind of topic on this group is that there are a lot more people that know history and military stuff to a significant degree then know music. At least in the way that it will change. I probably know the words to 75% of the songs sung by Elvis and the Beatles but I don’t know who wrote most of Elvises songs nor who produced any songs for either of them. But I either know or have books that tell me who the major officers where at pretty much any major battle in the Civil War. And I know or can find out enough about most of them to have a good guess how swapping them will effect a given battle. But who can say what guy would have walked through the door and gotten the opportunity to perform if Elvis was gone. Frankly there are thousands of better singers in the world than Elvis that never got the chance. But the combination of his abilities and the opritunities he got made him a superstar. But it is impossible to know who would have gooten that chance if he was not there. But there are only a handful of people that may have been promoted if Montgomery got ran over by a tank.

I’m not saying that nothing would change. There absolutely would be changes from neither artist existing. It’s just that fundamentally: You still have popular music derived from Black American musical traditions. You still have a push away from large swing-style bands and towards smaller guitar-based bands - especially since before the digital era the guitar is the most accessible music instrument for young people wanting to make music. You still have the Baby Boom yielding a much larger youth cohort than before - thus yielding a significant generational divide by the early to mid 1960s as they’ve grown up having not known the struggles of their parents or older siblings - and have more room tackling lifestyle changes without worry for economic precarity. You still have big labels and radio stations wanting to play “different music” for “different races” so to speak. And with that you still have white singers becoming popular for their heavily sanitized covers of black R&B songs ( looks at Pat Boone ). You still have the post-WWII dominance and saturation of American pop culture - including music - in Europe and across the globe. And since the UK and the Commonwealth have virtually zero language barrier with the US - music that imitates American musical traditions (twice removed from Black American roots) has the potential to take off. You still have the advancements in recording technology that gave artists room to make more experimental and groundbreaking music than before. Plus the steady rise of FM radio later in the 1960s to provide a market for more ambitious music. You still have the Sexual Revolution to loosen norms around sex. On top of the various other drivers of the counterculture. You still have the payola scandal and the burnout of 1950s rock stars causing the 1959-64 dearth in the quality of pop music. But that’s just structurally speaking. Aesthetically speaking, things could be shifted around - with some new genre inspired by surf rock and garage rock (though realistically not actually either one of them) blowing up out of nowhere by 1964-65 - and Pat Boone is the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll all the artists of the 1960s are inspired by in terms of singing style and aura. While British rock bands are basically seen as a store brand that only gains later appreciation in the social media era decades later a la Japanese city pop. But it would still fundamentally fit the bigger variables that had been brewing years or even decades before the mid 1960s.

While the absence of the Beatles (and particularly Lennon and McCartney) would deprive us of some very good songs, there were vast numbers of competent bands in Britain that could have filled the niche if given the opportunity- whether together or singly. The bigger impact would probably have been on the penetration of British artists into the USA [1], but that's quite likely to happen eventually because there's money to be made from big crowds of relatively wealthy teenagers who happen to hit on a good enough band. The other impact might have been on the pressure to become singer-songwriters, rather than just singers/performers. Again, money is a big driver so it's likely to happen sooner or later. Otherwise, US innovation is likely to remain largely unchanged (Iggy and the Stooges will still form, and the drivers for hippy culture and rock bands is still there). Meanwhile, the Rolling Stones would still be experimenting with blues and quality musicians like Buddy Holly, Carl Perkins will be filling the niche that Elvis is no longer dominating. In short, different but still broadly recognisable. [1] The Monkees are unlikely to be formed, but songs like Day Dream Believer are too good not to end up being a success, even if it takes a few cover versions to become a real hit.

No Beatles or Elvis? Hmmm the amateur musicologist in me (that's what happens when you're a musician, who has also played in rock bands) says that rock 'n roll would still exist. The chances are also good that you would still have its superstar in the 50s - I read years ago that there were plans to push Carl Perkins (he of "Blue Suede Shoes" fame) towards superstardom by Sun Records. He might have actually become one if he hadn't suffered a major injury (he was in a car crash that kept him out of commission for a long time). Sam Phillips and even Elvis stated that Carl was doing rockabilly before Elvis, and unlike Elvis, Carl was also a songwriter. Most musicians will tell you that having that skill gives you much more staying power - you're not just a performer, you can make money off or songwriting royalties. By the time Carl recovered from the car crash it was too late, Elvis had overshadowed him. Jerry Lee Lewis, courtesy of his flamboyant personality might have become the 50s rock 'n roll superstar (how long he would have lasted would have depended upon whether or not he was still foolish enough to marry his underage cousin). The 60s? Hmmm that's not so certain - in the early 60s, rock 'n roll seemed to be on it's way out (or at least heading towards just being a niche genre of music). What rock 'n roll there was on Top 40 radio was mostly bland, and barely even qualified as rock 'n roll (Frankie Avalon anybody?). The Beach Boys were making songs with lame-o lyrics ("Be True to Your School", etc.). Even in Europe it was only doing so-so - I remember reading an interview of Jimmy Page (who along with playing guitar in Led Zeppelin, and the Yardbirds, was an in-demand session guitarist in the early and mid 60s), where he stated that in the early 60s, it was hard to even find rock 'n roll recording sessions to play on. Without the Beatles, rock'n roll might have just kept on being 50s-style teen hearthrob music performed by Cliff Richard, instrumental music played by bands like The Shadows (who also happened to be Cliff Richard's backing band), and possibly music played by 50s American rock 'n roll musicians, who were going nowhere in the USA with their careers (Bo Diddly, Eddie Cochran, etc. performed extensively in Europe in the early 60s when their careers fizzled out in the US). One of the big elements of the Beatles that helped to propel them to stardom IMO, was that for its time (the early 60s), the Beatles' music was considered HARD ROCK. As a result, it had more energy to it than your typical music of the period, and people liked it. The Stones? They were in their infancy, playing what is to me, watered down blues, that sounded nowhere near as intense. That hard rock edge the Beatles had is what kick started rock 'n roll again, and resulted in a million bands wanting to sound like them (even in the US, after they were on the Ed Sullivan Show). No Beatles and IMO, rock 'n roll continues its decline into a niche music genre, with the occasional Top 40 hit by bland groups like Gary Pucket and The Union Gap, Gary Lewis and The Playboys, etc. Not much in the way of edgy, interesting music. In the US, Link Wray never charts as high as he did with "Rumble" (which was actually banned by radio stations because it was "too threatening - it'll incite people to riot"), and Lonnie Mack at most has a few very modest hits like he had with "Wham".

Oh, for the love of Pete, not THIS again.... I just don't understand how some on this board can analyze military events down to the level of minutiae where they can argue that if a particular German general farted at a given moment in 1940, the entirety of World War II would come out differently, and yet at the same time assume that popular culture would remain essentially unaltered without the presence of two of its most important figures. Just as one example: before the Beatles, there was no such thing as a "British rock and roll group" in the eyes of Americans, and particularly American record companies, radio programmers, and concert promoters. Cliff Richard, who was Britain's biggest rock and roll superstar prior to the Beatles, went absolutely nowhere in America. Americans knew that rock and roll had originated in the U.S., and they were very parochial about it - the assumption, and it was not often wrong, before the Beatles was that anything coming from Britain would be a poor copy of records American teenagers already owned. (And it WAS teenagers almost exclusively who listened to rock and roll in 1963; projecting one's own current cultural dynamics into the past is part of the reason one gets lost). No British rock group - not one - had broken in the U.S. before 1964. The Beatles themselves at first were turned down by Capitol, the American division of EMI, who held their recording contract in the UK; Capitol refused to issue their first four singles in the U.S. It took the "Beatlemania" phenomenon to convince Capitol that it was worth giving the Beatles a shot, which enabled Beatlemania to cross the Atlantic. I'm sorry, but it's not as if "Holliemania" or "Dave Clark Fivemania" simply takes the place of that. There's a whole set of intangibles here. You can't just assume that you like the Rolling Stones better, so they automatically take the place of the Beatles. It would never have worked like that. What happens to the Rolling Stones becomes essentially undefinable. And that's just one example. I didn't even address the fact of no Elvis - which probably would have meant no Beatles AND virtually none of the other British Invasion acts either. Removing Elvis from the picture (which automatically would remove the Beatles as we know them) changes the ENTIRE trajectory of popular music from that day to this, in well-nigh unpredictable ways. Period.
items.original_question: What if Modern Music without The Beatles and Elvis Presley. American Singer and Actor Elvis Presley and British Rock Band The Beatles are the most Influential musicians in existence. With the former codifying Rockabilly and is credited for advancing the Feminist movement in America, and the Latter spearheaded the British Invasion, increased public interest in Psychedelic Drugs, Asian Spirituality and heralded the Album Era. Let's say both the musician and the Band never had any interest in music, preventing the codifying of Rockabilly and The British Invasion. How would this influence modern music?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise fidelity: removing Elvis and The Beatles without erasing broader preconditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer consistently reasons from the specific premise that Elvis Presley and The Beatles do not exist or do not become musical actors, while preserving the wider historical conditions that produced modern popular music.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise inconsistently, erases unrelated history, or assumes modern music simply stops developing.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges the absence of Elvis and The Beatles but makes broad unsupported changes to unrelated social, technological, or musical conditions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves key background forces such as Black American musical roots, postwar youth culture, radio, labels, and recording technology, with some overreach.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates the missing artists from continuing structural drivers and avoids most butterfly-effect exaggeration.
criteria.9-10: Precisely maintains the historical baseline except where causally affected, distinguishing performer loss, songwriter loss, market niches, and institutional continuity.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage across musical, commercial, and social drivers
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the main mechanisms by which Elvis and The Beatles did or did not shape modern music, including genre development, songwriting, performance, markets, technology, and youth culture.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only fame or personal taste with no causal mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Covers one or two mechanisms, such as popularity or chart success, but neglects most music-industry and cultural drivers.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several relevant mechanisms, including rock and roll, British Invasion, singer-songwriters, or recording innovation, but unevenly.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple interacting mechanisms: covers versus songwriting, Black R&B roots, guitar bands, labels, radio, youth markets, and studio experimentation.
criteria.9-10: Integrates performer, composer, producer, industry, technological, racial, transatlantic, and generational mechanisms into a coherent account of likely musical change.

criteria.name: Differentiation of Elvis’s and The Beatles’ causal roles
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes Elvis Presley’s role as a performer and cultural popularizer from The Beatles’ role as songwriters, studio innovators, and catalysts for later rock and pop developments.
criteria.1-2: Treats Elvis and The Beatles as interchangeable celebrities or ignores one of them.
criteria.3-4: Notes that both were influential but gives little distinction between their types of influence.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes basic differences, such as Elvis popularizing rock and The Beatles writing songs, but does not trace implications far.
criteria.7-8: Explains why Elvis’s repertoire and image may be more replaceable while The Beatles’ compositions, albums, and British Invasion effects have deeper knock-on consequences.
criteria.9-10: Nuances both cases: Elvis’s racialized mainstreaming, performance style, and market role; The Beatles’ songwriting, album form, studio practice, peer competition, and global cultural signaling.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream coherence for modern music
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces consequences from the 1950s and 1960s through later genres, industry norms, and global pop without relying on disconnected speculation.
criteria.1-2: Provides scattered claims about later music with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Offers a simple linear story, such as one replacement artist changing everything, with weak links to later outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some plausible downstream effects, such as delayed British breakthrough, altered rock canon, or different singer-songwriter norms, but chains are incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Builds credible medium- and long-range chains linking substitute artists, genre niches, album culture, radio formats, counterculture, and later rock/pop evolution.
criteria.9-10: Presents a robust long-range scenario in which specific altered nodes are traced through later music while preserving broad continuity where structural forces dominate.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer appropriately signals uncertainty in an open counterfactual, avoids overconfident exact predictions, and remains internally consistent.
criteria.1-2: Makes dogmatic predictions, contradicts itself, or invents precise outcomes without justification.
criteria.3-4: Uses some hedging but still asserts implausibly specific charts, elections, genres, or artists as certain.
criteria.5-6: Generally avoids certainty and acknowledges replacement effects, but contains some unsupported or inconsistent claims.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes likely structural continuities from speculative aesthetic changes and flags unknowable substitutions.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence throughout, presents alternatives where appropriate, and maintains strict consistency about what follows from the missing artists.

items.model_answer:
Without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, modern popular music would probably still exist in recognizable form, but its development would have been slower, less unified, and shaped by different figures.

Elvis Presley did not invent rock and roll, but he became its first global mass-market symbol. He brought together rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and pop in a way that made rock acceptable to a huge white mainstream audience in the 1950s. Without Elvis, rock and roll would still have emerged through artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others. But its crossover into mainstream American and global youth culture might have been less sudden and less commercially explosive. Black pioneers may have received more direct recognition, though the music industry might also have found another white performer to play a similar crossover role.

Without The Beatles, the biggest change would be in the 1960s transformation of pop music into an album-centered, artist-driven, experimental form. The Beatles helped make it normal for bands to write their own songs, treat studio recording as an art form, explore psychedelia, and present popular music as culturally serious rather than just entertainment. Other artists—Bob Dylan, The Beach Boys, The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, The Who, Motown writers and producers, Jimi Hendrix, and later progressive and psychedelic bands—would still have pushed music forward. But the specific speed and scale of that shift would likely have been reduced.

The “British Invasion” would also have looked very different. British rock may still have reached the United States through The Rolling Stones, The Animals, The Who, or other groups, but The Beatles gave that movement its decisive commercial and cultural force. Without them, American rock, soul, folk, surf, and Motown might have remained more dominant for longer, and British bands may have had a smaller or later global impact.

Pop songwriting would likely be different too. The Beatles helped establish the model of the self-contained band: performers who wrote, arranged, recorded, and evolved their own material. Without them, the industry might have remained more dependent for longer on professional songwriting teams, producers, and label-controlled performers. Singer-songwriters and bands would still have risen, especially through folk and rock traditions, but the prestige attached to the “band as auteur” would be weaker.

Rock’s later genres would still exist, but with different lineages. Hard rock, metal, punk, indie, Britpop, power pop, psychedelic rock, progressive rock, and alternative rock all drew directly or indirectly from The Beatles or from the cultural space they helped create. Those genres would not disappear, because they also came from blues, garage rock, folk, soul, and experimental music. But their sound, mythology, and timing would be noticeably altered.

Popular culture itself would also be less centered on the idea of the pop musician as a generational icon. Elvis helped define the rebellious solo star; The Beatles helped define the band as a cultural movement. Without them, youth culture might have attached itself more strongly to other figures: Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Bob Dylan, James Brown, The Rolling Stones, The Beach Boys, Aretha Franklin, Motown groups, or later artists. The energy would still be there, but the symbolic history would be different.

In short, modern music would not be “missing rock” or “missing pop” entirely. The social forces behind them—youth markets, radio, television, racial musical exchange, recording technology, and postwar consumer culture—were too powerful. But without Elvis and The Beatles, rock and pop would likely have become less globally standardized, less quickly dominant, and less focused on the charismatic rock star and the self-writing band. Modern music would still be rich and innovative, but its canon, timelines, and central myths would be radically different.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.

items.model_answer:
If FDR had chosen an openly segregationist vice president in 1944, the main consequence is that when Roosevelt died in April 1945 the United States would have entered the last months of World War II and the early Cold War under a much more conservative, racially reactionary Democratic president than Harry Truman. The closest real-world analogue is James F. Byrnes of South Carolina, a serious 1944 contender who was a capable wartime administrator but also a Southern segregationist.

The immediate military outcome of World War II probably would not change much. Germany was already collapsing when FDR died, and Japan’s defeat was a matter of time. A segregationist Democratic president in 1945 would almost certainly still rely on the same generals, diplomats, and wartime bureaucracy. The atomic bomb would probably still be used against Japan, especially if the president were someone like Byrnes, who in real life favored a hard line toward Japan and the Soviet Union. The timing of Japan’s surrender might be very similar.

The bigger changes would come after the war.

Domestically, civil rights would be set back. Truman was not a civil-rights radical by later standards, but he did take historically important steps: he created the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, endorsed a federal civil-rights program, and desegregated the armed forces by executive order in 1948. A segregationist president would almost certainly not do those things. There would likely be no 1948 military desegregation order, no strong presidential civil-rights message, and no symbolic break between the national Democratic Party and the Jim Crow South. Federal judgeships, Justice Department priorities, and executive appointments would probably be more tolerant of segregation.

That could delay the national Democratic Party’s turn toward civil rights. The Black vote, which had been moving toward the Democrats since the New Deal, might shift more heavily toward Republicans or toward third-party liberal movements. Northern liberals, labor unions, and Black voters would be alienated if the Democratic president was visibly aligned with Southern segregationists.

The 1948 election would likely look very different. Truman’s actual 1948 campaign depended on rebuilding the New Deal coalition: labor, urban machines, farmers, Black voters, and enough of the South. A segregationist incumbent might keep the Deep South more unified behind the Democrats, so there might be no Dixiecrat revolt like Strom Thurmond’s. But he would probably lose strength in the North and West. Henry Wallace or another liberal third-party candidate might do better, while Republicans such as Thomas Dewey would have a stronger chance of winning the presidency. In that scenario, the Democrats might preserve the white South but lose the national majority.

On foreign policy, the early Cold War might be at least as hard-line as it was under Truman, possibly more so. A figure like Byrnes was skeptical of the Soviet Union and helped shape the confrontational tone of 1945–46. The Truman Doctrine, containment, NATO, and the Marshall Plan might still emerge, because they were driven by broad geopolitical pressures, not just Truman personally. But the style could be different: less idealistic language about democracy and freedom, more blunt anti-communism, and perhaps less concern about how American racism damaged U.S. credibility abroad.

There might also be changes on specific postwar issues. A segregationist Southern Democrat might be less sympathetic to recognizing Israel quickly in 1948 than Truman was. He might also be more conservative on labor policy and economic reconversion, possibly accepting measures Truman resisted or vetoed, such as stronger anti-union legislation.

The largest long-term effect would be on civil rights and party realignment. Truman’s civil-rights moves helped begin the process by which the national Democratic Party slowly became identified with civil rights and the South began drifting away. A segregationist president in 1945 could delay that split. The Democratic Party might remain longer as an uneasy coalition of Northern New Dealers and Southern segregationists. But the contradiction would not disappear. The civil-rights movement, Black migration to Northern cities, Cold War pressure, and Supreme Court litigation would still force the issue eventually.

So the short answer is: World War II probably ends much the same way, including likely use of the atomic bomb, but the postwar Democratic Party, early civil-rights policy, and perhaps the 1948 election change substantially. A segregationist successor to FDR would probably slow federal civil-rights progress, weaken the Democrats among Northern liberals and Black voters, and make a Republican victory in 1948 more likely.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.
