criteria.7-8: Reasonably situates a redesigned Merlin P-40 as better than Allison P-40s but likely inferior to the Merlin Mustang in range/aerodynamics.
criteria.9-10: Gives well-calibrated comparative outcomes, e.g. P-40F-like gains, possible 400+ mph with two-stage Merlin, yet still constrained versus P-51 by drag and range.

criteria.name: Industrial, production, and strategic downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of longer-range consequences: Merlin supply constraints, Curtiss production choices, RAF/USAAF needs, competition with P-47/P-51/Spitfire, and likelihood of cancellation or limited adoption.
criteria.1-2: Ignores production, engine availability, and procurement consequences entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions production or supply in passing but does not connect them to likely program outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes Merlin scarcity or competing aircraft but gives only a shallow downstream assessment.
criteria.7-8: Explains how Merlin allocation, established P-51 superiority, and Curtiss production realities would limit impact.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent long-range chain from design choice to production bottlenecks, variant decisions, procurement cancellation risk, and limited strategic effect.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, flags uncertainties in engine variant/design assumptions, and remains internally consistent about what a Merlin-designed P-40 could and could not achieve.

items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the start around the Rolls-Royce Merlin, it would probably have been a better high-altitude fighter, but it still would not have become a P-51 Mustang.

The main historical weakness of the P-40 was not that it was a bad airplane; it was that its Allison V-1710 engine had a single-stage, single-speed supercharger in most versions. At low and medium altitude the P-40 was sturdy, fast enough, and useful, especially in North Africa, China-Burma-India, and the Pacific. But above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet it lost performance badly compared with Merlin-powered Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later Mustangs.

A Merlin-designed P-40 would have had better altitude performance from the beginning. With a Merlin III, XX, 45, or later Packard-built Merlin, it would have climbed better, retained power higher up, and had a higher service ceiling. It would have been more competitive against the Bf 109E/F and Japanese fighters at medium altitude, and less confined to low-level fighting. In British service especially, it would have been more valuable as a general-purpose fighter rather than mainly as a fighter-bomber and low-to-medium-altitude aircraft.

But the improvement would have had limits. The P-40’s airframe came from the P-36 lineage and had relatively high drag compared with newer designs. Its wing, radiator installation, fuselage shape, and general aerodynamic refinement were not in the same class as the Spitfire or the later P-51. Simply installing a Merlin would not give it the Mustang’s laminar-flow wing, long-range internal fuel capacity, excellent radiator ducting, or low-drag airframe. Historically, the Merlin-powered P-40F and P-40L did exist, and while they were better at altitude than Allison P-40s, they were not revolutionary. They did not turn the P-40 into a first-rank high-altitude escort fighter.

If Curtiss had designed the aircraft around the Merlin from the outset, rather than adapting the engine later, the result would probably have been somewhat better than the real P-40F. The nose, cooling system, center of gravity, and fuselage could have been optimized earlier. It might have been a cleaner, better-balanced aircraft with fewer compromises. Performance might plausibly have landed somewhere between the historical P-40F and early Mustang: useful, rugged, and faster at altitude than the Allison versions, but still not equal to the best contemporary fighters once the war advanced.

The bigger problem would have been production and engine supply. In 1938–1940 the United States did not have large numbers of Merlins available. Britain needed Merlins urgently for Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later bombers. Packard-built Merlin production did not mature until later. If Curtiss had committed the P-40 to the Merlin early, the fighter might have been delayed, produced in smaller numbers, or forced into competition with British priorities. One reason the Allison-powered P-40 mattered historically was that it was available in quantity when the Allies badly needed modern fighters.

So the likely outcome is this: a Merlin P-40 designed from the beginning would have been a more capable aircraft, especially above medium altitude, and it might have had a stronger reputation. It would have been less obviously inferior to the Bf 109 at altitude and more flexible in Allied service. But it would still have been constrained by the basic Curtiss airframe and by Merlin availability. It would not have replaced the Spitfire, and it would not have matched the later P-51 as a long-range escort. Its greatest effect would have been to make the early Allied fighter inventory somewhat stronger, not to change the course of the air war by itself.

nodes.text: If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the start around the Rolls-Royce Merlin,
it would probably have been a better high-altitude fighter,
but it still would not have become a P-51 Mustang.
The main historical weakness of the P-40 was not that it was a bad airplane;
it was that its Allison V-1710 engine had a single-stage, single-speed supercharger in most versions.
At low and medium altitude the P-40 was sturdy, fast enough, and useful,
especially in North Africa, China-Burma-India, and the Pacific.
But above roughly 15,000–20,000 feet it lost performance badly compared with Merlin-powered Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later Mustangs.
A Merlin-designed P-40 would have had better altitude performance from the beginning.
With a Merlin III, XX, 45, or later Packard-built Merlin, it would have climbed better, retained power higher up, and had a higher service ceiling.
It would have been more competitive against the Bf 109E/F and Japanese fighters at medium altitude,
and less confined to low-level fighting.
In British service especially, it would have been more valuable as a general-purpose fighter
rather than mainly as a fighter-bomber and low-to-medium-altitude aircraft.
But the improvement would have had limits.
The P-40’s airframe came from the P-36 lineage and had relatively high drag compared with newer designs.
Its wing, radiator installation, fuselage shape, and general aerodynamic refinement were not in the same class as the Spitfire or the later P-51.
Simply installing a Merlin would not give it the Mustang’s laminar-flow wing, long-range internal fuel capacity, excellent radiator ducting, or low-drag airframe.
Historically, the Merlin-powered P-40F and P-40L did exist,
and while they were better at altitude than Allison P-40s,
they were not revolutionary.
They did not turn the P-40 into a first-rank high-altitude escort fighter.
If Curtiss had designed the aircraft around the Merlin from the outset, rather than adapting the engine later,
the result would probably have been somewhat better than the real P-40F.
The nose, cooling system, center of gravity, and fuselage could have been optimized earlier.
It might have been a cleaner, better-balanced aircraft with fewer compromises.
Performance might plausibly have landed somewhere between the historical P-40F and early Mustang:
useful, rugged, and faster at altitude than the Allison versions,
but still not equal to the best contemporary fighters once the war advanced.
The bigger problem would have been production and engine supply.
In 1938–1940 the United States did not have large numbers of Merlins available.
Britain needed Merlins urgently for Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later bombers.
Packard-built Merlin production did not mature until later.
If Curtiss had committed the P-40 to the Merlin early,
the fighter might have been delayed, produced in smaller numbers, or forced into competition with British priorities.
One reason the Allison-powered P-40 mattered historically was that it was available in quantity when the Allies badly needed modern fighters.
So the likely outcome is this:
a Merlin P-40 designed from the beginning would have been a more capable aircraft, especially above medium altitude,
and it might have had a stronger reputation.
It would have been less obviously inferior to the Bf 109 at altitude
and more flexible in Allied service.
But it would still have been constrained by the basic Curtiss airframe
and by Merlin availability.
It would not have replaced the Spitfire,
and it would not have matched the later P-51 as a long-range escort.
Its greatest effect would have been to make the early Allied fighter inventory somewhat stronger,
not to change the course of the air war by itself.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

items.model_answer:
Assuming the intended reference is the PT-109 disaster in 1943, the most likely consequence of JFK dying then is that the Kennedy family never produces a president in the 1960s, and several major events of U.S. political history unfold differently.

John F. Kennedy’s death in 1943 would have mattered far beyond the loss of one naval officer because his later political career depended heavily on the PT-109 survival story. That episode became central to his image: courage under pressure, physical endurance despite illness, and youthful heroism in war. Without surviving it, he never becomes a congressman in 1946, never defeats Henry Cabot Lodge for the Senate in 1952, never becomes a national Democratic figure, and never wins the presidency in 1960.

The Kennedy family’s ambitions would probably have been badly damaged. Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. originally expected his eldest son, Joseph Kennedy Jr., to become president, but Joe Jr. died in 1944. If JFK had already died in 1943, the family would have lost both of its plausible presidential heirs within a year. Robert Kennedy was talented but much younger and lacked the independent political base he later gained as JFK’s campaign manager and attorney general. Ted Kennedy was younger still and would not automatically have inherited JFK’s Senate path. The “Kennedy dynasty” might still have existed socially and financially, but probably not as a presidential dynasty.

The immediate military outcome of World War II would not change. PT-109 was a small episode in the Solomon Islands campaign, and JFK’s death would not alter the Pacific war. Its importance is political and symbolic, not strategic.

The biggest change comes in 1960. Without JFK, the Democratic nomination likely goes to someone else: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Stuart Symington, or possibly Adlai Stevenson again. Richard Nixon’s chances of winning the presidency would probably improve. JFK barely beat Nixon in the real 1960 election, and his appeal—youth, television skill, Catholic ethnic urban support, and the Kennedy campaign machine—was crucial. Against a different Democrat, especially one less effective on television or less able to unite northern liberals and urban machines, Nixon may well have won.

If Nixon became president in 1961, U.S. policy would change in several areas, though not always in predictable ways. On Cuba, the Bay of Pigs might either be cancelled, handled with more direct military support, or produce a different crisis. The Cuban Missile Crisis as we know it might not happen, because it depended partly on Khrushchev’s assessment of JFK after the Bay of Pigs and Vienna summit. A Nixon administration might look tougher, which could deter Soviet missiles in Cuba—or provoke a different confrontation.

Civil rights would probably move more slowly. JFK himself was cautious on civil rights until events forced his hand, but his assassination gave Lyndon Johnson a powerful moral and political opening to push the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965. Without JFK’s presidency and martyrdom, and without LBJ inheriting the White House in that exact way, major civil-rights legislation might still pass because the movement was strong and national pressure was rising, but it could be delayed, weaker, or politically configured differently.

Vietnam is uncertain. JFK had expanded the advisory role but had not committed large U.S. combat forces before his death. Nixon was strongly anti-communist, as was nearly every major Cold War politician, so a Nixon presidency could still escalate in Vietnam, perhaps earlier or in a different form. Conversely, Nixon’s later reputation as a hardliner might have given him more political room to avoid a massive ground war. The safest answer is that Vietnam would remain a major danger point, but the exact path of escalation would differ.

The space program would also likely be altered. JFK’s 1961 commitment to land a man on the Moon before the decade’s end was a personal presidential decision shaped by Cold War competition and political theater. Without JFK, the Apollo program might receive less urgency and funding. A Moon landing by 1969 becomes less likely, though U.S.-Soviet space competition would still continue.

So the short answer is: JFK’s death in 1943 would not change World War II, but it would likely prevent the Kennedy presidency, weaken or delay the Kennedy family’s political rise, improve Nixon’s chances in 1960, and significantly alter the timing and shape of civil rights legislation, Cuba policy, Vietnam, and the space race. The United States would still be a Cold War superpower facing the same broad pressures, but the symbolic and political architecture of the 1960s would be very different.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, the personal computer revolution would still have happened, but it likely would have been slower, more fragmented, and less dominated by Microsoft and Intel.

The IBM PC mattered less because it was technically extraordinary and more because IBM legitimized the personal computer for business. Before 1981, microcomputers already existed: Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80, CP/M machines, and others. Hobbyists, schools, and some small businesses were already using them. But many large companies did not fully trust personal computers until IBM entered the market. IBM’s name made PCs acceptable in corporate purchasing departments.

Without the IBM PC, business adoption of personal computers would probably have continued, but with no single dominant standard emerging as quickly. The early 1980s market might have remained divided among Apple, CP/M-based systems, Commodore, Tandy, various business machines, and possibly UNIX workstations. Software developers would have had to support more platforms, which would have slowed the rise of mass-market business software.

Microsoft’s history would be especially different. MS-DOS became central because IBM chose it for the IBM PC, and then IBM-compatible clones spread it everywhere. Without that deal, Microsoft might still have been important through BASIC, applications, and later operating systems, but it probably would not have gained the same early operating-system monopoly. Digital Research’s CP/M or CP/M-86 might have remained more influential. Alternatively, a UNIX-like operating system could have gained more ground in business computing.

Intel’s dominance would also be less certain. The IBM PC helped make the Intel x86 architecture the default for business computing. Without IBM’s machine and the clone market that followed, Motorola 68000 chips, Zilog processors, or other architectures might have had a stronger chance. Apple’s Macintosh, based on the Motorola 68000, might have faced less pressure from cheap IBM-compatible PCs and could have gained more business share, though Apple’s higher prices and closed ecosystem would still have limited it.

The clone industry might not have developed in the same way. One of the most important consequences of the IBM PC was that it was relatively open and easy to copy. Companies like Compaq, Dell, and many others built IBM-compatible machines, driving prices down and creating a huge standardized hardware market. Without the IBM PC, there may have been no equivalent “PC-compatible” standard in the early 1980s, or it might have emerged later around another platform.

This would have affected software too. Programs like Lotus 1-2-3, WordPerfect, dBASE, and later Windows benefited from the large IBM-compatible market. Without that common platform, software markets would have been more scattered. Graphical interfaces might have arrived differently: Apple’s Macintosh, Atari ST, Amiga, or UNIX workstations could have shaped user expectations more strongly. Windows might not have become the default desktop environment, or it might have emerged much later in a different form.

The broader economy would still have moved toward personal computing because the underlying forces were strong: microprocessors were getting cheaper, memory was improving, businesses wanted productivity tools, and consumers wanted affordable computers. But the specific “Wintel” world — Microsoft Windows running on Intel-compatible hardware — was not inevitable. It was greatly accelerated by IBM’s entry and the clone ecosystem that followed.

So the most likely result is not a world without personal computers, but a world where the PC industry is more pluralistic for longer. Apple might be stronger, CP/M or UNIX might play a larger role, Microsoft might be less dominant, Intel might not become the default architecture, and corporate computing might shift from terminals and minicomputers to desktops more gradually. The IBM PC did not create personal computing, but it strongly determined the standard form it took.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. It doesn't need to be very successful, as they only had about 2000 inhabitants and Argentina had a population of about 30 million. As long as 3000 people move in, the locals become a minority. That may lead to ethnic tensions down the line, but they are just too few people in a too isolated place and facing a country that earned a reputation by going against one of the world's leading military powers and winning IITL.

Argentina would have gone as far as She could (and probably beyond) to accommodate them. It is of course possible that someone in the Islands would misbehave. That person would be crushed. The whole Argentina (Anaya) assumption was the Goa* Hypothesis. They are not going to come, there is not going to be a war, AND our US friends** shall help us. They were very, as in very, very, conscious of their international public reputation. Had they won the situation of the Kelpers and what the world was shown would be one of their primary preoccupations. As in fact it was during the war * https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Goa ** Argentina, and it's armed forces, was used by the Reagan Administration in the dirty wars in Centro America. Galtieri*** was absolutely convinced that he was an personal friend to most in the Pentagon. And most probably he was right. *** (He was not the one that was all out for Operation Rosario **** that was Anaya that made it an condition on the Navy supporting Galtieri when he, mini, couped Viola and take charge of the Junta) **** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_invasion_of_the_Falkland_Islands
items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.

items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the Falklands War in 1982, the islanders would almost certainly not have been treated as a population with a right to choose their own political future. Argentina’s position was that the Falklands/Malvinas were Argentine territory occupied by Britain, and that the islanders were a transplanted British population rather than a distinct people entitled to self-determination.

In the short term, they would probably have lived under Argentine military administration. Based on the actual Argentine occupation in 1982, this would likely have meant curfews, censorship, restrictions on movement, searches, detention of some civilians, and close surveillance, especially of anyone seen as pro-British. The occupation was not generally genocidal or openly murderous toward civilians, and Argentina had strong reasons to avoid mass violence because it wanted international recognition of its sovereignty claim. But the islanders would have been a distrusted subject population under an authoritarian military regime.

In the longer term, Argentina would likely have tried to “Argentinize” the islands: Spanish-language administration and schooling, Argentine law, Argentine officials, settlement from the mainland, and pressure on islanders to accept Argentine sovereignty and perhaps Argentine citizenship. Some islanders might have stayed under protest, but many would probably have emigrated to Britain or elsewhere, either voluntarily or under indirect pressure. Their British political identity and institutions would not have been protected in the way they were after Britain retained control.

So the most likely outcome is not mass killing or immediate wholesale expulsion, but loss of political rights as British Falkland Islanders, military control at first, and gradual pressure to assimilate or leave. The islands’ British character would probably have been deliberately weakened over time.

items.question: What If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank?
human_answers: Let’s first think about the hypothetical scenarios that fit the “conditions” you mentioned. 1. Joseon modernizes before or at the same time as Japan. The relationship between Korea and Japan isn’t bad, but Japan is unable to colonize Korea because Korea becomes strong enough to resist. 2. Japan loses the First Sino-Japanese War or the Russo-Japanese War, and therefore fails to expand into Korea. For each of these conditions, Japan’s situation would be drastically different. In particular, if Japan were to lose a war, the "extent of its defeat" would make a huge difference. However, in my view, if Japan had developed in this way, there’s a high chance that the "Pacific War and other major conflicts" would never have occurred. There wouldn’t have been such "dramatic growth" as in real history—but there also wouldn’t have been such "catastrophic destruction" either. Ultimately, this is something that depends on the imagination of whoever envisions it. Honestly, I think it’s quite possible that Japan could still have developed to the level of a "modern G7 nation". Of course, it’s not inevitable.

East Asia would be completely different without Japanese expansion. Just to keep this in 1900 let's say they beat China but lose to Russia in 1905. I think that a Japan that doesnt even fight the 1894 war with China would be in too alien a modern world for a comparison with OTL to be very useful (mainly since no Chinese defeat in the 1894 war could lead to among other things a surviving Qing dynasty IMO). The Japanese public is highly demoralized by the loss against Russia, Korea remains an idependent country playing off Russian and Japanese influence, and Japan maintains an alliance with the UK and US. Japan not getting militarily or colonially involved in mainland Asia probably reduces the level of overall "momentum" that Japan is able to sustain as a growing world power. Many types of industries go hand in hand in their development and a Japan that does not pursue a world-class navy is probably also not going to be able to justify a world-class heavy industry to go with it. A weaker Japan is also taken less seriously and most importantly takes itself less seriously. I believe they would be somewhat simil啊r to Thailand or the modern day Philippines. Maybe they'd end up like OTL Taiwan and get really deep into some high tech sectors like semiconductors.

You are absolutely right, and it would be a natural effect to expect. Looking at your chart reminds of peculiarities of public opinion in the region in OTL however: Notice the contrast between China and Korea's Favorable-Unfavorable ratios and the opposing ratios of the South Asian and Southeast Asian countries, including 3 Southeast Asian countries Japan occupied in WWII? I have often heard people assert Japan is hated "throughout Asia" because of WWII, or is hated wherever its Army occupied anyplace during the war, but a closer inspection shows this is mainly a China and Korea thing. And for China, while with real historical basis, it's a generationally cultivated and amplified 21st century thing-- Polls were not so lopsidedly negative in the China of the 70s, 80s, and most of the 90s. There may even be some of that in South Korea also, with Japan a highly partisan issue amplified by the left-leaning party since the democratization of the late 80s, development of competitive partisan politics, and Kim Dae-Jung's breakthrough to political power, because the South Korean left's best revenge against supporters of former military dictators is to characterize them as part of continued lineage of 'collaborators' with Japan. items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.

items.model_answer:
Yes, it plausibly could have reached something like G7 rank without expanding into China, Korea, Taiwan, or Russian-held spheres, but it would have depended on remaining sovereign, politically stable, and plugged into world trade. Empire was helpful to Meiji and imperial Japan in some ways, but it was not the fundamental reason Japan later became a top-tier industrial economy.

The strongest evidence is that postwar Japan actually became a G7 economy after losing the entire empire. Its 1950s–1970s growth was based mainly on the home islands: a large literate population, strong state institutions, high savings, industrial organization, technology importation, export competitiveness, and access to American and global markets. Korea, Taiwan, Manchuria, and Sakhalin were no longer part of Japan when it became the world’s second-largest capitalist economy.

That said, losing or avoiding expansion would have changed the path. The victories over Qing China and Russia gave Japan prestige, security buffers, indemnities, markets, and confidence. The Qing indemnity after 1895 helped Japan’s finances and gold-standard policy; Taiwan and Korea provided food, raw materials, markets, and strategic depth; Manchuria later became important for coal, iron, railways, and heavy industry. Without those, Japan’s industrialization would likely have been slower and more dependent on peaceful trade for food, raw materials, and energy.

But empire also imposed huge costs. Expansion pushed Japan toward militarism, continental overextension, confrontation with China, Britain, the Netherlands, the Soviet Union, and ultimately the United States. The wars of the 1930s–1945 destroyed capital, killed millions, invited blockade and bombing, and ended in occupation. A non-expansionist Japan that avoided those catastrophes might have been poorer in strategic resources but richer in accumulated capital and international trust.

So the answer depends on the counterfactual version. If Japan simply modernizes but stays commercially oriented, like a larger version of the Netherlands, Sweden, or later South Korea/Taiwan, then yes: with its population, literacy, administrative capacity, and industrial policy, it could plausibly have become one of the world’s seven largest advanced economies by the late twentieth century, perhaps later or somewhat smaller than actual Japan but still in the G7 range. If instead Japan tries to expand and is badly defeated by China or Russia, suffers indemnities, political destabilization, or foreign coercion, then its rise could be delayed or derailed.

In short: Japan did not need empire to become a G7-level economy, but it did need security, markets, and access to resources. Peaceful integration into the world economy could have substituted for empire; catastrophic failed wars probably could not.

items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). This gets you raid warning, fighters get into the air in time to meet the raid, and the ships in port and ready to take the punch. That is not done due any specific intelligence about an attack it is simply done as a response to the war warnings of late November. Between fighter defenses and AA fire and planes not making it back to the carriers the Japanese lose somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2 of their attacking aircraft. Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. That scenario has the US forces on island ready to take the punch and the US has about 180 attack aircraft of various types ready to throw at the KB to include roughly the equivalent of seven squadrons of US Navy and US Marine Corps dive bombers the most effective weapon in the US arsenal. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. Kido Butai trundles back home to Japan, undetected by US aircraft.. This may seem like a "what if Japan declared war, and did not attack Pearl Harbor" scenario but it is not. The key difference is, what if Japan launched surprise attacks all over Asia without declaring war, and its most powerful naval assets were non-combat effective for the first 25 days of the war? Comments?

I'm not too familiar either with how much intelligence the US had on Japan pre-Pearl Harbor, but I do know that a Japanese submarine was sunk by the US just hours before Pearl Harbor, and the message either was ignored or received too late to mobilize the dock. I could totally see an early warning, through this incident, cause Pearl Harbor to mobilize and allow for Japanese pilots to lose the element of surprise. Assuming the Japanese ships aren't found and only the planes are destroyed, this would make Japan more cautious against the US, since the Pacific Fleet wouldn't be as weak as it was after Pearl Harbor in our timeline. Additionally, because of the warning, there might be less civilian causalities and so, in the United States, there is anger at being attacked, there wouldn't be the rallying cry of "OMG THEY MURDERED A BUNCH ON INNOCENT AMERICANS!" But, overall, Pearl Harbor not being totally destroyed is definitely an interesting and plausible scenario that would have an impact on WWII.

If the attack on Pearl Harbor had completely failed, Japan would probably have been in a much worse strategic position almost immediately, while the United States would still almost certainly have entered World War II.

The key point is that Japan’s attack was meant to buy time. By crippling the U.S. Pacific Fleet, Japan hoped to seize the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, and other resource-rich territories before America could respond effectively. If Pearl Harbor failed—meaning the U.S. battleships, aircraft, fuel facilities, and repair yards remained intact, and especially if Japanese aircraft or carriers suffered heavy losses—Japan would have gained the worst possible outcome: it would have provoked the United States without seriously weakening it.

America would still have declared war. Even a failed attack on a U.S. naval base would have been an act of war, and Japan was also attacking other Western possessions across the Pacific at the same time. Public outrage would likely have been intense, though perhaps less emotionally overwhelming than after the real disaster. The slogan “Remember Pearl Harbor” might have had less power, but the political result would probably have been the same: the United States enters the war against Japan.

The immediate military effects would depend on how the attack failed. If Japan simply missed its targets and escaped, the U.S. Pacific Fleet would have been stronger, but not automatically able to stop Japan’s early offensives. American battleships were slow, vulnerable to air attack, and operating far from major forward bases. The Philippines were still exposed, and Japan still had strong land-based airpower in the western Pacific. So Japan might still have captured much of Southeast Asia, including the oil-rich Dutch East Indies.

But the U.S. would have had far more options. With Pearl Harbor’s battleships, aircraft, fuel tanks, and repair facilities intact, the U.S. Navy could have responded faster and with greater confidence. Japanese operations around the Philippines, Wake Island, and the central Pacific would have faced more pressure. The U.S. might have attempted earlier counterattacks or used its surviving surface fleet to complicate Japan’s expansion.

If the failure also meant Japan lost many carrier aircraft—or, even more dramatically, lost some of its aircraft carriers—the consequences would have been enormous. Japan’s carrier force was its main offensive weapon in 1941–42. Heavy losses there could have prevented or weakened later Japanese operations such as the Indian Ocean raid, the attack toward Port Moresby, and the Midway operation. In that case, Japan’s early momentum might have collapsed much sooner, and the United States could have moved onto the offensive earlier than it did historically.

Germany’s role probably would not change much. In reality, Hitler declared war on the United States after Pearl Harbor. If Japan still attacked the U.S., even unsuccessfully, Germany likely would still have declared war, or U.S.-German naval conflict in the Atlantic would have escalated anyway. So the United States probably still becomes a full participant in both the Pacific and European wars.

Domestically, the failed attack might have reduced some of the shock and humiliation that shaped American wartime culture. However, anti-Japanese fear and anger would still have been strong. Policies like Japanese American internment might still have happened, though possibly with somewhat less public pressure if Hawaii had not suffered devastating losses.

Overall, a completely failed Pearl Harbor attack would not save Japan. It would likely make Japan’s position worse. The United States would still enter the war, but with more of its Pacific strength intact. Japan’s early conquests might still occur, but they would be harder to consolidate, and the U.S. counteroffensive would likely begin sooner or with greater strength. The most likely result is the same final outcome—Japan’s defeat—but potentially faster and at lower cost to the United States.

human_answers: The one thing that keeps coming to me is Nixon would have the greatest meltdown in political history, screaming bloody murder then the Eastern Establishment has screw him for a third and final time. Even in OTL 68 a lot of the GOP had in fact become very weary over backing Nixon over his defeats in 1960, and 1962 in California. Now this last minute scandal, Nixon messing with the peace talks, cost him and the Republicans the election for a third time. At the very best, Tricky Dick might become a Secretary of State under a future Republican president and a Statesman, but the White House is forever gone. GOP swings back to the Rockefeller Republicans like George Romney and Nelson Rockefeller himself, but could also swing to Reagan. McGovern quickly makes a peace deal for Vietnam and pulls out. The South eventually falls. But we wash our hands of that conflict. McGovern would see to a second wind of the Great Society and likely see to a very liberal and Leftist Supreme Court along with many other Judges and at least some mild liberal reforms passed in Congress.

items.original_question: The Highest Patriotism: What if George McGovern became President in 1968 ​ The initial frontrunner for the Democratic nomination in 1968 was President Johnson of course, but an insurgent primary challenge from one Senator Eugene McCarthy set off a spark that would blow open a wide power vacuum in the Democratic party following Johnson's withdrawal from consideration. Johnson had endorsed Hubert Humphrey, his ambitious VP, but he chose not to run in the primaries, instead gaining support through backroom deals with delegates to win at the convention. This led to a bitter primary fight between McCarthy and Robert F. Kennedy, who had jumped into the race shortly before Johnson's withdrawal. As the primaries carried on, this fight would all come to a head with the hotly-contested California primary. Both campaigns put valiant efforts and loads of funding into this contest, but in the end, McCarthy would narrowly prevail, winning 45% to Kennedy's 42% and taking all of California's delegates. Kennedy would immediately announce his withdrawal from the nomination after the loss, but refused to make an endorsement. When it came to the convention, however, most of Kennedy's delegates coalesced around McCarthy, leading to a deadlocked convention between him and Humphrey. Kennedy had only privately backed McCarthy, even though he hated the man. With the convention at an impasse, Kennedy looked for an alternate who could emerge as a compromise candidate, despite his own ego making him hurt that no matter what, it wasn't going to be him. That man was none other than Senator from South Dakota George Stanley McGovern. McGovern was a Kennedy ally who had served as his brother's director for Food for Peace and an ambassador to the Peace Corps his brother founded. However, he was also firmly of the anti-war wing of the party and was more amenable to McCarthy and his delegates than Kennedy, whom McCarthy deeply despised. McCarthy vowed to stay in, but as more and more Kennedy-turned-McCarthy delegates flipped to McGovern, he saw the writing on the wall. After six more ballots, McCarthy would release his delegates, with all but a few holdouts voting for McGovern on the next ballot. However, the race was not over yet. There still was not an agreed upon consensus, and it would take more backroom dealing to put McGovern over the hump. To that, Kennedy looked to the Texas delegation, which was backing Humphrey, led by the old friend of his brother's, Governor John Connally. Kennedy aimed to make a deal with Connally to give his delegates over to McGovern in exchange for major concessions. Initially resistant, and more and more concessions being offered, Connally would finally accept the offer on one singular condition; he would be made VP. With the two coming to an agreement, Texas would announce the switch of its delegates to McGovern, putting him over the line to win the nomination after 10 ballots, and Connally was selected as McGovern's running mate. Republican nominee Richard Nixon had a strong lead in early polls, and it looked as if the McGovern/Connally ticket was heading for a demolishment. Some polls even had McGovern losing Texas despite Connally's presence on the ticket. But slowly McGovern chipped at Nixon. Nixon was seen as a crooked insider and someone who would do anything to win, while McGovern appeared to be more honest in his approach. However, the race still remained in Nixon's favor weeks before the election, despite McGovern's best efforts. Then, a bombshell emerged. Johnson, who had only tacitly supported McGovern, if only for his buddy Connally becoming VP if they won, had leaked to the press that Nixon attempted to sabotage the peace talks occurring in Vietnam. McGovern didn't wish to make the campaign dirty, but he still called the reports "troubling" and placed serious question into his opponent's integrity while not outright placing guilt, which helped his honest image even further, and painted an even greater contrast between the two men . In the end, it was close, but... McGovern/Connally (Democratic) - 279 electoral votes, 42.62% Nixon/Agnew (Republican) - 182 electoral votes, 41.04% Wallace/LeMay (American Independent) - 77 electoral votes, 16.01% ​ ...the last second scandal proved to be just enough for McGovern to win this election by the slimmest of margins. If he had lost any of the states of California, Illinois, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Texas, or Wisconsin, with Texas being decided by just 1.04% for him and only winning 39.74% of the vote there, this election would have been thrown to the House of Representatives, and all of them, decided by only a few points each, had flipped, than Nixon would have won an outright majority himself. George McGovern was never meant to win this election, but through a deadlocked convention, backroom deals, and scandals, it was the honest prairie man that triumphed over them all.

items.model_answer:
If George McGovern had become president in 1968, the largest and most immediate change would have been Vietnam. A McGovern presidency would likely have treated opposition to the war not as disloyalty but as, in his own moral vocabulary, “the highest patriotism.” The United States probably would have moved toward withdrawal years earlier, with fewer American deaths, less bombing of Indochina, and no Nixon-style expansion of the war into Cambodia. But the political cost at home would have been enormous, and McGovern would probably have been blamed by conservatives and many moderates for “losing” Vietnam.

For the scenario to happen, the Democratic convention in 1968 would have had to reject Hubert Humphrey after Robert Kennedy’s assassination and nominate McGovern as an antiwar compromise candidate. He then would have needed to defeat Richard Nixon while George Wallace split the conservative vote. That is unlikely, but not impossible in a very narrow Electoral College outcome.

As president, McGovern would probably have announced a rapid de-Americanization of the war: a bombing halt, direct negotiations with Hanoi, pressure on South Vietnam to accept a political settlement, and a timetable for U.S. troop withdrawal. He would not have invaded Cambodia in 1970, and the Kent State crisis as we know it likely would not have happened. The antiwar movement would have lost some of its central target, though radical unrest would not have disappeared overnight. The war might have ended for the United States by 1970 or 1971 rather than 1973.

The harder question is what happened afterward in Vietnam. McGovern would have hoped for a negotiated settlement, perhaps involving a coalition government or neutralization of South Vietnam. But without continued massive U.S. military support, South Vietnam’s position would likely have deteriorated. A communist victory might have come earlier than 1975. The difference is that it would have come after fewer years of American bombing, fewer U.S. casualties, and probably less destruction in Cambodia and Laos. McGovern’s critics would have called this surrender; his defenders would have called it a necessary end to an unwinnable war.

Domestically, McGovern would have tried to extend the Great Society in a more explicitly egalitarian direction. He cared deeply about hunger, poverty, farm policy, Native American issues, and civil rights. His administration likely would have supported stronger anti-poverty programs, expanded food assistance, national health insurance debates, and campaign-finance reform. But he would have faced a Congress still dominated by Democrats who were not all liberals. Southern Democrats and Republicans would have blocked much of his most ambitious agenda. He would have had moral authority with liberals, but not necessarily the legislative skill or congressional base that Lyndon Johnson had.

Race and law-and-order politics would have been a major problem for him. In 1968, the country was shaken by riots, assassinations, urban crime, and white backlash. Nixon exploited those fears through “law and order” and the Southern Strategy. If McGovern were president instead, that backlash would not vanish; it would probably intensify. Republicans would portray him as soft on crime, soft on communism, and captive to student radicals. The conservative realignment of white working-class and Southern voters might have happened even faster.

The Supreme Court could have changed significantly. Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist. McGovern would almost certainly have chosen more liberal justices. The Warren Court’s liberal direction might have lasted longer, affecting criminal procedure, civil rights, reapportionment, school desegregation, abortion, and executive power. A McGovern Court would likely have been more skeptical of police power and more protective of individual rights than the actual Burger Court became.

Foreign policy beyond Vietnam would have been more complicated. McGovern was not isolationist; he was a World War II bomber pilot and a serious critic of militarized foreign policy. He likely would have pursued détente with the Soviet Union and arms control, perhaps similar in broad direction to Nixon and Kissinger but with less secrecy and less emphasis on great-power manipulation. Opening relations with China might have been delayed, because Nixon’s anti-communist credentials made it easier for him to make that move. McGovern might have wanted engagement with China, but he would have faced harsher domestic attacks for it.

Economically, ending the war earlier might have reduced some federal pressure and social strain, but it would not have eliminated the structural problems of the 1970s. Inflation, the weakening of Bretton Woods, industrial competition, and the coming oil shock would still have posed serious challenges. McGovern was more economically populist than technocratic. He might have expanded social spending while cutting defense, but if inflation worsened, he would have been politically vulnerable. A Republican victory in 1972 or 1976 would have been very likely if the economy weakened and Vietnam ended badly.

The biggest political consequence is that there would be no Nixon presidency as we know it: no Watergate, no Nixon enemies list, no Nixonian Cambodia incursion, and no Nixon appointments reshaping the Court. But there also might be no Democratic recovery. A McGovern presidency beginning in 1969 could have made him, rather than Nixon, the central figure associated with defeat in Vietnam, inflation, racial conflict, and national disorder. The Republican Party might have gained power afterward under someone like Ronald Reagan earlier than in actual history.

So the most likely outcome is a morally clearer but politically fragile presidency. McGovern would have ended or sharply reduced American involvement in Vietnam sooner, saving lives and avoiding some of the darkest escalations of the Nixon years. He would have tried to make American politics more humane, anti-militarist, and egalitarian. But he would have governed a country not yet ready for his kind of liberalism, and the backlash against him might have accelerated the conservative turn of the 1970s and 1980s.

edus.text: If George McGovern had become president in 1968,
the largest and most immediate change would have been Vietnam.
A McGovern presidency would likely have treated opposition to the war not as disloyalty but as, in his own moral vocabulary, “the highest patriotism.”
The United States probably would have moved toward withdrawal years earlier, with fewer American deaths, less bombing of Indochina, and no Nixon-style expansion of the war into Cambodia.
But the political cost at home would have been enormous, and McGovern would probably have been blamed by conservatives and many moderates for “losing” Vietnam.
For the scenario to happen, the Democratic convention in 1968 would have had to reject Hubert Humphrey after Robert Kennedy’s assassination.
The convention would have had to nominate McGovern as an antiwar compromise candidate.
He then would have needed to defeat Richard Nixon while George Wallace split the conservative vote.
That is unlikely, but not impossible in a very narrow Electoral College outcome.

As president, McGovern would probably have announced a rapid de-Americanization of the war: a bombing halt, direct negotiations with Hanoi, pressure on South Vietnam to accept a political settlement, and a timetable for U.S. troop withdrawal.
He would not have invaded Cambodia in 1970, and the Kent State crisis as we know it likely would not have happened.
The antiwar movement would have lost some of its central target, though radical unrest would not have disappeared overnight.
The war might have ended for the United States by 1970 or 1971 rather than 1973.
The harder question is what happened afterward in Vietnam.
McGovern would have hoped for a negotiated settlement, perhaps involving a coalition government or neutralization of South Vietnam.
But without continued massive U.S. military support, South Vietnam’s position would likely have deteriorated.
A communist victory might have come earlier than 1975.
The difference is that it would have come after fewer years of American bombing, fewer U.S. casualties, and probably less destruction in Cambodia and Laos.
McGovern’s critics would have called this surrender; his defenders would have called it a necessary end to an unwinnable war.
Domestically, McGovern would have tried to extend the Great Society in a more explicitly egalitarian direction.
He cared deeply about hunger, poverty, farm policy, Native American issues, and civil rights.
His administration likely would have supported stronger anti-poverty programs, expanded food assistance, national health insurance debates, and campaign-finance reform.
But he would have faced a Congress still dominated by Democrats who were not all liberals.
Southern Democrats and Republicans would have blocked much of his most ambitious agenda.
He would have had moral authority with liberals, but not necessarily the legislative skill or congressional base that Lyndon Johnson had.
Race and law-and-order politics would have been a major problem for him.
In 1968, the country was shaken by riots, assassinations, urban crime, and white backlash.
Nixon exploited those fears through “law and order” and the Southern Strategy.
If McGovern were president instead, that backlash would not vanish; it would probably intensify.
Republicans would portray him as soft on crime, soft on communism, and captive to student radicals.
The conservative realignment of white working-class and Southern voters might have happened even faster.
The Supreme Court could have changed significantly.
Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist.
McGovern would almost certainly have chosen more liberal justices.
The Warren Court’s liberal direction might have lasted longer, affecting criminal procedure, civil rights, reapportionment, school desegregation, abortion, and executive power.
A McGovern Court would likely have been more skeptical of police power and more protective of individual rights than the actual Burger Court became.
Foreign policy beyond Vietnam would have been more complicated.
McGovern was not isolationist; he was a World War II bomber pilot and a serious critic of militarized foreign policy.

He likely would have pursued détente with the Soviet Union and arms control, perhaps similar in broad direction to Nixon and Kissinger but with less secrecy and less emphasis on great-power manipulation.
Opening relations with China might have been delayed, because Nixon’s anti-communist credentials made it easier for him to make that move.
McGovern might have wanted engagement with China, but he would have faced harsher domestic attacks for it.
Economically, ending the war earlier might have reduced some federal pressure and social strain.
But it would not have eliminated the structural problems of the 1970s, including inflation, the weakening of Bretton Woods, industrial competition, and the coming oil shock.
McGovern was more economically populist than technocratic, and he might have expanded social spending while cutting defense, but if inflation worsened, he would have been politically vulnerable.
A Republican victory in 1972 or 1976 would have been very likely if the economy weakened and Vietnam ended badly.

The biggest political consequence is that there would be no Nixon presidency as we know it: no Watergate, no Nixon enemies list, no Nixonian Cambodia incursion, and no Nixon appointments reshaping the Court.
But there also might be no Democratic recovery.
A McGovern presidency beginning in 1969 could have made him, rather than Nixon, the central figure associated with defeat in Vietnam, inflation, racial conflict, and national disorder.
The Republican Party might have gained power afterward under someone like Ronald Reagan earlier than in actual history.
So the most likely outcome is a morally clearer but politically fragile presidency.
McGovern would have ended or sharply reduced American involvement in Vietnam sooner, saving lives and avoiding some of the darkest escalations of the Nixon years.
He would have tried to make American politics more humane, anti-militarist, and egalitarian.
But he would have governed a country not yet ready for his kind of liberalism, and the backlash against him might have accelerated the conservative turn of the 1970s and 1980s.

He cared deeply about hunger, poverty, farm policy, Native American issues, and civil rights.
His administration likely would have supported stronger anti-poverty programs, expanded food assistance, national health insurance debates, and campaign-finance reform.

Southern Democrats and Republicans would have blocked much of his most ambitious agenda.

The conservative realignment of white working-class and Southern voters might have happened even faster.

Nixon appointed Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell, and William Rehnquist.
