failures.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?
human_answers: Note: Parts of this answer will be copied from this one . However, this is a different scenario than that one. Note: I do not claim that this answer is realistic, nor that everything would happen the way I say it would. This is, of course, impossible to predict. Anyway, the point of divergence here is 378 AD, with the battle of Adrianople. Battle of Adrianople You see, Rome could have won this battle quite decisively. They had numerical parity, if not superiority, to the Gothic forces. They had great heavy cavalry. Valens had a large amount of additional reinforcements marching in from the west as well. They likely would have arrived within the next few days. Had the two forces linked up, they would have likely beaten the Goths. Why did I have the Romans win at Adrianople? The Roman defeat at Adrianople and the resulting Gothic invasions devastated the Balkans, to the point where they were somewhat depopulated. This is avoided in this timeline. This also avoids the Goths rising up in revolt within the Empire later on. With the Balkans in a much better position, the Romans are able to largely keep the Huns at bay, forcing them west. The Huns were defeated in battle by the Western Romans and their allies in 451 AD, so I could see the Eastern Romans doing the same here. Next, Theodosius the Great recognizes Eunegius as Emperor in 394, rather than killing and deposing him. This avoids the problem of Honorius becoming Emperor and also doesn’t kill over a third of the western army. Eunegius agrees to let Flavius Stilicho become Magister Militum of the west in exchange for being recognized as Emperor. Stilicho would survive longer in this timeline due to Honorius not rising to power, allowing him to better contain the barbarians invading the Empire. He would represent a bridge between the barbarians living within the Empire, allowing them to be more easily assimalated and showing that the two could coexist. Flavius Aetius would also survive longer, giving Rome a strong military leader to hold the Empire together. Next, Majorian is not betrayed in 460 AD, and his fleet is not destroyed. This allows him to retake North Africa, giving Western Rome fresh sources of manpower, taxes, food, and resources. Majorian finds out about Ricimier’s plots and has him executed. His replacement would be loyal and competent. Majorian would stabalize Italy and North Africa, and implement his reforms to the imperial administration. This would make the Empire more stable. Majorian would implement laws to whip the decedant and lazy upper class back into shape, reinvigorate pride in the Roman state, and reintroduce native Italians into the army. Majorian’s successor, likely Julius Nepos, would continue his reforms, enforcing and expanding upon them. Roman Empire in 460 AD. In this timeline, Carthage is under Roman rule as well. Under Majorian’s successors, Gaul and most of Hispania would still be lost, but the Empire would survive. Julius Nepos comes to power in the mid-late 470s, continuing the reforms of Majorian and strengthening the Empire. He would fortify the borders and choose a competent successor, who would continue the reforms of Majorian and Nepos. Majorian, Nepos, and their successors would recognize that the Empire could not rely on slavery, and that it needed to bolster its population in order to survive. Therefore, they would implement more efficient farming practices and the use of technology such as water wheels and mills in order to make the production of flour more efficient. They would also update architectural codes and improve living standards in order to increase stability and keep more people alive and healthy. They would massively revamp sanitation systems to reduce the risk of disease and improve healthcare for pregnant mothers in order to bolster the population further. They would also choose a competent successor, who would likely free most remaining slaves to increase the conscriptable, taxable population. Barbagel water mill complex During this time monuments and architecture would be restored. Propaganda would hearken back to the old days and the resilience of the Roman people, reinvigorating pride in the Empire. Leo I in the East would die a few years later than in our timeline, helping out the West. The West largely goes on as a regional power until Justinian comes along. He would officially reunify the East and West, although there would still be two emperors. Without Italy being devastated by the Gothic wars, its population thrives, and the Roman spirit is reignited in the East as well. Justinian implements the reforms of the West all across the Empire, and Rome reaches a new technological golden age. Hispania and southern Gaul are retaken for the Empire, and the whole of North Africa up to the Atlantic is under Roman control as well. The Justinian Plague is still devastating, but with the improved sanitation and without the devastation of the Gothic wars, Rome is still going strong. The Plague would drive demand for labor up as the population declines, allowing the middle class to grow and seeing the further implementation of technology into the everyday lives of Romans. Women would be allowed to hold more jobs and to work in factories, and would slowly gain more power and rights in society from there. In this timeline, with the Balkans secured and giving Rome much greater manpower than it had in our world, Germanus would be able to destroy the Persians at Antioch, making Persia rethink Rome’s weakness. The Persians would sue for peace, restoring the “Eternal Peace” they had signed with Rome not long before. They would have to make several concessions, allowing Rome to fortify the border. In this timeline, Germanus would not have to fight the Ostrogoths in Italy, and would thus not fall ill. He would become Emperor after Justinian, and after him would be Justin Germanus, who would be another competent ruler. These two would further expand on the reforms of their predecessors, upholding them and giving them time to stick. IRL Rome under Justinian With large sources of manpower from North Africa, the Balkans, and Italy, Rome is not percieved as weak by Persia. In this timeline, Phokas would not rise to power and severely weaken the Empire, as Justin Germanus would not order him to camp north of the Danube for the winter. Maurice would still rise to power after Justin, and would be a fairly competent Emperor as he was in our timeline. After Maurice, Heraclius would not want to see the Empire split between Maurice’s sons and would rise to power. Heraclius was also fairly competent. Without Phokas, and with Persia having been stopped by Germanus decades earlier, the Persians wouldn’t attack the Romans. When the Arabs explode out of the Arabian peninsula, Rome would abandon Gaul and lose Hispania and parts of North Africa. However, they would still hold Carthage, Egypt, and the Levant. They’d also lose bits of the northern Balkans to the Slavs and Avars. However, they’d still hold much of the Balkans. Persia, due to not being exhausted by fighting Rome, would be in a stronger position, and would survive the Arab invasions, though with a loss of territory. In the same way Rome was Europe’s shield during the middle ages, Persia would be Rome’s shield, taking blow after blow and lessening the effects of these invasions on the Roman Empire. The balance of power within the Empire would still shift east, with Constantinople being the capital. The Empire would closely resemble the Eastern Roman/Byzantine Empire of our timeline, but with more Latin influence. During this time, northern Europe still largely develops as it did in our timeline, with the Kingdom of the Franks still emerging and splitting. Hispania is still slowly reconquered by the Europeans, but this time the Romans would participate. Eventually they’d end up with what would be Aragon in our timeline. Much of the middle ages in Europe would be Roman tributary states paying the Romans in exchange for protection. The Pope, chafing under Roman rule, would flee and set up a new branch of Christianity, namely Catholicism. The Romans are able to hold back the Turks as well, keeping them out of the Empire. They win at Manzikert. Rome has entered a period of slow but steady decline, as it did in our timeline. It’s still surviving and prospering, but beginning to rot from the inside. The Great Schism never happens, and neither do the Crusades. Rome is one of the most technologically advanced nations on the planet, being near a state of industrialization. They would have rudimentary air conditioning, sanitation, advanded plumbing and running water, all in every apartment building. They would have hospitals and universities. Their military would be formidable. Factory-like complexes would be common, using water power to produce flour and goods. Slavery would come to be regarded as the mark of a less advanced civilization. Basil II would reinvigorate the Empire, bringing back Roman pride and defeating the Bulgars. He would reform the Empire, and leave it in a much stronger position than it was before his reign. In this timeline, he would choose a competent successor, similarly to Germanus and Justinian. Europe and the Middle East in 1025 AD In 1190, the Romans beat the Bulgarians at the battle of Trinova. This leads to Isaac II not being deposed and the Roman army not being demoralized like in our timeline. Alexios III does not rise to power, and the 4th Crusade never happens, as Alexios IV never needs to contact the crusaders to depose Alexios III. The Romans would have good relations with Hungary to the north. In the 1200s, the Mongol invasions would happen. Whatever Persion/Turkish state that would exists east of Rome would take the brunt of the blow, but Rome would still be hit fairly hard. They wouldn’t be devastated, but they wouldn’t be able to brush it off either. The Black Death would also be devastating, but experience with plagues and sanitation would somewhat mitigate the effects. Like the Justinian Plague before, the Black Death would again grow the middle class, increasing their power within society. The Romans would recover. Mongol expansion The world in 1250 The Turks would still carve out an Empire like they did in our timeline, leading to several wars with the Romans. They would very nearly succeed in taking Constantinople in 1453, but Rome would be able to drive them back. Roman propaganda would once again hearken back to the determination of the Roman people and the strength and culture of classical Rome. There would be a resurgance in classical ideas, innovation, and technology and philosophy, as well as the arts. This would spread throughout Europe, sparking the Renaissance. Rome would reconquer what territory it lost to the Turks, and even expand in some places. Constantine XI and his successor would implement broad reforms to protect from invasions and to make it so that the internal rot that had weakened Rome would not happen again. The 100 Years War ends the way it did in our timeline, and Poland-Lithuania still emerges, as does something like the Tutonic Order. In this timeline, they would fight in the Reconquista before eventually getting evicted and moving up to the Baltic region to stamp out paganism there. Europe in 1450 Rome for centuries would dominate East-West trade, leading the Iberian kingdoms impoverished. They would search for new trade routes, and would travel around Africa and eventually find the Americas. Now the race is on to colonize the New World. In the early 16th century, Rome would conquer down to the Horn of Africa and set up client kingdoms. This would give them access to the lucrative Indian Ocean trade routes. Rome at this point would be incredibly advanced, rich, and prosperous. Huge factory complexes and industrial scale agricultural and mining operations would exist. Roman towns and cities would be among the cleanest in the world. By now almost every building would have a flush toilet and sink. Plumbing would be common in towns as well as cities. Gunpowder weapons would be appearing. Analog computers would be used. The printing press would allow ideas to spread rapidly, spreading technology. The world in 1550 Protestantism would be spreading throughout the northern lands of Europe, and in the early 1610s Germany would be ripped apart by religous war. The Hapsburgs would control Austria, Germany, and Spain, and in a bid to exploit the Hapsburg’s weakness, the French, Romans, and Russians would fight them. The Romans and Russians in particular would support the Protestants against the Catholics, who were enemies of Roman Orthodoxy. The war would end with Germany and Spain crippled, the former of which would be reduced to a messy confederation of states. The Romans would annex Hungary. Brandenburg, Bavaria, and Prussia would come to dominate Germany. Meanwhile, for the past few centuries England, Spain, Portugal, Rome, France, and Holland have been setting up colonies in the Americas. The Romans would not partake in the Atlantic Slave Trade, viewing slavery as the mark of a less advanced civilization. The Portugese would colonize Brazil. The French and British colonies would grow fast in the Americas. Meanwhile, Brandenburg would become a dominant power in Germany alongside Bavaria and Prussia. The three would become close allies, hoping to unite Germany. They would attempt to annex Transnistria, leading to the Seven Years War. The world at the start of the Seven Years War The British side of the war would be: Prussia Brandenburg Bavaria Britain Portugal Rome Russia The French side of the war would be: Austria France Spain Persia Poland Holland The war would be even larger here than in our timeline. Russia would move into Poland-Lithuania, gaining territory until the Polish stop them with a defensive trench line. The Romans would move against the Persians/Turks, pushing them back and taking Armenia. They would advance into Arabia. The British and French would fight in the Americas, and the Romans would advance against the Spanish in both the New World and Old World. The British would seize Spanish islands in the Carribean. The armies of Prussia, Bavaria, and Brandenburg initially push the Austrians back, but get bogged down. After the first winter in Europe, spring offensives begin. However, inspired by Poland, the other powers have built trench lines and fortresses, bogging down any advance. The British and French would fight in India. The Dutch would fight the British, hoping to protect their interests in India. After years of brutal war, Poland is carved up by Prussia and Russia. The Americas largely shake out the way they did in our timeline. Austria is weakened. Rome annexes Persia and Arabia entirely. The Romans would industrialize fairly easily, soon after the British. They had the technology, and the Romans were historically nothing if not adaptable, and during the Medieval era were able to change their institutions to fit the changing world around them. The American colonies still become independent following the Great War. Following a trade dispute in the Indian Ocean due to British control of India, relations between Rome and Britain sour. Rome starts to ally with France and supports the Americans in response. They would also support the native tribes, hoping to stop America from threatening Roman interests in the Americas. The Romans would sell Corsica to France just in time for Napoleon to be born, and the Napoleonic wars still happen. Rome allies with France due to soured relations with Britain. When France invades Russia, however, the Romans turn on Napoleon and deal his empire the death blow. However, the other European powers are mad at the Romans, and force territorial concessions. The Romans lose land both at home and overseas, notably in Iberia and Africa. During their time as a Napoleonic ally, the Roman senate would gain much more power, and the Emperor’s power would be reduced. The Emperor would still be powerful, but they would have to share power with the Senate. The world after the Napoleonic Wars The Romans are embittered by this loss of land. Brandenburg and Prussia would rise in power immensely following this war, becoming the dominant forces in Germany. They would become the de-facto leader of the German Confederation, and would eventually unify Germany in the 1860s and 70s during and after the Franco-German war. During the 1850s, a dispute between ethnic Romans and Slavs in the Crimean Peninsula leads to the Crimean War. Russia and Rome would had been traditional allies for centuries by this point, but Russian expansionism would sour relations between the two. The British and French would intervene on Rome’s side, and the war would ultimately not accomplish anything. In the 1870s, France is devastated by the Franco-Prussian war. The Romans take the opportunity to invade and occupy France, a hugely controversial move. They also annex Spain and Portugal, and move deeper into North Africa. Without the French, the British take the Congo and French West Africa and Indochina. France, Spain, and Portugal are all very rebellious, and fight for independence for decades. However, the Romans are determined to hold on to them. The world in 1914 Then comes the 20th century, the graveyard of empires. While many would say that nationalism would rip the Empire apart, I disagree. In our timeline, even after the Roman Empire died in 1453, the people living in the lands it occupied considered themselves Roman up until well into the 19th century. With a much stronger Roman state and culture, Rome would not succumb to nationalism like so many other Empires would. In 1914, a rogue nationalist assasinates Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Everyone in Europe has been itching to beat each other up, and this is a conventient excuse. Austria blames the Romans and declares war. Russia joins Austria. rubrics.question_focus: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and Roman survival mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines how the Roman Empire avoids collapse and whether that survival path is historically plausible for late antiquity rather than simply assuming uninterrupted Roman power.
criteria.1-2: Gives no concrete divergence point or relies on magic, vague inevitability, or an unchanged empire lasting effortlessly to 2020.
criteria.3-4: Names a broad reason Rome survives but gives little connection to real late Roman crises such as succession, fiscal strain, military pressure, or administrative division.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible divergence or reform path addressing some key causes of decline, though with gaps or oversimplified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Builds survival from historically grounded changes in military, fiscal, succession, frontier, and administrative systems, with mostly plausible tradeoffs.
criteria.9-10: Defines a precise, well-justified survival pathway that addresses Western and Eastern Roman vulnerabilities, barbarian integration, internal legitimacy, economy, and frontier defense without making Roman success automatic.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence from antiquity to 2020
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer sustains a coherent sequence of cause and effect across major eras instead of jumping from ancient Rome to a modern superstate without intermediate mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Skips most historical development or presents disconnected claims about the modern world.
criteria.3-4: Includes some chronological stages but relies on large unexplained leaps, anachronisms, or unmotivated outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several eras with a recognizable causal chain, though some transitions are thin or overly deterministic.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a mostly coherent timeline through late antiquity, medieval, early modern, industrial, and modern periods, showing how earlier changes constrain later outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust, era-by-era causal chain where demographic, military, institutional, religious, technological, and geopolitical developments interact plausibly over fifteen centuries.

criteria.name: Coverage of major downstream historical effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores the main consequences of a surviving Roman Empire for Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, religion, language, colonialism, industrialization, and global power by 2020.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only one or two superficial effects, such as everyone speaking Latin or Rome being powerful.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few downstream effects but omits several central domains such as Christianity, Islam, medieval Europe, colonialism, or modern geopolitics.
criteria.5-6: Addresses multiple major domains, though some are brief, generic, or not clearly tied to Roman survival.
criteria.7-8: Substantively covers most major domains, including religion, languages, state formation, warfare, trade, colonization, technology, and modern international order.
criteria.9-10: Explores a broad and balanced set of downstream effects, including second-order consequences for Islam, the papacy, Slavic/Germanic states, European colonial powers, nationalism, world wars, decolonization, and the 2020 balance of power.

criteria.name: Plausibility of institutional, economic, technological, and social evolution
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains how a Roman state could adapt its institutions, economy, technology, and society over time rather than remaining a static ancient empire.
criteria.1-2: Depicts Rome as essentially unchanged for 1,500 years or assumes implausible technological/social outcomes without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges some adaptation but treats Roman institutions, slavery, citizenship, urban life, or technology in a simplistic or anachronistic way.
criteria.5-6: Gives reasonable mechanisms for some changes, such as bureaucracy, military reform, language shifts, trade, sanitation, or industrialization, but leaves key tensions unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Shows credible institutional and social adaptation, including changing imperial authority, military recruitment, taxation, religion, urban systems, labor, and economic modernization.
criteria.9-10: Presents a nuanced model of Roman transformation into a modern state, explaining constitutional change, identity formation, labor systems, technological diffusion, industrialization, public health, and economic integration with historically plausible constraints.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, contradiction control, and avoidance of overdetermined history
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the speculative nature of the scenario responsibly, avoids internal contradictions, and does not simply replay real-world history unchanged despite a radically altered Roman survival.
criteria.1-2: States outcomes with unjustified certainty, contains major contradictions, or copies real history wholesale despite the changed premise.
criteria.3-4: Shows occasional caution but includes many deterministic claims, inconsistent borders/events, or real-world events that occur without plausible causes.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent and acknowledges uncertainty, though some events are too conveniently preserved or contradicted by earlier assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, flags alternative possibilities, and keeps most claims internally consistent with the altered Roman geopolitical landscape.
criteria.9-10: Consistently distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradiction; explains why familiar events would change or persist; and treats long-range history as contingent rather than inevitable.

failures.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]

failures.question: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?
human_answers: Here’s our aircraft: [Image: image] The Cessna 172 Skyhawk, probably the most common plane in the world. Here’s our pilot: [Image: image] Here’s what happens when the aircraft is launched above the surface of the 32 largest Solar System bodies: [Image: image] In most cases, there’s no atmosphere, and the plane falls straight to the ground. (If it’s dropped from one kilometer, in a few cases, the crash will be slow enough that the pilot may survive—although the life-support equipment probably won’t.) There are nine Solar System bodies with atmospheres thick enough to matter: Earth—obviously—Mars, Venus, the four gas giants, Saturn’s moon Titan, and the Sun. Let’s take a closer look at what would happen to a plane on each one. The Sun: This works about as well as you'd imagine. If the plane is released close enough to the Sun to feel its atmosphere at all, it's vaporized in less than a second. Mars: To see what happens to aircraft on Mars, we turn to X-Plane (http://www.x-plane.com/desktop/home/?utm_expid=25103718-8). X-Plane is the most advanced flight simulator in the world. The product of 20 years of obsessive labor by a hardcore aeronautics enthusiast who uses capslock a lot when talking about planes, it actually simulates the flow of air over every piece of an aircraft’s body as it flies. This makes it a valuable research tool, since it can accurately simulate entirely new aircraft designs—and new environments. In particular, if you change the X-Plane config file to reduce gravity, thin the atmosphere, and shrink the radius of the planet it can simulate flight on Mars (http://www.x-plane.com/adventures/mars.html). (Note: Thank you to Tom J and the folks in the X-Plane community for their help with aerodynamic calculations in different atmospheres.) X-Plane tells us that flight on Mars is difficult, but not impossible. NASA knows this, and has considered surveying Mars by airplane (http://marsairplane.larc.nasa.gov/). The tricky thing is that with so little atmosphere, to get any lift, you have to go fast. You need to approach Mach 1 just to get off the ground, and once you get moving, you have so much inertia that it’s hard to change course—if you turn, your plane rotates, but keeps moving in the original direction. The X-Plane author compared piloting Martian aircraft to flying a supersonic ocean liner. Our Cessna 172 isn’t up to the challenge. Launched from 1 km, it doesn’t build up enough speed to pull out of a dive, and plows into the Martian terrain at over 60 m/s (135 mph). If dropped from four or five kilometers, it could gain enough speed to pull up into a glide—at over half the speed of sound. The landing would not be survivable. Venus:Unfortunately, X-Plane is not capable of simulating the hellish environment near the surface of Venus. But physics calculations give us an idea of what flight there would be like. The upshot is: Your plane would fly pretty well, except it would be on fire the whole time, and then it would stop flying, and then stop being a plane. The atmosphere on Venus is over 60 times denser than Earth’s, which is thick enough that a Cessna moving at running speed would rise into the air. Unfortunately, the air it’s rising into is hot enough to melt lead. The paint would start melting off in seconds, the plane’s components would fail rapidly, and the plane would glide gently into the ground as it came apart under the heat stress. A much better bet would be to fly above the clouds. While Venus’s surface is awful, its upper atmosphere is surprisingly Earthlike. 55 kilometers up, a human could survive with an oxygen mask and a protective wetsuit; the air is room temperature and the pressure is similar to that on Earth mountains. You need the wetsuit, though, to protect you from the sulfuric acid. (I’m not selling this well, am I?) The acid's no fun, but it turns out the area right above the clouds is a great environment for an airplane (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20030003716_2002108457.pdf), as long as it has no exposed metal to be corroded away by the sulfuric acid. And is capable of flight in constant Category-5-hurricane-level winds, which are another thing I forgot to mention earlier. Venus is a terrible place. Jupiter: Our Cessna can’t fly on Jupiter; the gravity is just too strong. The power needed to maintain level flight is three times greater than that on Earth. Starting from a friendly sea-level pressure, we’d accelerate through the tumbling winds into a 275 m/s (600 mph) downward glide deeper and deeper through the layers of ammonia ice and water ice until we and the aircraft were crushed. There's no surface to hit; Jupiter transitions smoothly from gas to solid as you sink deeper and deeper. Saturn: The picture here is a bit friendlier than on Jupiter. The weaker gravity—close to Earth’s, actually—and slightly denser (but still thin) atmosphere mean that we’d be able to struggle along a bit further before we gave in to either the cold or high winds and descended to the same fate as on Jupiter. Uranus: Uranus is a strange, uniform bluish orb. There are high winds and it’s bitterly cold. It’s the friendliest of the gas giants to our Cessna, and you could probably fly for a little while. But given that it seems to be an almost completely featureless planet, why would you want to? Neptune: If you’re going to fly around one of the ice giants, Neptune (Motto: “The Slightly Bluer One”) is probably a better choice than Uranus. It at least has some clouds to look at before you freeze to death or break apart from the turbulence. Titan: We’ve saved the best for last. When it comes to flying, Titan might be better than Earth. Its atmosphere is thick but its gravity is light, giving it a surface pressure only 50% higher than Earth’s with air four times as dense. Its gravity—lower than that of the Moon—means that flying is easy. Our Cessna could get into the air under pedal power. In fact, humans on Titan could fly by muscle power. A human in a hang glider could comfortably take off and cruise around powered by oversized swim-flipper boots—or even take off by flapping artificial wings. The power requirements are minimal—it would probably take no more effort than walking. The downside (there’s always a downside) is the cold. It’s 72 kelvin on Titan, which is about the temperature of liquid nitrogen. Judging from some numbers on heating requirements for light aircraft, I estimate that the cabin of a Cessna on Titan would probably cool by about two degrees per minute. The batteries would help to keep themselves warm for a little while, but eventually the craft would run out of heat and crash. The Huygens probe, which descended with batteries nearly drained (taking fascinating pictures (http://www.beugungsbild.de/huygens/huygens.html) as it fell), succumbed to the cold after only a few hours on the surface. It had enough time to send back a single photo (http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/New_images_from_Titan) after landing—the only one we have from the surface of a body beyond Mars. If humans put on artificial wings to fly, we might become Titan versions of the Icarus story—our wings could freeze, fall apart, and send us tumbling to our deaths. [Image: image] But I've never seen the Icarus story as a lesson about the limitations of humans. I see it as a lesson about the limitations of wax as an adhesive. The cold of Titan is just an engineering problem. With the right refitting, and the right heat sources, a Cessna 172 could fly on Titan—and so could we.

failures.question: What If a Stereo Flew Past at Twice the Speed of Sound?
human_answers: Yes. Technically, anyway. It would be pretty hard to hear. The basic idea is pretty straightforward. The stereo is going faster than its own sound, so it will reach you first, followed by the sound it emitted one second ago, followed by the sound it emitted two seconds ago, and so forth. [Image: image] The problem is that the stereo is moving at Mach 2, which means that two seconds ago, it was over a kilometer away. It’s hard to hear music from that distance, particularly when your ears were just hit by (a) a sonic boom, and (b) pieces of a rapidly disintegrating stereo. Wind speeds of Mach 2 would messily disassemble most consumer electronics. The force of the wind on the body of the stereo is roughly comparable to that of a dozen people standing on it: [Image: image] An ordinary stereo wouldn’t make it, but one with some kind of ruggedized high-strength casing might be able to survive. If we put together a durable, heavy-duty stereo and launch it on a ballistic trajectory, it will only be traveling at supersonic speeds for the first 150 meters or so. This means that the target will hear a maximum of about a third of a second of reversed music. This phenomenon is actually confirmed in the 2008 paper Reproduction of Virtual Sound Sources Moving at Supersonic Speeds in Wave Field Synthesis (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/230702229_Reproduction_of_Virtual_Sound_Sources_Moving_at_Supersonic_Speeds_in_Wave_Field_Synthesis), which says that the sound wave field “contains a component carrying a time-reversed version of the source’s input signal”. The sonic boom would be the first thing the target would hear. It would be followed by several sounds played over one another, including both reversed music (rising slightly in pitch as it fades out) and forward-playing music (which would play at half speed and an octave too low), followed by the crash of a stereo demolishing your neighbor’s shed. Which means that if you’re playing one of those albums containing secret demonic messages, the result will be the strangest listening experience of your life: [Image: image]

failures.question: What If We Launched a One-Way Mission to Voyager 1 Today?
human_answers: Voyager I is farther from Earth than any other manmade object. After getting a pair of gravitational kicks from Jupiter and Saturn, it’s headed out of the Solar System at a pretty high speed, and nothing else we’ve built is on track to pass it. Strangely, as of the day I’m writing this, Voyager is actually getting closer (http://voyager.jpl.nasa.gov/where/) to us, because Earth is in a part of its orbit where it’s approaching Voyager faster than Voyager is fleeing. But in a few months, we’ll swing around the Sun and Voyager will again be getting farther away. [Image: image] It has a 35-year head start, so it would be hard to catch. But catching up isn’t the problem. New Horizons, the spacecraft currently headed out of the Solar System by way of Pluto, is never going to catch up to Voyager—it’s not moving fast enough and it’s headed in the wrong direction. But it could have. The reason Voyager is moving so fast is that it got gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn, while New Horizons only got one from Jupiter. [Image: image] Gravity assists aren’t paradoxical magic. It’s just like bouncing a tennis ball off a passing truck. Gyroscopes, on the other hand, ARE magic. If New Horizons had ditched the Pluto objective and waited for the right planetary alignment (the 2030s look promising), it could have swung by Jupiter and Saturn, then caught up to Voyager in as little as a century or two! (Assuming we could manage to hit Voyager from that far away. But I bet we could; our rocket scientists are pretty good at rocket science.) Of course, getting there’s the easy part. The hard part is getting back. Voyager weighs a little less than a ton and is moving away at 17 kilometers per second (if it were in the atmosphere, that would be Mach 50). And since it’s out in interstellar space, there are no speeding Jupiters to grab on to. Stopping Voyager is going to take a lot of fuel. It’s what engineers call the tyranny of the rocket equation (http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition30/tryanny.html): As the amount that you want to change your speed (“delta-v”) goes up, the fuel required increases exponentially. The equation tells us that to turn the 720-kilogram Voyager around, we’re going to need at least 30 tons of fuel. But to get that fuel out there, we need even more fuel. And to get that fuel, we need even more fuel. (This is where the tyrannical rocket equation gets its exponential term.) In fact, to rescue Voyager, we’d have to launch a fleet of—at minimum—60 New Horizons-sized spacecraft loaded with nothing but fuel. Could we do it? Sure. There are a couple plausible ways. Instead of building five to ten dozen fuel-laden Titan IIIEs, we could just build a fleet of ten or fifteen Saturn Vs, and do the whole thing with fewer launches. But however we did it, it would be a massive and expensive operation similar in scale to the Apollo program. The difference between the launch vehicle we’d used to get Voyager out of the Solar System and the fleet we’d need for a round trip is striking: [Image: image] Fortunately, there’s one way around the tyranny of the rocket equation: Ditch the rockets. Ion engines—which use electric fields to accelerate exhaust gas to high speeds—are far more efficient than chemical rockets, and they make accelerating to high speeds much more plausible. The reason we’re not using them for everything is that they produce very little thrust, so it takes a long time to get up to speed. It’s like if you had a car that gets amazing mileage but has a one-horsepower engine. (Actually, are you sure that’s not just a horse?) Ion engines are great; the current ones just take forever to get you moving. But since catching Voyager is going to take a long time anyway, ion engines are fine. We could launch a probe (like this one (https://web.archive.org/web/20150910020454/http://trs-new.jpl.nasa.gov/dspace/bitstream/2014/13644/1/00-0010.pdf)), send it out to Voyager, latch on, turn everything around, and let it spend a few decades slowing Voyager down. Once Voyager had lost nearly all its speed, the Sun’s gravity would take over, and the probe would begin a long slow slide toward the inner Solar System. This would take about 200 years, and with some extremely careful nudges, we could make sure it falls in an Earth-crossing orbit. Two centuries later, Voyager would reach Earth and, with no way to slow down, burn up in our atmosphere, because we didn’t think to send out an aerobraking shell with the rescue craft. So that was a waste of a few centuries of work and billions upon billions of dollars. [Image: image] Maybe a better idea would be to borrow a salvage vessel and set sail for the coast of New South Wales, Australia. There, in the waters off Jervis Bay, the Australian Royal Navy ship Voyager sank in 1964 after an accidental collision. That one’s probably easier to retrieve. [Image: image]

failures.question: What If You Drained the Oceans through a 10-Meter Hole at Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]

failures.question: What If You Tried to Hold an Airplane to the Ground with a Rope?
human_answers: Ah, the Just Cause 2 scenario (http://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=just+cause+2+plane+grapple). At takeoff, a 747's four engines can each generate 281.57 kN of thrust. I have no real sense for what that number means, so let's put it in different terms: [Image: image] A 747 with all engines at full could roughly balance the weight of a dangling blue whale. With all that weight, how thick would the cable need to be? Surprisingly, not all that thick! A cable a little over an inch in diameter would do it.[1]Bethlehem Wire Rope General Purpose Catalog (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) Let's suppose you don't have a cable lying around. What else could you use? If you're into fishing, you might have some fishing line. A typical line for saltwater fishing might have a 50-100 lb strength,[2]West Marine: Selecting Fishing Line (http://www.wwwrope.com/product_pdfs/GP_CAT.pdf) so it would take a brigade of several thousand people armed with fishing rods to restrain the plane. [Image: image] If you don't have fishing line, there's one thing you probably do have: Hair. While hair isn't as strong as steel, it's just about the strongest material in your body,[3]Examples of the Tensile Strength of Materials (http://web2.clarkson.edu/class/me380/materials_tenstrength.pdf) with a tensile strength rivaling or exceeding that of bone.[4]Properties of Textile Fibers (http://www.academia.edu/2179355/Properties_of_Textile_Fibers) This tensile strength is why performers are able to hang by their hair at the circus. In fact, from a materials standpoint, it's actually more impressive that performers are able to hang by their arms. Based on these hair strength figures, a piece of hair three inches in diameter would be strong enough to restrain a 747.[5]If you wanted to measure the strength of a strand of hair, you could use the device described by US Patent #4628742A (http://www.google.com/patents/US4628742), "Tensile strength tester for hair" Hairs that big around are hard to come by.[6]... I hope. Since most of us have many small hairs, instead of one big hair ... [Image: image] ... we'd need to get a lot of hairs and bundle them together. Given that individual hairs can support about 50 grams of weight, we'd need roughly 20 heads of hair to restrain the aircraft. [Image: image] Conclusion: Restraining a plane with a cable would be pretty easy. Further conclusion: Blue whales are not typically covered in hair,[8]Although they are mammals, most whales do not have coats of hair like land mammals typically do (http://bioweb.uwlax.edu/bio203/s2012/olson_rile/adaptation.htm) but if we transplanted the hair from at least 20 human heads onto a blue whale ... [Image: image] ... it would have enough hair to perform acrobatics at a circus.

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Bottom Inch of a Massive Mountain Vanished?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Immediate Kinematics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise as a massive mountain suddenly losing its bottom inch, leaving a one-inch unsupported gap that closes under gravity, and computes or qualitatively estimates the short fall accurately.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats the mountain as disappearing, exploding, floating, or collapsing from summit height without justification.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes a small vertical drop but gives highly implausible timing, speed, or motion, or ignores gravity-driven closure.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that the mountain drops only about one inch and the motion is brief, but with little quantitative grounding.
criteria.7-8: Gives plausible estimates for closure time and impact speed, e.g. tens of milliseconds and under 1 m/s, with mostly sound reasoning.
criteria.9-10: Accurately derives or explains the one-inch free fall, about 70 ms closure time, and modest impact speed while avoiding overstatement.

criteria.name: Impact, Stress, and Seismic Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly analyzes the mechanical impact of the mountain landing after a one-inch fall, including stress waves, rock strength, seismic shaking, and earthquake-triggering uncertainty.
criteria.1-2: Claims inevitable continent-scale destruction, no effect at all, or other outcomes incompatible with the small drop and huge mass.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impact or earthquake effects but with vague, exaggerated, or physically inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the impact would create noticeable shaking and stress but likely not catastrophic damage by itself.
criteria.7-8: Explains that rock can generally withstand the added stress, with local cracking and shaking comparable to a small earthquake, while noting possible triggered seismicity.
criteria.9-10: Balances the modest direct impact with the nonzero chance of triggering an existing fault, distinguishing induced seismic release from impact energy itself.

criteria.name: Local Hazards and Material Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of near-field effects specific to a one-inch mountain-wide gap, including air expulsion, dust and rock jets, cracking, sound, vibration, and danger to people at or near the base.
criteria.1-2: Ignores local hazards or invents unrelated effects such as lava, nuclear fireballs, or universal liquefaction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions danger nearby but gives little mechanism or focuses only on generic earthquake damage.
criteria.5-6: Covers some local effects such as a jolt, noise, dust, or rock fracture, but misses key gap-closure hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains that compressed/expelled air, debris, dust, and cracking near the gap may be more dangerous locally than the fall itself.
criteria.9-10: Provides a vivid but physically grounded account of local hazards, including high-speed air/debris expulsion, lightning-like crack/rumble sounds, minor cracking, and risk to nearby observers.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer traces downstream consequences from the initial vanishing inch through immediate impact, local damage, possible seismic triggering, and broader human/geological effects without skipping causal links.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected conclusions with no causal chain or jumps directly to apocalyptic/global outcomes from the one-inch event.
criteria.3-4: Has a partial chain but relies on unsupported leaps, such as assuming total mountain collapse or global climate effects.
criteria.5-6: Gives a reasonable immediate-to-local sequence but treats longer-range effects shallowly or inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a coherent sequence from gap creation to fall, impact, vibrations, local hazards, and conditional earthquake effects.
criteria.9-10: Builds a clear, conditional, multi-stage causal narrative that separates likely local outcomes from rarer long-range seismic consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control

failures.question: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?
human_answers: The answers to these questions all hinge on the same idea. It's an idea I've touched on in other articles, but today I want to focus on it specifically: The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard to get to orbit because you have to go so fast. Space isn't like this: [Image: image] Space is like this: [Image: image] Space is about 100 kilometers away. That's far away—I wouldn't want to climb a ladder to get there—but it isn't that far away. If you're in Sacramento, Seattle, Canberra, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Phnom Penh, Cairo, Beijing, central Japan, central Sri Lanka, or Portland, space is closer than the sea. Getting to space[1]Specifically, low Earth orbit, which is where the International Space Station is and where the shuttles could go. is easy. It's not, like, something you could do in your car, but it's not a huge challenge. You could get a person to space with a small sounding rocket the size of a telephone pole. The X-15 aircraft reached space[2]The X-15 reached 100 km on two occasions, both when flown by Joe Walker. just by going fast and then steering up.[3]Make sure to remember to steer up and not down, or you will have a bad time. [Image: image] But getting to space is easy. The problem is staying there. Gravity in low Earth orbit is almost as strong as gravity on the surface. The Space Station hasn't escaped Earth's gravity at all; it's experiencing about 90% the pull that we feel on the surface. To avoid falling back into the atmosphere, you have to go sideways really, really fast. The speed you need to stay in orbit is about 8 kilometers per second.[4]It's a little less if you're in the higher region of low Earth orbit. Only a fraction of a rocket's energy is used to lift up out of the atmosphere; the vast majority of it is used to gain orbital (sideways) speed. This leads us to the central problem of getting into orbit: Reaching orbital speed takes much more fuel than reaching orbital height. Getting a ship up to 8 km/s takes a lot of booster rockets. Reaching orbital speed is hard enough; reaching to orbital speed while carrying enough fuel to slow back down would be completely impractical.[5]This exponential increase is the central problem of rocketry: The fuel required to increase your speed by one km/s multiplies your weight by about 1.4. To get into orbit, you need to increase your speed to 8 km/s, which means you'll need a lot of fuel: $ 1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\times1.4\approx 15$ times the original weight of your ship. Using a rocket to slow down carries the same problem: Every 1 km/s decrease in speed multiplies your starting mass by that same factor of 1.4. If you want to slow all the way down to zero—and drop gently into the atmosphere—the fuel requirements multiply your weight by 15 again. These outrageous fuel requirements are why every spacecraft entering an atmosphere has braked using a heat shield instead of rockets—slamming into the air is the most practical way to slow down. (And to answer Brian's question, the Curiosity rover was no exception to this; although it used small rockets to hover when it was near the surface, it first used air-braking to shed the majority of its speed.) How fast is 8 km/s, anyway? I think the reason for a lot of confusion about these issues is that when astronauts are in orbit, it doesn't seem like they're moving that fast; they look like they're drifting slowly over a blue marble. But 8 km/s is blisteringly fast. When you look at the sky near sunset, you can sometimes see the ISS go past ... and then, 90 minutes later, see it go past again.[6]There are some good apps and online tools to help you spot the station, along with other neat satellites. My favorite is ISS Detector (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.runar.issdetector), but if you Google you can find lots of others. In those 90 minutes, it's circled the entire world. The ISS moves so quickly that if you fired a rifle bullet from one end of a football field,[7]Either kind. the International Space Station could cross the length of the field before the bullet traveled 10 yards.[8]This type of play is legal in Australian rules football. Let's imagine what it would look like if you were speed-walking across the Earth's surface at 8 km/s. To get a better sense of the pace at which you're traveling, let's use the beat of a song to mark the passage of time.[9]Using song beats to help measure the passage of time is a technique also used in CPR training, where the song "Stayin' Alive" is used to . suppose you started playing the 1988 song by The Proclaimers, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles). That song is about 131.9 beats per minute, so imagine that with every beat of the song, you move forward more than two miles. In the time it took to sing the first line of the chorus, you could walk from the Statue of Liberty all the way to the Bronx: [Image: image] It would take you about two lines of the chorus (16 beats of the song) to cross the English Channel between London and France. The song's length leads to an odd coincidence. The interval between the start and the end of I'm Gonna Be is 3 minutes and 30 seconds,[10]Based on timing from the official Youtube video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tbNlMtqrYS0) and the ISS is moving at 7.66 km/s. This means that if an astronaut on the ISS listens to I'm Gonna Be, in the time between the first beat of the song and the final lines ... [Image: image] ... they will have traveled just about exactly 1,000 miles.

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Spacecraft Used Rockets to Slow to a Few Miles per Hour during Reentry?

criteria.name: Core counterfactual framing: reentry speed is orbital speed, not falling-from-height speed
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly identifies that the spacecraft must shed roughly orbital horizontal velocity before it can descend gently, and that altitude alone is not the main difficulty.
criteria.1-2: Treats reentry mainly as falling from high altitude; misses orbital sideways speed or implies only small braking is needed.
criteria.3-4: Mentions high speed but only vaguely; does not clearly distinguish orbital velocity from vertical descent speed.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that orbital spacecraft move around 7-8 km/s and must lose that speed, but explanation is partial or imprecise.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that staying in orbit requires large sideways velocity and that rocket-braking to a few mph means removing most of it.
criteria.9-10: Uses the orbital-speed insight as the central causal premise, explicitly correcting the intuition that space is hard mainly because it is high up.

criteria.name: Rocket-equation and fuel-mass consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures why carrying enough propellant to slow from orbital speed to a few mph is impractical, including compounding mass penalties.
criteria.1-2: Claims rockets could simply slow the craft without addressing fuel mass, or gives physically impossible fuel assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Says it would need 'a lot of fuel' but gives no mechanism for why this becomes prohibitive.
criteria.5-6: Explains that propellant requirements are very large and reduce payload, but lacks rocket-equation-style compounding.
criteria.7-8: Accurately describes exponential or multiplicative mass growth from needing propellant to brake, plus propellant to carry that propellant.
criteria.9-10: Connects the full mission penalty: reaching orbit while carrying deorbit/braking fuel is vastly harder, making near-zero-speed reentry impractical compared with aerobraking.

criteria.name: Atmospheric entry, heat shield, and aerobraking mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains how normal reentry uses the atmosphere to dissipate kinetic energy and how rocket braking would change heating, trajectory, and landing dynamics.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the atmosphere or incorrectly says heat shields are unnecessary simply because rockets exist.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heat or air resistance but does not explain their role in removing orbital energy.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that heat shields/aerobraking normally shed most speed, with rockets only possibly used near landing.
criteria.7-8: Explains that slowing before dense atmosphere would greatly reduce heating but requires enormous propellant; also notes remaining descent/terminal landing issues.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent entry sequence comparing normal aerobraking with powered braking, including energy dissipation, heating reduction, trajectory control, and final low-speed descent.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects on spacecraft design and mission feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows consequences beyond the immediate maneuver, including launch mass, payload, staging, cost, safety, and practical alternatives.
criteria.1-2: Stops at a yes/no claim with little discussion of broader mission impacts.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few impacts such as cost or weight but without causal connection to the counterfactual.
criteria.5-6: Connects extra propellant to reduced payload and larger launch vehicles, with some discussion of operational tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Traces a plausible chain from braking requirement to bigger boosters, staging/tankage, lower payload fraction, cost, reliability, and landing architecture.
criteria.9-10: Integrates system-level consequences and alternatives, explaining why spacecraft use heat shields, parachutes, lift, or small terminal rockets rather than full powered orbital deceleration.

criteria.name: Quantitative plausibility, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses reasonable scales and avoids internal contradictions while being appropriately cautious about edge cases.
criteria.1-2: Contains major numerical errors or contradictions, such as confusing mph with km/s or saying orbit requires escape velocity.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but includes misleading numbers, overconfident claims, or inconsistent statements about gravity, speed, or fuel.
criteria.5-6: Uses broadly reasonable figures and caveats but may be approximate or omit important limitations.
criteria.7-8: Provides consistent order-of-magnitude reasoning, e.g. orbital speed near 8 km/s and huge delta-v/fuel needs, with sensible caveats.
criteria.9-10: Maintains precise, internally consistent reasoning throughout, distinguishes idealized from practical cases, and handles exceptions such as suborbital flights or propulsive landers without undermining the main conclusion.

failures.question: What If You Tried to Print the Entire English Wikipedia in Real Time?
human_answers: This many: [Image: image] That's surprisingly few printers! But before you try to create a live-updating paper Wikipedia, let's look at what those printers would be doing ... and how much they'd cost. Printing Wikipedia People have considered printing out Wikipedia before. A few years ago, student Rob Matthews printed every Wikipedia featured article (http://www.brandnew.uk.com/wikipedia-as-a-printed-book/), creating a book several feet thick. Of course, that's just a small slice of the best of Wikipedia; the entire encyclopedia would be a lot bigger. Wikipedia user Tompw (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Tompw) has set up a page (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Size_in_volumes) for calculating the size of the whole English Wikipedia in printed volumes. It would currently fill a lot of bookshelves. Keeping up with the edits would be harder. Keeping up The English Wikipedia currently receives about 125,000 to 150,000 edits each day, or 90-100 per minute.[1]ToolServer: Edit rate (http://toolserver.org/~emijrp/wmcharts/wmchart0001.php) We could try to define a way to measure the "word count" of the average edit, but that's hard bordering on impossible. Fortunately, we don't need to—we can just estimate that each change is going to require us to reprint a page somewhere. Many edits will actually change multiple pages—but many other edits are reverts, which would let us put back pages we've already printed.[2]The filing system for this would be staggering (http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IBM_card_storage.NARA.jpg). One page per edit seems like a reasonable middle ground. For a mix of photos, tables, and text typical of Wikipedia, a good inkjet printer might put out 15 pages per minute. That means you'd only need about six printers running at any given time to keep pace with the edits. The paper would stack up quickly. Using Rob Matthews' book as a starting point, I did my own back-of-the-envelope estimate for the size of the current English Wikipedia. Based on the average length of featured articles vs. all articles, I came up with an estimate of 300 cubic meters for a printout of the whole thing.[3]That's a little larger than Tompw's estimate, but I'm assuming they're printed straight from the browser, which is less compact and includes images. By comparison, if you were trying to keep up with the edits, you'd print out 300 cubic meters every month. $500,000 per month Six printers isn't that many, but they'd be running all the time. And that gets expensive. The electricity to run them would be cheap—a few dollars a day. The paper would be about one cent per sheet, which means you'll be spending about a thousand dollars a day. You'd want to hire people to manage the printers 24/7, but that would actually cost less than the paper. Even the printers themselves wouldn't be too expensive, despite the terrifying replacement cycle. But the ink cartridges would be a nightmare. Ink A study by QualityLogic[4]QualityLogic: Cost of Ink Per Page Analysis (http://www.qualitylogic.com/tuneup/uploads/docfiles/QualityLogic-Cost-of-Ink-Per-Page-Analysis_US_1-Jun-2012.pdf), June 2012 found that for a typical inkjet printer, the real-life cost of ink ran from 5 cents per page for black-and-white to around 30 cents per page for photos. That means you'd be spending four to five figures per day on ink cartridges. You definitely want to invest in a laser printer. Otherwise, in just a month or two, this project could end up costing you half a million dollars: [Image: image] But that's not even the worst part. If, someday, Wikipedia decides to go dark (http://sys01-public.msnbc.msn.com/technology/wikipedia-goes-dark-piracy-bill-protest-day-117714) again, and you want to join the protest ... [Image: image] You'll have to get a crate of markers and color every page solid black yourself. I would definitely stick to digital.
